The only literature text actually read is the search-result snippets: Mellmann regime list plus rolling and cascading Fr bands via a citing paper; Henein 1983 abstracts; Ding 2001 abstract; DEM-thesis summary; patents, FEECO and theses on sticking and agglomeration. Everything else is (a) recalled from training knowledge, marked 'NOT VERIFIED' with low or medium confidence, or (b) derived here by calculation (scratchpad/kilnB/calc.py), marked as derived. The user can send a follow-up to continue searching, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION. Priority items to verify next:
1. Mellmann 2001 Table 1 (slumping, slipping, cataracting bands; transition criteria equations).
2. Henein 1981 thesis and 1983 papers (Bed Behavior Diagram values; dynamic angles of limestone and sand).
3. Pe and D_ax values from Sai et al. 1990, Bongo Njeng et al. 2015 and Gao et al. 2013.
4. Active-layer delta/h from Boateng & Barr 1997, Ding et al. 2001 and Mellmann et al. 2004.
5. The Weimar 2006 thesis (sand and PE rotary kiln pyrolysis).
6. Angle of repose of polyolefin pellets and flakes.
7. Carrier/plastic ratios in sand or ball heat-carrier kilns.

KEY PHYSICS AND SYNTHESIS.
(1) Regime. Pyrolysis kilns (D 0.3-2 m, 1-5 rpm) sit at Fr about 1e-4 to 1e-2, which is the rolling band (D = 1 m: Fr 5.6e-4 at 1 rpm, 5.0e-3 at 3 rpm, 1.4e-2 at 5 rpm). Slumping appears at low Fr and low fill; slipping appears on smooth walls with low-friction pellets. The important effect of rotation is not axial speed but transverse renewal:
- Wall contact time is t_c = 2 eps/omega, about 3-15 s.
- The passive layer carries solids up the wall.
- The active layer returns them at several times the wall speed (flux balance Q = (omega/2)[R^2 - (R cos eps + delta)^2]).
- Exposed chord length is 2R sin(eps).
These feed the wall-to-bed penetration and radiation models in Topic C.

(2) Axial transport.
- Saeman/Kramers ODE: dh/dz = tan(theta)[3Phi_v/(4 pi n R^3)(2h/R - h^2/R^2)^-1.5 - tan(beta)/sin(theta)], z from discharge, BC h(0) = dam height or about dp.
- This ODE is the right continuum model. It handles dams and variable Phi_v(z) as mass is lost to vapour.
- In the shallow-bed limit it reduces exactly to Sullivan's USBM formula: coefficient (180/pi^2) sin(theta) vs 1.77 sqrt(theta), identical at 35 deg and within 13% for 25-45 deg. This is a ready-made validation test.
- Worked example (300 kg/h, D = 1 m, L = 10 m, 2 deg, 3 rpm, theta = 35 deg): fill about 2% and tau = 17.6 min; Sullivan gives 17.5 min. A 0.10 m dam raises tau to 22.1 min; a 0.15 m dam raises it to 29.8 min.
- The 5-20% fill quoted for kilns requires higher throughput, lower slope or rpm, or dams. Fill must be checked, since Saeman gives absurd fills (38%) for 1000 kg/h at 1 rpm and 2 deg.
- RTD: use a 1D axial dispersion model with Danckwerts BCs. The Pe value is NOT verified; use plug flow by default plus a sensitivity run at Pe about 50-200 (own choice) until literature values are retrieved.

(3) Plastic-specific behaviour (mostly NOT verified; derived scaling).
- Along the kiln the charge passes through three states: free-flowing pellets or flakes (granular rolling bed, theta about 25-35 deg unverified); a sticky melt above Tm (about 105-170 C) with zero-shear viscosity 1e2 to 7e3 Pa s at 300 C (from our previous brief); and, once random scission is advanced (>380-400 C), a low-viscosity liquid (1e-3 to 1e-2 Pa s).
- The drag-out estimate h* = sqrt(mu U/(rho g)) shows why the middle state is the problem: at mu >= 10 Pa s the shell can carry films of 1.6-16 cm round the circumference. That gives wall coating, insulating crusts, rings acting as uncontrolled dams (they change h(z) and tau via the same ODE) and agglomerates bonded by melt bridges.
- The patents and vendor notes confirm the mechanisms qualitatively: melt as binder, wall sticking, ring formation, choking, wall layer as thermal barrier, higher rpm as a remedy.
- When the melt is cracked it behaves as a liquid pool with a flat surface (theta about 0) and a sub-mm wall film. Its axial transport is then gravity-driven open-channel or overflow flow, not Saeman.
- Inert carriers (sand, steel or ceramic balls) keep the bed granular. The melt coats carrier surfaces, so Saeman applies to the carrier with its own theta, and the carrier scours the wall. Carrier ratios and sizes were not found. Wet-granular cohesion raises the angle of repose and can turn rolling into slumping or balling, which is an agglomeration risk.

(4) Modelling recommendation for Colab and a T4.
- Use a continuum model, not DEM, for the reactor.
  (a) Axial 1D grid (200-500 cells): Saeman ODE for h(z) with variable Phi_v(z) from the pyrolysis mass loss, plus solids-state transport by plug flow or dispersion. Mark a phase-state flag per cell (granular / sticky / liquid) from T and viscosity. In sticky cells, add a wall-coating thermal resistance; in liquid cells, switch to an open-channel pool.
  (b) Transverse sub-model per cell: analytic rolling-bed kinematics (Mellmann/Khakhar). It gives t_c, chord length, covered arc 2 eps, active-layer thickness (delta/h sensitivity 0.1-0.35 until verified) and a surface-renewal frequency for heat transfer. Include an automatic regime check from Fr and fill against the Mellmann table, with a warning outside rolling.
  (c) Optional quasi-2D DEM slice, for the video and a transverse-regime check only: a periodic slab a few diameters thick, 5e3 to 5e4 spheres of dp 4-6 mm, reduced E about 1e6-1e7 Pa, the real Fr, and 3-10 revolutions. Implement with custom GPU kernels (NVIDIA Warp, Taichi or Triton). Plain PyTorch per-contact tensor ops are about 10x slower (estimate).
- Full-kiln DEM is infeasible. It needs 4e6 to 3e7 pellets (more with sand) and about 1e6 time steps per revolution at 3 rpm (Rayleigh dt about 2e-5 s), so 1e5 particles costs about 15 min/rev even with good kernels (own throughput estimate of about 1e8 particle-steps/s on a T4, unverified). Residence times of 15-60 min mean hundreds of revolutions.
- Validation tests available without new data:
  - Sullivan vs Saeman consistency.
  - Fr regime placement.
  - Henein scaling group.
  - Dam effect on hold-up.
  - The DEM-slice dynamic angle and active-layer flux against the kinematic balance.

CONFLICTS AND SPREAD. Mellmann's rolling and cascading bands overlap (1e-3 to 1e-2), so the boundary there depends on fill and material. A search summary also mentioned 'Fr about 0.001 for slipping to cascading', which is inconsistent with the table's slipping band and probably refers to a specific material or criterion. Sullivan vs Saeman differ by up to about 13% for theta away from 35 deg. Deeper beds or dams raise Saeman's tau well above Sullivan (+26% to +70% in the example).

equations.name: Sullivan (USBM 1927) mean residence time
equations.expression: t = 1.77 * L * sqrt(theta) / (p * D * n)
equations.variables: t [min]; L kiln length [ft]; theta dynamic angle of repose [deg]; p kiln slope [deg]; D kiln diameter [ft]; n [rpm]. Perry-type versions add a factor F for constrictions (not verified)
equations.validity: Unconstricted kilns without lifters; reported to fail at low inclination (Zhang et al. 2018); empirical
equations.source: Sullivan, Maier, Ralston (1927) USBM TP 384 (via secondary transcription)

equations.name: Saeman / Kramers–Croockewit bed-depth ODE
equations.expression: dh/dz = (3*tan(theta)*q_v)/(4*pi*n*R^3) * (2*h/R - (h/R)^2)^(-3/2) - tan(beta)/cos(theta)   [equivalently tan(theta)*{ 3 q_v/(4 pi n R^3) (...)^(-3/2) - tan(beta)/sin(theta) }]
equations.variables: h local bed depth [m]; z axial coordinate from discharge towards feed (integrate upstream) [m]; q_v volumetric solids flow [m3/s] (= Mdot/rho_bulk); n rotation [rev/s]; R inner radius [m]; theta dynamic angle of repose; beta kiln inclination
equations.validity: Rolling/cascading bed, steady flow, free-flowing solids; boundary condition at discharge = dam height or Specht F0 correlation; Lebas 1995 found it best for bed-depth profiles; ~20 % MRT error reported for MSW
equations.source: Saeman (1951) Chem. Eng. Prog. 47:508; Kramers & Croockewit (1952); form cross-checked against Specht et al. 2010 as quoted

equations.name: Bed cross-section, filling degree and MRT from bed profile
equations.expression: cos(eps) = 1 - h/R ; A(h) = R^2*(eps - sin(eps)*cos(eps)) ; f = A/(pi R^2) ; tau = (1/q_v) * integral_0^L A(h(z)) dz ; hold-up = rho_bulk * integral A dz
equations.variables: eps half central (fill) angle [rad]; A bed cross-sectional area [m2]; f filling fraction [-]; tau MRT [s]
equations.validity: Geometric identity; plug-flow MRT definition (hold-up/feed), used by Liu & Specht and the Rutgers FCC work
equations.source: Geometry (standard); MRT = hold-up / mass flow as used in Liu & Specht 2006, Navodia 2018

equations.name: Discharge-end filling correlation
equations.variables: F0 filling degree at discharge [-]; Bd bed depth number built from Mdot, n, R, beta, rho_s, theta (exact grouping not obtained)
equations.validity: Inclination 1°–4°; kilns 0.25–0.4 m ID; authors claim tested Bd range covers industrial kilns
equations.source: Specht et al. (2010) Powder Technol. 197:17–24

equations.name: Rotational Froude number and Henein scaling
equations.expression: Fr = omega^2 * R / g ; Fr_mod = Fr * (D/d_p)^0.5 ; rolling: 1e-4 < Fr < 1e-2 (Mellmann), 5e-4 < Fr < 2e-2 (Henein)
equations.variables: omega = 2*pi*n/60 [rad/s]; R inner radius [m]; g 9.81 m/s2; D kiln diameter; d_p particle diameter
equations.validity: Free-flowing beds, fill > ~10 % for rolling; slumping–rolling critical Fr scales with d/D (Liu, Specht, Mellmann 2005)
equations.source: Mellmann (2001); Henein et al. (1983)

equations.name: Penetration model for covered wall-to-bed heat transfer
equations.expression: h_pen = 2 * sqrt(k_b * rho_b * c_b / (pi * t_c)) ; t_c = (2*eps)/(2*pi*n) = eps/(pi*n)
equations.variables: k_b, rho_b, c_b bulk conductivity, density, heat capacity; t_c contact time of a wall element under the bed [s]; eps half fill angle [rad]; n [rev/s]
equations.validity: Continuum bed, contact time long vs particle thermal time; over-predicts for coarse particles/short contact (needs contact resistance); trends: h rises with n, falls with fill
equations.source: Penetration theory as quoted from Bongo Njeng et al. 2018 / Herz et al. 2012

equations.name: Extended penetration model with gas-gap contact resistance (Li et al. 2005; Schlünder–Mollekopf type)
equations.expression: h_cw-cb = [ chi * d_p / k_g + 0.5 * sqrt(pi * t_c / (k_b * rho_b * c_b)) ]^-1 , 0.096 < chi < 0.198 ; general series form 1/h = 1/h_ws + 1/h_pen
equations.variables: chi gas-film thickness factor [-]; d_p particle diameter [m]; k_g gas conductivity [W/mK]; other symbols as above
equations.validity: Second term = 1/h_pen (consistent with penetration model); first term reconstructed from a garbled abstract snippet — verify against Li, Ma, Yao, Chem. Eng. Technol. 2005; Herz 2012 reports good agreement of this class of model
equations.source: Li S.Q., Ma L.B., Wan W., Yao Q. (2005) Chem. Eng. Technol. 28:1480 (abstract)

equations.name: Tscheng & Watkinson wall-to-bed correlation (dimensionless penetration fit)
equations.expression: h_cw-cb = 11.6 * (k_b / l_psi) * ( n * R^2 * psi / alpha_b )^0.3 , l_psi = R * psi (covered arc length)
equations.variables: k_b bed conductivity; alpha_b bed thermal diffusivity [m2/s]; psi fill (covered) angle [rad]; R radius [m]; n rotation rate
equations.validity: Fit to published data; exact grouping/exponent placement recovered from garbled secondary text — verify before use; Herz 2012 reports it deviates strongly from their measurements
equations.source: Tscheng & Watkinson (1979) as reproduced by Bongo Njeng et al. 2018 and Hanein-type kiln models

equations.name: Isothermal first-order conversion time (TGA check)
equations.expression: k(T) = k0 * exp(-Ea/(R_g*T)) ; t_X = -ln(1 - X)/k ; e.g. t90 = ln(10)/k
equations.variables: k0 [s^-1]; Ea [J/mol]; R_g = 8.314 J/mol/K; X conversion
equations.validity: Westerhout HDPE: 400–450 °C, 70–90 % conversion (k0 = 1.9e13, Ea = 220 kJ/mol); above 450 °C TGA heat-transfer limited
equations.source: Westerhout et al. (1997)

equations.name: Overall wall-to-load heat transfer (lumped validation metric)
equations.expression: q_wall = U * (T_wall,in - T_load) ; U from measured wall flux (thermocouple pairs across shell) or energy balance
equations.variables: U overall coefficient [W/m2K]; T_wall,in inner wall temperature; T_load bed/waste temperature
equations.validity: Definition used by Suzuki & Okazaki 2008 (k_m-w, 22–55 W/m2K) and Nhuchhen 2016 (13.2–20.9 W/m2K); not the same as local contact h (hundreds of W/m2K)
equations.source: Suzuki & Okazaki (2008); Nhuchhen et al. (2016)

ACCESS LIMITATION (important): in this session WebFetch failed on every host (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND, including wikipedia/mdpi/sciencedirect) and curl through the proxy returned 'CONNECT tunnel failed, 403'. So NO full text was read. Every number above comes from WebSearch (extended) summaries of abstracts, highlights, figure captions or full-text snippets. 'abstract-only' means the number is in the abstract or highlights. 'secondary' means a search summary of a citing paper or of a full-text snippet. Several full texts are open and should be downloaded in Colab or by a person to pull the tables: Henein 1983 (U. Alberta PDF); Santos 2016 (SciELO); Moumin 2021 (DLR elib); Nafsun HEFAT 2014 (UP repository); Hanein 2017 supplementary (digitised Barr T4 and Tscheng data); Pichler 2021 Mendeley dataset; Kodera 2021 Table 1; Qasim 2025 (Chalmers/DiVA); Jaworski 2023 (PMC); Fedorova 2025 MDPI review (it reproduces Sullivan's tables); Westerhout 1997 (Twente); the ANSAC thesis (core.ac.uk); Bhatt 2026 (PMC).

WHAT IS STILL MISSING: (a) No measured tau or bed-depth table was obtained that pairs one D, L, slope, rpm, feed, material and measured value from a clean, consistent source. The closest are the Chutwiboonkun 2021 torrefaction kiln (D 0.3 m, L 6 m, palm kernel shell; 38.6–86.9 min at 1–3 rpm, 1°, 2 lifters), whose abstract contradicts itself, and the Kramers & Croockewit and Liu & Specht rigs, for which we have geometry and trends but no values. Recommendation: use the Kramers rig (0.197 m × 1.78 m) and the Bäbler model kiln (0.4 m × 2 m, 3°, 2.5 cm dam, 30 kg/h, 2 rpm) as fully specified cases. Check them code-to-code against Sullivan, the Saeman ODE and the Pichler dataset now. Replace them with measured values once the Fedorova review or Liu & Specht tables are fetched. (b) No numeric Herz/Nafsun contact h values were obtained; only conditions and trends. One unattributed snippet gives 900–2400 W/m²K for quartz sand at 20 % fill, which is too uncertain to use. (c) No measured axial bed/gas/wall profiles were obtained for a plastic-pyrolysis kiln. Barr T4 and Tscheng A11 (inert sand) are the only well-documented open thermal cases, and their numbers sit in Hanein 2017's supplementary files. (d) The slumping Fr bounds (10^-5–10^-3) and the cascading–cataracting bound (0.3–0.36) are commonly quoted, but neither was verified here.

CONFLICTS AND SPREADS:
- Rolling regime: Mellmann gives 1e-4 to 1e-2 and Henein gives 5e-4 to 2e-2. Use both as an uncertainty band.
- Overall U vs contact h: these are not comparable quantities.
  - Overall wall-to-load U for waste/torrefaction kilns is 13–55 W/m²K (Nhuchhen 13.2–20.9; ANSAC 31–35; Suzuki 22–55 and 38.6–50.1 with lifters).
  - The medical-waste kiln wall-to-bed h is 147.6–241.8 W/m²K.
  - The local contact h from penetration models is typically hundreds of W/m²K.
  - The model should report both the local h and the effective U (shell to bed, including the gas path) so the comparison is like for like.
- Model disagreement on h: Herz 2012 states that literature h models differ by up to 3×. One review says Wes, Tscheng–Watkinson and Schlünder–Mollekopf deviate strongly from measurements, while other citations say Schlünder–Mollekopf and Li 2005 agree well. Expect ±50 % uncertainty on h.
- Isothermal HDPE kinetics:
  - At 450 °C, t90 is 15.7 min (Westerhout first-order) vs 13.5 min (Jiang k1), which agree within 15 %.
  - At 500 °C, Westerhout extrapolates to 1.5 min vs 4.2 min from Jiang, a factor of about 3. Westerhout says data above 450 °C are heat-transfer-limited in TGA.
  - This matters for the kiln because plastic residence times are tens of minutes. Reaction is fast compared with solids transport above about 470 °C, so heat transfer, not kinetics, controls conversion. Check this with the RS-L2 kinetics already in the code (E 238/215/179/180 kJ/mol).
- Kodera 2021: 'Run A' (PP, 64.2 wt% gas) is a separate run from the 650/700/750 °C series.
- Liu/Dai/Li 2026: the HDPE gas-yield numbers were attached to a page title belonging to a different paper. Verify the DOI before showing them on a slide.

MODELLING RECOMMENDATIONS:
- Transport: 1-D Saeman/Kramers bed-depth ODE, with a dam boundary condition or F0 = 1.75 Bd^0.5. Add axial dispersion for the RTD.
- Transverse regime: from Fr and filling. Flag slipping below about 10 % fill, consistent with the heat-carrier result where 5 % fill slips and more than 10 % rolls.
- Wall-to-bed heat transfer: penetration model plus a gas-gap contact resistance (Li 2005, χ 0.096–0.198), with Tscheng–Watkinson as a sensitivity case.
- Fill limit: keep fill at 10–20 %. h falls as fill rises (Moumin; Zhou 182→154 W/m²K for 11→38 %).
- Plastic melting: the plastic melt wets the wall and agglomerates, which changes bed mobility. The available data (Suzuki: lifters raise U by about 17–30 %) only bound this effect.

PROPOSED VALIDATION LADDER (targets and tolerances):

Level 0, code verification (must pass before any physics comparison):
- (i) Global mass and energy balances close to <0.1 %.
- (ii) The bed-depth ODE reproduces the analytic normal depth (dh/dz = 0 for long kilns) to <1e-4 relative. The observed order of accuracy matches the integrator.
- (iii) Penetration conduction into a semi-infinite slab vs the erfc solution, <1 %.
- (iv) Axial-dispersion RTD vs the analytic Danckwerts open/closed solution: mean and variance within 1 %.
- (v) Isothermal first-order TGA vs exp(-kt) to 1e-6. Non-isothermal DTG peak vs the existing calibration (475/465/455/420 °C at 10 K/min), ±2 K.
- (vi) Radiation enclosure view-factor sums = 1, and the two-surface analytic exchange to <1 %.
- (vii) Grid/step independence: tau and outlet T change <1 % on refinement.

Level 1, component validation:
- (a) MRT vs Sullivan and Kramers on the Kramers rig and the torrefaction kiln: ±25 %. The Saeman class shows about 20 % error vs measured MSW data.
- (b) Discharge filling vs F0 = 1.75 Bd^0.5: ±15 %.
- (c) Regime classification matches the Mellmann/Henein maps. Rolling must be predicted for 5e-4 < Fr < 1e-2 at fill >10 %. Treat the transition Fr as uncertain by about a factor of 2.
- (d) Wall-to-bed h vs Herz-type data, once fetched: ±50 %, with the correct trends (dh/dn > 0, dh/dfill < 0, dh/d(dp) < 0).
- (e) Effective U for a plastic-waste kiln falls within 22–55 W/m²K at about 555 °C wall (Suzuki). Lifters at 2.7 rpm give +17 %, and 4.0 rpm gives about 50 W/m²K, ±25 %.
- (f) Isothermal HDPE t90: 13–16 min at 450 °C (±30 %); 1.5–4.2 min at 500 °C (within the literature band).
- (g) Gas-solid convection against the Tscheng & Watkinson envelope (inert sand): bed temperature RMSE ≤15–20 K once the digitised data are loaded.

Level 2, system validation:
- (a) Barr T4 axial bed/gas/wall profiles: RMSE ≤30–50 K, with the bed–inner wall temperature coupling reproduced.
- (b) Code-to-code vs Pichler 2021 cases at matching D, L/D, Fr and Pe: bed height and MRT within 10 %, bed and wall temperatures within 20 K.
- (c) Bäbler reference kiln (0.4 m × 2 m, 3°, 2.5 cm dam, 2 rpm, 30 kg/h): qualitative reproduction of the bed-temperature plateau and overshoot.
- (d) Plastic product yields:
  - PP gas: 58.5/64.4/66.1 wt% at 650/700/750 °C (Kodera), ±5 wt% absolute.
  - HDPE gas: 32.6 → 56.3 wt% from 480 → 600 °C (Liu/Dai/Li), ±5 wt% absolute.
  - Polyolefin oil yield should peak near 500 °C and decline as secondary cracking raises gas.
  - Semi-pilot mixed-plastics yields at 500 °C: oil 43 wt% and char 16 wt%, ±7 wt%.
- (e) Batch kiln trend check (Zhou 2025): raising the heat-source temperature from 750 to 850 °C should shorten completion from 5.04 to 2.28 h and raise gas from 35.6 to 39.3 %. Target: trend correct and within ±30 %.
- (f) Pilot energy-balance sanity: surface losses are 29–52 % of input at about 150 kW pilot scale and 11–16 % at industrial scale (Qasim 2025). The model's loss fraction at pilot scale should fall in this band.

Report every comparison with the source's conditions. Where only trends are available, state that plainly in the video.

C_heat.topic: TOPIC C: heat transfer in rotary kilns, with the focus on indirectly (externally) heated pyrolysis kilns for plastic waste. Covers covered-wall-to-bed contact, gas convection, freeboard radiation, regenerative wall, external heating and losses, bed and melt conductivity, and typical values at 450-650 °C wall temperature.

findings.parameter: Measured covered-wall-to-bed contact HTC alpha_WS,lambda versus 4 models (indirectly heated batch drum)
findings.context: Drum D = 0.6 m, L = 0.45 m, 2 mm steel wall, three electric heaters totalling 4.5 kW, wall up to about 200 °C, fill F = 20 %, 16 type-K thermocouples on a rotating rod. Bed properties (Table 1): steel dp 2.0 mm, rho 4827 kg/m3, cp 465 J/kgK, lambda 1.37 W/mK; animal powder 0.4 mm / 574 / 1538 / 0.12; clinker 4.5 mm / 1478 / 917 / 0.20; expanded clay 3.0 mm / 432 / 769 / 0.12; glass beads 2.0 mm / 1680 / 800 / 0.25; quartz sand 0.2 mm / 1590 / 1080 / 0.30. Regression deviation is about 20 %. Expanded clay (low density, lambda 0.12) is the closest analogue to a plastic-flake bed and gives 27-54 W/m2K.
findings.source: Nafsun A.I., Herz F., Specht E., Scherer V., Wirtz S. (2014) The contact heat transfer in rotary kilns and the effect of material properties. HEFAT2014, Orlando, pp. 2112-2118, Table 2
findings.evidence: Table 2 and Table 1 read in the full PDF text. Conclusion: 'good agreement between the experimental measurements and the models developed by Schlunder et al. [11] and Li et al. [7]'. The Tscheng model 'shows significantly lower values ... could not be validated' for animal powder. Wes 'away from the accuracy range for higher rotational speeds'.

findings.parameter: Contact HTC behaviour: dominant mode, trends and model spread
findings.value: In indirectly heated kilns, contact heat transfer from the covered wall is dominant. In directly heated kilns it is up to 20 % of the heat to the bed. The HTC rises with rpm (shorter contact time) and with bed density, conductivity and heat capacity. It falls as particle diameter rises, because the wall-to-first-layer contact resistance grows. Literature models differ quantitatively by up to a factor of three.
findings.context: OvGU Magdeburg / Hochschule Anhalt (Specht, Herz) experimental programme, including polydisperse beds
findings.source: Nafsun et al. 2014 HEFAT (above); Herz F., Hochschule Anhalt 'Rotary Drums' research brochure (2019), sections 'Contact Heat Transfer' and 'Regenerative Heat Transport'
findings.evidence: Nafsun: 'In indirectly heated rotary kilns, the contact heat transfer from the covered wall to the covered solid bed is dominant. Contact heat transfer also contributes up to 20%... in directly heated rotary kilns [2]'. Herz brochure: models 'differ quantitatively to a factor of three'.

findings.parameter: Li et al. (2005) gas-film parameter chi
findings.value: chi = 0.096 to 0.198 as sand dp rises from 157.5 to 1038 um (Li's optimum about 0.10). Colin's fit: chi = 1.59e-7 dp^2 - 7.58e-5 dp + 1.05e-1 (dp in um), giving chi = 0.59 for 2 mm wood chips. chi = 0.59 clearly improved the prediction of measured charge temperature. With Wes or Lehmberg, the charge temperature was strongly overpredicted.
findings.context: An electrically heated pilot kiln for wood torrefaction (shell 4 m long). Colin also reports that Herz et al. found Li's model to be the only one fitting their data: sand, glass and copper beads, 0.5-2.5 mm, 1-6 rpm, 10-20 % fill.
findings.source: Colin B. (2014) PhD thesis, Ecole des Mines d'Albi-Carmaux, tel-01162630, Eq. 42 and Eq. 70, Fig. 54-55; Li S.-Q., Ma L.-B., Wan W., Yao Q. (2005) Chem. Eng. Technol. 28(12):1480-1489
findings.evidence: Thesis full text: 'chi augmente de 0,096 a 0,198 quand le diametre des particules dp (ici du sable) augmente de 157,5 a 1038 um'; 'la valeur de chi est alors 0,59'. The SimCem code docstring independently gives 'around 0.1, but is in the range 0.096-0.198'.

findings.parameter: Overall inner-wall-to-waste HTC k_m-w and shell heat flux, externally (flue-gas) heated pyrolysis kiln
findings.value: Wall 555 °C: k_m-w rose from 22 to 55 W/m2K as the waste heated, and radial wall heat flux was about 11 kW/m2. Wall 630 °C: 27 to 55 W/m2K, with a maximum flux of 16.5 kW/m2. Wall-to-waste dT just after feeding was about 450 K (555 °C case) and about 520 K (630 °C case). Waste reached 460 °C 30 min after feeding. Heating gas was held at 800 °C, then 700 °C once the cylinder reached 600 °C.
findings.units: W m-2 K-1; kW m-2; K
findings.context: Batch kiln, SUS310S inner cylinder 25 mm thick, ID 1 m, L 1.5 m, flue-gas jacket with a 34 mm gap and outer insulation. Simulated MSW (dry basis): 30 % paper, 25 % wood, 15 % PE, 15 % PP, 5 % PS, 10 % grain, plus 10 % moisture. k_m-w = q_m / (A (T1 - Tw)), where A is the whole inner surface. It is a lumped coefficient that includes contact, wall-to-bed radiation and convection. The closest literature analogue for a KINTEK-type plastic kiln.
findings.source: Suzuki T., Okazaki T., Yamamoto K., Nakata H., Fujita O. (2008) Improvements in Pyrolysis of Wastes in an Externally Heated Rotary Kiln (Measurements of the Overall Heat Transfer Coefficient from the Wall to Wastes), J. Thermal Sci. Technol. 3(3):523-531, doi 10.1299/jtst.3.523
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'When the mean temperature of the kiln's inner wall was 555 °C, km-w rose from 22 W/m2K to 55 W/m2K'. Section 3.4: 'the heat flux qm was about 11 kW/m2... in the 630 °C case... 16.5 kW/m2 at a maximum'.

findings.parameter: Effect of lifters and rpm on k_m-w (same kiln)
findings.value: Six lifters 200 mm high: mean k_m-w rose from 38.6 to 45.3 W/m2K at 2.7 rpm, and to 50.1 W/m2K at 4.0 rpm. Lifters mattered most in the pyrolysis phase of the plastic-based components.
findings.context: Wall 555 °C, batch externally heated kiln (Table 1 conditions: 555 °C, 2.7 rpm, 6 lifters, 200 mm)
findings.source: Suzuki T. et al. (2008) J. Thermal Sci. Technol. 3(3):532-539 (Experimental Study on Heat Transfer Enhancement), doi 10.1299/jtst.3.532
findings.evidence: Abstract text in the PDF: 'the mean value of km-w increased from 38.6 W/m2K to 45.3 W/m2K at 2.7 rpm... increased to 50.1 W/m2K when the rotating speed was increased to 4.0 rpm'

findings.parameter: Overall HTC, waste-tyre horizontal rotary pyrolysis furnace
findings.value: Highest 16.89 W/m2K (3 rpm, powdered tyre plus carborundum). Spiral fins raised the 'comprehensive' coefficient from 12.78 to 16.32 W/m2K. Above 2 rpm, contact between material and wall was sufficient. Oil yield was 46.1 %.
findings.context: Horizontal externally heated rotary furnace, tyre feed (closest elastomer analogue)
findings.source: Ma H., Bai Y., Ma S., Zhou Z. (2025) Energies 18(15):4028
findings.evidence: Abstract quote: 'the overall heat transfer coefficient was the highest, which was 16.89 W/(m2·K)... increased from 12.78 W/(m2·K) to 16.32 W/(m2·K)'

findings.parameter: Overall HTC in a laboratory indirectly heated kiln
findings.value: 74-107 (internal heat-transfer area 1.7 m2)
findings.context: Patent family on maximising throughput of indirectly heated rotary kilns; the bed material was not seen
findings.source: US 8298406 / US 9371486 'Method and apparatus for maximizing throughput of indirectly heated rotary kilns'
findings.evidence: Web-search summary of the patent text only. Google Patents returned a block page.

findings.parameter: Spread of literature wall-to-solid HTC values (same input data)
findings.value: Debacq (2001) compilation: Tscheng 185, penetration theory 130, Wachters 44, Dumont 30, Imber 0.1-0.2, Lybaert 0.08, a factor of about 2000. For Thammavong's pilot nominal conditions: penetration theory 285, Tscheng 302, Dumont 34, Wachters 95. Measured h_sp in that pilot was only 4.4-51.3 and was ill-conditioned (some balances gave negative values).
findings.context: CEA/CNAM electrically heated pilot kiln, sand, no lifters. Measured h_sg was about 2.2-4.8 W/m2K (about 4 nominal). The measured trend did not follow the rpm proportionality of penetration theory.
findings.source: Thammavong P. (2010) PhD thesis, UPMC Paris 6 / CNAM, Tableau 3, Tableau 35 and Chapter IV
findings.evidence: 'varient de 0,08 W m-2 K-1 [Lybaert, 1987] a 185 W m-2 K-1 [Tscheng, 1979] ; soit un facteur d'environ 2000'; Tableau 35 values; result tables with hsg 3.07, 2.99... and hsp 5.1, 4.4, 4.7, 23.3, 33.4, 33.8, 43.9, 51.3

findings.parameter: Apparent HTC stages, MSW components in an externally heated rotary kiln
findings.value: The apparent HTC is highest in the moisture-evaporation stage, then drops to a minimum. It stays about constant in pre-pyrolysis, rises in the violent-pyrolysis stage and falls at the end. At 3 r/min the pre-pyrolysis plateau disappears. Heating rates were (22±2) and (32±2) °C/min. Numeric HTC values were not in the abstract.
findings.context: Paper, fabric, biomass and MSW without inerts
findings.evidence: English abstract read on the journal page

findings.parameter: DERIVED typical covered-wall coefficients for a D = 1 m kiln at fill 15 % (half fill angle 54.2°, contact time 18.1 / 6.0 / 3.0 s at 1 / 3 / 6 rpm)
findings.value: Penetration only (no contact resistance): flake bed (k 0.10, rho 350, c 2000) 70 / 122 / 172; denser flakes (0.15 / 450 / 2200) 102 / 177 / 251; molten pool (0.20 / 750 / 2600) 166 / 287 / 406; char or carbon-black bed (0.10 / 400 / 1000) 53 / 92 / 130; sand heat carrier (0.30 / 1590 / 1080) 191 / 330 / 467. Li model for a flake bed with kg = 0.053: dp 0.5 mm, chi 0.1 gives 66 / 109 / 148; dp 2 mm, chi 0.1 gives 56 / 83 / 104; dp 4 mm, chi 0.1 gives 46 / 63 / 75; dp 4 mm, chi 0.59 gives 17 / 19 / 20. Tscheng form, flake bed: 32 / 45 / 56.
findings.units: W m-2 K-1 (per covered wall area)
findings.context: My own calculation (scratchpad kilnB/htcalc.py). Bed properties are assumed, not measured. The Tscheng argument n R^2 beta/a comes out at 5e4-5e5, above the about 1e4 limit noted for that correlation, so Tscheng is extrapolated here. The calculated values bracket the measured Suzuki lumped 22-55 and the expanded-clay 27-54.
findings.source: Derived from the Nafsun Eq. 3 penetration model, Li et al. 2005 (SimCem form) and the Tscheng & Watkinson form (wally form)
findings.evidence: Python calculation, reproducible

findings.parameter: Tscheng & Watkinson gas-to-exposed-bed and gas-to-exposed-wall Nusselt correlations
findings.value: Nu_gb = 0.46 Re^0.535 Re_w^0.104 eta^-0.341; Nu_gw = 1.54 Re^0.575 Re_w^-0.292 (Nu = h D_e / k_g). Validity: 1600 < Re < 7800 and 20 < Re_w < 800. Measured h_gw is independent of fill. h_gb falls slightly with fill. Slope and gas flow rate have no important effect on h_gb. Solids feed rate and inclination had no impact on h_gw.
findings.context: Tscheng's experimental kiln: L 2.5 m, D 0.19 m, 0.4-6 rpm, slope 1.36-4.1°, about 1120 K (Thammavong Tableaux 8 and 10), directly heated by hot gas. SPREAD: Colin (2014) prints the gas-wall exponent on Re as 0.535 instead of 0.575 (probably a typo) and writes eta as (Hz/100). SimCem attributes the same equations to Li et al. 2005 Eqs. 8-9.
findings.source: Tscheng S.H., Watkinson A.P. (1979) Can. J. Chem. Eng. 57(4):433-443, as reproduced in Hared (2007) Eqs. 2.13 and 2.15, SimCem kiln.hpp and wally HtcTscheng1979; Fakt et al. (2025) Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. (PMC12023457)
findings.evidence: Hared: 'Nugp = 1.54Re0.575 Re−0.292'; 'Nugp = 0.46Re0.535 Re0.104 Xr−0.341'. SimCem docstring: 'This requires 1600<Re_g<7800 and 20<Re_w<800'. Fakt: 'solids feed rate and kiln inclination had no impacts on the gas-to-wall heat transfer coefficient'.

findings.parameter: Gorog / turbulent-pipe gas-to-wall convection and measured or assumed gas-side values
findings.value: Nu = 0.036 Re^0.8 Pr^0.33 (d/Z)^0.055 for 10 < Z/d < 400, turbulent. On the Carling coke kiln (Re > 40000) this gives h_gw ≈ 10 W/m2K. h_gs was taken as 10 W/m2K. Barr found h_gs/h_gw of 1 to 2. Rotation speed and grain size have no significant effect on gas convection. Gorog gas-solid: h_gs = 0.4 (m_g/S_g)^0.62, with m_g in kg/h, for Re 2e5-5e5.
findings.context: In a pyrolysis kiln the sweep or vapour flow is weak, so Re is usually laminar and convection is minor. Colin also gives the Seghir-Ouali laminar correlation (see equations).
findings.source: Patisson F., Lebas E., Hanrot F., Ablitzer D., Houzelot J.-L. (2000) Coal pyrolysis in a rotary kiln: Part II, Metall. Mater. Trans. B 31B:391-402 (HAL preprint), Eq. 14; Colin (2014) Eqs. 25 and 29
findings.evidence: 'Applied to the Carling kiln, this gives hcgw ≈ 10 W m−2 K−1... Barr found a ratio of 1 to 2... hcgs = 10 W m−2 K−1'

findings.parameter: Freeboard radiation: locality, beam length, gray-gas error
findings.value: Radiative exchange is effectively confined to the kiln cross-section: flux between surfaces (or gas and a surface) more than one diameter apart axially is negligible. Mean beam length L_m = 0.95 (D - H). With a gray gas, the error on gas-solid exchange is under 20 % when solid and wall emissivities exceed 0.8. At pyrolysis gas temperatures the gas can no longer be treated as gray (Beckmann). Radiation is often considered negligible below 300-400 °C (Colin).
findings.context: Gorog, Brimacombe, Adams (1981) Metall. Trans. B 12B:55-69 and (1983), as summarised
findings.source: Lebas E. (1995) PhD thesis, INPL Nancy (Eq. IV.2 and section IV.1.1); Colin (2014) section III.4.2; Beckmann M., Fontana A., Gehrmann H.-J. (2003) Sheffield symposium paper (TU Dresden)
findings.evidence: Lebas: 'le flux entre deux surfaces... distantes suivant l'axe de plus d'un diametre est negligeable'; 'Lm = 0,95 (D - H)'; 'Lorsque les emissivites du solide et de la paroi sont superieures a 0,8, l'erreur... est inferieure a 20 %'. Beckmann: 'the gas radiation can no longer be assumed to be gray'.

findings.parameter: Emissivities
findings.value: Coal or char during pyrolysis: 0.9-1 measured by optical pyrometer (Lecerf), literature 0.8-1. Inner kiln wall coated with carbon or graphite: chosen arbitrarily between 0.8 and 1. Outer oxidised steel shell: 0.9. Stably oxidised type 347 stainless: 0.87-0.91 (600-2000 °F). Haynes C 0.90-0.96, X 0.85-0.88, 25 0.85-0.89. Flame-sprayed alumina 0.69-0.44 and zirconia 0.62-0.44 (800-2000 °F). wally code defaults: bed 0.8, refractory 0.8, environment 0.8.
findings.context: No measured emissivity was found for plastic flakes, PE melt or plastic-derived char at pyrolysis temperature. The SUS310S drum value was not found either; 347 is the nearest stainless proxy.
findings.source: Lebas (1995) section IV.1.1.2; Patisson et al. (2000); Wade W.R. (1959) NASA memo, NTRS 19980228304; wally rotary_kiln.py defaults
findings.evidence: NASA abstract: 'type 347 stainless steel for which the total hemispherical emissivity varied from 0.87 to 0.91 for temperatures from 600 F to 2,000 F'. Patisson: 'heavily oxidized steel. The emissivity εwo is taken equal to 0.9'. Lebas: 'valeurs comprises entre 0,9 et 1'.

findings.parameter: DERIVED radiative wall-to-bed potential (black-body, linearised)
findings.value: Wall 450 / bed 350 °C: h_rad 69.6 W/m2K, flux 7.0 kW/m2. Wall 550 / bed 400 °C: 95.9 and 14.4. Wall 650 / bed 450 °C: 128.4 and 25.7. Wall 650 / bed 500 °C: 139.5 and 20.9. Multiply by an effective exchange factor of about 0.6-0.85 and by the chord/exposed-wall view factor.
findings.units: W m-2 K-1; kW m-2 (per bed-surface area)
findings.context: My calculation, h = sigma (T1^2+T2^2)(T1+T2). It shows radiation from the free wall to the bed surface is of the same order as covered-wall contact at 450-650 °C. Both must be modelled.
findings.source: Derived (scratchpad kilnB/htcalc.py)
findings.evidence: Python calculation

findings.parameter: Regenerative wall heat transfer: depth of periodic temperature oscillation
findings.value: Refractory concrete (rho 2230 kg/m3, cp 1150 J/kgK, lambda 1.6 W/mK): only the first 15 mm are significantly affected. The uncovered-wall surface temperature varies by at most 75 °C. A 2 cm steel shell has about 300 times less resistance than 20 cm refractory. Specht and Herz group: the penetration depth in the wall is 'a few millimeters'. A thin active layer plus a stationary inactive layer is modelled as semi-infinite, and the analytical model agrees with FVM/FEM.
findings.context: Gorog, Adams, Brimacombe (1982) Metall. Trans. B 13:153-163 is the reference (closed access, not read). The Agustini (2006) OvGU thesis is behind an anti-bot wall and was not read.
findings.source: Patisson et al. (2000) section D; Herz F. Hochschule Anhalt 'Rotary Drums' brochure (2019), 'Regenerative Heat Transport'
findings.evidence: Patisson: 'only the first 15 millimeters of the wall are significantly affected... variations at the surface of the uncovered wall do not exceed 75°C'. Herz: 'temperature penetration depth in the wall with a few millimeters is relatively low'.

findings.parameter: DERIVED steel-shell regenerative penetration depth and contact temperature
findings.value: delta = sqrt(a P / pi): SUS310S (assumed k 19 W/mK, a 4.4e-6 m2/s) 9.1 / 5.3 / 3.7 mm at 1 / 3 / 6 rpm; carbon steel (assumed k 38) 12.4 / 7.2 / 5.1 mm. Effusivity is about 9100 for SUS310S and about 265 for a flake bed (W s^0.5 m-2 K-1), so the wall surface keeps about 97 % of its excess temperature on contact.
findings.context: An unlined steel shell in an indirectly heated kiln is nearly isothermal around the circumference. Contact resistance and bed penetration control. A lumped wall node with thermal mass is adequate. In Suzuki's 25 mm SUS310S wall, the dT measured across the two inner layers was only 6.5-8.5 °C.
findings.source: Derived (scratchpad kilnB/htcalc.py); Suzuki et al. 2008 (JTST 3:523) for the measured dT
findings.evidence: Python calculation; property values assumed

findings.parameter: Outside coefficients, shell emissivity and losses
findings.value: Natural convection from Ozisik as printed: h_cwa = 0.26 W/m2K (suspiciously low). Forced convection 3-40 W/m2K for a 1-28 m/s cross wind. Measured on the Carling kiln: 17 W/m2K at 10.6 m/s. Outer shell emissivity 0.9. wally default h_env = 8 W/m2K. DERIVED insulation loss: 200 mm at k 0.08 W/mK and 650 °C gives about 240 W/m2; 150 mm at k 0.10 gives about 400 W/m2.
findings.context: Directly fired coke kiln (Patisson). For a jacketed or furnace-enclosed pyrolysis kiln, the loss is through the jacket insulation.
findings.source: Patisson et al. (2000) section III-B; wally rotary_kiln.py; derived
findings.evidence: 'gave a value of hcwa = 0.26W m−2 K−1 for natural convection and 3 ≤ hcwa ≤ 40W m−2 K−1 for forced convection... hcwa = 17W m−2 K−1, corresponding to a wind speed of 10.6 m s-1'

findings.parameter: External heating: achievable shell heat flux and design practice
findings.value: Measured through a flue-gas jacket: 11 kW/m2 (wall 555 °C) to 16.5 kW/m2 maximum (630 °C), with heating gas at 700-800 °C. Vendors: indirect kilns are unlined, with a heat-resistant alloy shell. The shell is often at or above 1200 °F (649 °C), and shell-to-solids radiation prevails. A pilot patent kiln used a centrifugally cast HH-alloy shell in a 54 kW electric furnace with 4 zones. DERIVED electric radiant heater to shell: heater 750 / shell 600 °C gives 17.5-23.3 kW/m2 (eps_eff 0.6-0.8); 850/650 gives 29.4-39.2; 950/700 gives 45.6-60.9.
findings.context: For a 450-650 °C wall, a realistic sustained shell flux is about 5-20 kW/m2. It is limited by wall-to-bed U (about 20-100 W/m2K) times dT (about 100-250 K), not by the heater.
findings.source: Suzuki et al. (2008) JTST 3:523; FEECO technical pages (search summary); derived
findings.evidence: Suzuki full text; vendor statements from search summaries only

findings.parameter: Pilot externally heated kiln with PE (CUTEC / TU Dresden)
findings.value: Wall temperatures staged at 300 / 400 / 500 / 500 °C. Feed 90 kg/h sand plus 10 kg/h PE. N2 at about 0.8 Nm3/h. Model reaction enthalpy 'assumed with 4.600 kJ/kg' (as printed). Sand heating rates on the measured profiles were 10-159 K/min. The model uses the Mollekopf penetration approach plus the Adams-Brimacombe radiation model.
findings.context: A heat-carrier (sand) kiln for PE. Validation profiles were in figures only.
findings.source: Beckmann M., Fontana A., Gehrmann H.-J. (2003) Mathematical Modeling and Experimental Investigation of the Pyrolysis of Waste in Rotary Kilns, 4th Int. Symp. Waste Treatment Technologies, Sheffield
findings.evidence: Fig. 6 caption and text: 'staging of the wall temperatures of 300/ 400/ 500/ 500 °C with 90 kg/h sand and 10 kg/h PE... nitrogen... about 0.8 Nm3/h. The reaction enthalpy ΔRh was assumed with 4.600 kJ/kg'

findings.parameter: Polymer melt thermal conductivity and diffusivity
findings.value: Diffusivity of molten LDPE 6.92e-7 and molten PP 5.53e-7 m2/s near Tm. A prior verification judged these about 4-6x higher than typical (about 1.2e-7). Melt conductivity (handbook / Moldflow-type, unverified): HDPE 0.22-0.26, LDPE 0.20-0.24, PP 0.15-0.19, PS 0.14-0.17, liquid waxes and oils 0.08-0.12 W/mK at 300-450 °C. Trend from Santos et al. (2005): for semi-crystalline polymers k falls with T up to melting, then tends to rise. For amorphous PS and HIPS, k is about constant up to softening, then rises slightly.
findings.context: Used for the molten pool and the wall-film resistance
findings.source: Yanez et al. (2013) Ing. Investig. 33(2):5-8 (prior-session full-text check); Santos W.N. dos et al. (2005) Polimeros 15(4):289-295 (hot-wire, HDPE/LDPE/PP/PS/HIPS); prior-topic property compilation
findings.evidence: Santos full text read this session (values only in figures). Yanez abstract: 'alpha = 6.92x10^-7 m2/s for LDPE and alpha = 5.53x10^-7 m2/s for PP'.

findings.parameter: Effective conductivity of a plastic-flake bed
findings.value: No measured value was found in the open literature. A derived Zehner-Schlunder estimate (no radiation, porosity 0.5-0.6, N2) gives 0.05-0.14, about 0.08-0.12 at 300-450 °C. The solid polymer is PE 0.3-0.5 and PP 0.17-0.22. The analogue expanded-clay bed in the Nafsun drum is 0.12.
findings.context: The bed conductivity sets the penetration resistance. The low effusivity of flakes (about 265) is why covered-wall coefficients for plastics are at the low end (about 30-120 W/m2K).
findings.source: Prior Topic G/H derived calculation (Zehner-Schlunder); Thermtest note; Nafsun et al. 2014 Table 1
findings.evidence: Derived calculation and secondary data

findings.parameter: Heat transfer to or through a molten plastic layer on the wall
findings.value: Second-hand value: wall HTC for molten plastics is about 1000 W/m2K in a rotary kiln versus about 4000 W/m2K in a falling-film reactor. Patent: rubbery or plastic feed forms an adhering layer that, in externally heated kilns, can block heat transfer so badly that operation soon becomes impossible; scrapers are used. A Chinese plastic-kiln study cites the 'low thermal conductivity and sticky nature of plastic waste' as the reason for a sand heat carrier. DERIVED film resistance: h_film = k_m / delta gives 100 W/m2K for 2 mm at k 0.2, and 40 W/m2K for 5 mm.
findings.context: No measured melt-film coefficient specific to a rotary kiln was found. Zhang et al. (2022) CEJ 445:136686 (DEM-CFD of plastic pyrolysis in a rotary furnace) is closed access and was not read.
findings.source: Applied Energy 2021 semi-batch melting model (HAL hal-04652254, search summary); US 4147505 scraper patent (search summary); Gao & Bao 2020 (prior topic); derived
findings.evidence: Search summaries; the HAL PDF returned an anti-bot page

findings.parameter: Dominant heat transfer mode at 450-650 °C wall, indirectly heated plastic kiln
findings.value: Covered-wall contact conduction (about 20-170 W/m2K on the covered area for flakes or melt, lower bound for coarse flakes) and free-wall-to-bed-surface radiation (black-body h_rad about 70-140 W/m2K) are both first-order. Gas convection is minor: about 2-10 W/m2K (measured 2.2-4.8 in an unswept pilot; 10 assumed in a directly fired kiln). Measured lumped wall-to-waste U is 22-55 W/m2K (Suzuki), 38.6-50.1 with lifters, and 13-17 W/m2K for tyres.
findings.context: This is a synthesis of the findings above. Radiation's share rises with temperature and with lifter cascading.
findings.source: Synthesis of Suzuki 2008, Nafsun 2014, Thammavong 2010, Patisson 2000 and derived calculations
findings.evidence: Synthesis

equations.name: Fill degree and fill angle
equations.expression: F = A_bed/A_drum = (gamma - sin(gamma) cos(gamma))/pi ; gamma = arccos(1 - h/R)
equations.variables: F fill fraction; gamma half filling angle [rad]; h bed depth [m]; R drum radius [m]
equations.validity: Flat bed surface (rolling mode, chord approximation)
equations.source: Nafsun et al. 2014 HEFAT, Eq. (1)

equations.name: Penetration (Schlunder) coefficient into the covered bed
equations.expression: alpha_S,pen = 2 * sqrt(rho_S c_p,S lambda_S / (pi t_contact)) ; t_contact = gamma/(pi n)
equations.variables: rho_S, c_p,S, lambda_S bulk bed density, heat capacity, conductivity; n rotation rate [rev/s]; gamma half filling angle [rad]. Equivalent: t_c = 2 gamma/omega.
equations.validity: Constant wall temperature, quasi-continuum bed, well-mixed passive layer. Overpredicts for coarse particles and short contact times unless a contact resistance is added in series.
equations.source: Nafsun et al. 2014, Eq. (3); same form as Wes et al. 1976 (Colin 2014 Eq. 39) and Lybaert (Hared Eq. 2.19)

equations.name: Series contact model for covered wall to bed
equations.expression: alpha_WS,lambda = 1/(1/alpha_WS,contact + 1/alpha_S,pen)
equations.variables: alpha_WS,contact wall-to-first-particle-layer coefficient; alpha_S,pen penetration coefficient
equations.validity: General (Schlunder 1984)
equations.source: Nafsun et al. 2014, Eq. (2)

equations.name: Schlunder-Mollekopf wall-to-first-layer contact coefficient (as printed)
equations.expression: alpha_WS,contact = tau_W alpha_WP + (1 - tau_W) * (2 lambda_G/d_P) / (sqrt(2) + (2 l_G + mu_P)/d_P) + alpha_WP,rad
equations.variables: tau_W surface coverage factor; alpha_WP gas-gap conduction coefficient wall-particle (Schlunder 1971, involves the modified free path); lambda_G gas conductivity; d_P particle diameter; l_G modified free path of gas molecules; mu_P mean surface roughness; alpha_WP,rad gap radiation coefficient
equations.validity: Monodisperse spheres. The grouping of the denominator was reconstructed from garbled PDF text. Check it against Schlunder & Mollekopf, Chem. Eng. Process. 18 (1984) 93-111 or the VDI Heat Atlas before coding. The sub-expression for alpha_WP was not obtained.
equations.source: Nafsun et al. 2014, Eq. (4)

equations.name: Li et al. (2005) wall-to-bed model with gas film
equations.expression: Nu = h d_p/k_g = 1/(chi + 0.5 sqrt(pi/Pe)) ; Pe = (d_p/k_g)^2 * rho_b c_b k_b * omega/theta ; equivalently 1/h = chi d_p/k_g + 0.5 sqrt(pi theta/(k_b rho_b c_b omega))
equations.variables: chi film-thickness factor (0.096-0.198 for 157.5-1038 um sand); d_p particle diameter; k_g gas conductivity; k_b, rho_b, c_b bed properties; theta bed central angle (= 2 gamma) [rad]; omega angular speed [rad/s]
equations.validity: Fitted to sand and soda; best fit to Herz and Nafsun data for dp up to about 1 mm. For 2 mm wood chips Colin used chi = 0.59.
equations.source: Li S.-Q., Ma L.-B., Wan W., Yao Q. (2005) Chem. Eng. Technol. 28:1480-1489, as implemented in SimCem kiln.hpp (Nu_bed_wall_Li_etal_2005, Pe_bed_wall_Li_etal_2005) and Colin 2014 Eq. 42

equations.name: Colin chi(dp) fit
equations.variables: dp particle diameter [um]
equations.validity: Fitted to Li's 157.5-1038 um points and extrapolated to 2 mm (chi = 0.59). Not valid for flakes larger than about 2 mm.
equations.source: Colin B. (2014) thesis, Eq. 70

equations.name: Tscheng & Watkinson wall-to-bed correlation
equations.expression: h_cw = 11.6 * (k_b/(R beta)) * (n R^2 beta / a_b)^0.3   [wally form]  ;  Patisson form: h_cws = 11.6 (lambda_eff/A_wc) Go^0.3, Go = omega alpha d_wi^2/(2 a_eff), A_wc = alpha d_wi/2
equations.variables: k_b effective bed conductivity; a_b bed diffusivity; R radius; beta (= alpha) bed central angle [rad]; n rotation rate; d_wi inner diameter
equations.validity: The argument is reportedly limited to about 1e4 (wally code comment). The grouping differs by a factor of 2 between the two secondary sources (n versus omega), so verify against Can. J. Chem. Eng. 57 (1979) 433-443. Nafsun found it too low for fine powders (fictitious gas film).
equations.source: wally/Kilnerys HtcTscheng1979.h_wb; Patisson et al. 2000 Eq. 20

equations.name: Lehmberg et al. (1977) wall-to-bed with gas layer
equations.expression: h = sqrt(lambda_s rho_s c_p,s / t_c) * ( 2/sqrt(pi) - 1/(h' sqrt(a_s t_c)) + exp(h'^2 a_s t_c) erfc(h' sqrt(a_s t_c)) / (h' sqrt(a_s t_c)) )
equations.variables: h' wall-related transfer parameter (gas-layer) [1/m]; a_s bed diffusivity; t_c contact time
equations.validity: Overpredicted wood-chip temperatures in Colin's pilot. The form was reconstructed from PDF text.
equations.source: Colin 2014 Eq. 41, citing Lehmberg, Hehl, Schugerl, Powder Technol. 18 (1977) 149-163

equations.name: Hydraulic diameter of the freeboard
equations.expression: D_e = 0.5 D [ (2 pi - theta + sin theta) / (pi - theta/2 + sin(theta/2)) ]  (wally: D_e = 0.5 D f(1,beta)/f(2,beta), f(n,b) = (3-n) pi - b/n + sin(b/n))
equations.variables: D drum diameter; theta bed central angle
equations.validity: Partly filled cylinder
equations.source: Tscheng & Watkinson 1979, via Colin 2014 Eq. 23 and wally code

equations.name: Tscheng & Watkinson gas-to-bed and gas-to-wall Nusselt numbers
equations.expression: Nu_gb = 0.46 Re^0.535 Re_w^0.104 eta^-0.341 ; Nu_gw = 1.54 Re^0.575 Re_w^-0.292 ; Re = rho_g u_g D_e/mu_g ; Re_w = rho_g omega D_e^2/mu_g ; h = Nu k_g/D_e
equations.variables: eta fill fraction; u_g axial gas velocity; omega angular speed
equations.validity: 1600 < Re < 7800 and 20 < Re_w < 800 (SimCem). Laboratory kiln 0.19 m x 2.5 m, 0.4-6 rpm. In a slow-sweep pyrolysis kiln Re is often below 1600, so these are extrapolated.
equations.source: Tscheng & Watkinson (1979) via Hared 2007 Eqs. 2.13 and 2.15, SimCem and wally

equations.name: Turbulent gas-to-wall (Gorog / pipe-flow) correlation
equations.variables: d inner diameter; Z axial distance or length
equations.validity: Turbulent, 10 < Z/d < 400
equations.source: Patisson et al. 2000 Eq. 14; Colin 2014 Eq. 25

equations.name: Gorog gas-to-solid
equations.variables: m_g gas mass flow [kg/h]; S_g flow cross-section (as given by Colin)
equations.validity: Re 2e5-5e5. Dimensional; check units in the original.
equations.source: Colin 2014 Eq. 29 citing Gorog et al.

equations.name: Seghir-Ouali laminar gas-to-wall
equations.variables: Re axial; Re_w rotational Reynolds
equations.validity: Re 0-3e4; Re_w 1.6e3-2.77e5. Suits low-flow pyrolysis kilns better.
equations.source: Colin 2014 Eq. 27

equations.name: Mean beam length (Gorog et al. 1981, Eq. 50)
equations.variables: D diameter; H, h bed depth
equations.validity: Kiln cross-section
equations.source: Lebas 1995 Eq. IV.2; SimCem pathLength(); wally (Hanein 2016 usage)

equations.name: Cross-section view factors, wall p and solid s
equations.expression: F_ss = 0 ; F_sp = 1 ; F_ps = S_l/S_pd ; F_pp = 1 - S_l/S_pd
equations.variables: S_l bed chord (surface) length; S_pd exposed (uncovered) wall arc length
equations.validity: Gray diffuse surfaces, no axial exchange
equations.source: Colin 2014 Eq. 30, citing Gorog et al.

equations.name: Manitius exchange factors (within 5 % of Gorog's rigorous model)
equations.expression: Phi_rgs = sigma E_gs A_s (T_g^4 - T_s^4), E_gs = eps_g eps_s ; E_gw = eps_g eps_w ; E_ws = eps_w eps_s (1 - eps_g)
equations.variables: eps_g gas emissivity; eps_s bed; eps_w wall
equations.validity: Gray gas
equations.source: Patisson et al. 2000 Eq. 12

equations.name: Two-surface plus gray-gas radiation network (SimCem)
equations.expression: Conductances: eps_b A_b/(1-eps_b), (1-eps_g) A_b, eps_g A_b, eps_w A_w/(1-eps_w), eps_g A_w ; potentials sigma T_b^4, sigma T_w^4, sigma T_g^4 ; A_w = R(2 pi - theta), A_b = chord length
equations.variables: per unit kiln length; eps_g from Hottel charts with L_m
equations.validity: SimCem notes that Li et al. 2005 incorrectly used the covered perimeter for A_b
equations.source: SimCem kiln.hpp rad_fluxes()

equations.name: Linearised radiation coefficient
equations.expression: h_rad = eps sigma (T1^2 + T2^2)(T1 + T2)
equations.variables: T in K
equations.validity: Gray surfaces
equations.source: SimCem h_rad_simple()

equations.name: Measured overall wall-to-waste coefficient
equations.expression: q_m = lambda_m (T2 - T1) / ((D1/2) ln(D2/D1)) ; k_m-w = q_m/(A_m (T1 - T_w))
equations.variables: T1, T2 inner and outer wall temperatures; D1, D2 diameters; A_m whole inner area; T_w waste temperature
equations.validity: Lumped. Includes contact, radiation and convection. Based on the whole inner area.
equations.source: Suzuki et al. 2008 JTST 3:523, Eqs. (1)-(2)

equations.name: External shell radiation loss
equations.expression: Phi_rwa = A_wo eps_wo sigma (T_wo^4 - T_a^4), A_wo = pi d_wo ; Phi_cwa = h_cwa A_wo (T_wo - T_a)
equations.variables: eps_wo = 0.9 (oxidised steel)
equations.validity: Gray shell to infinite surroundings
equations.source: Patisson et al. 2000 Eqs. 13 and 17

equations.name: Regenerative thermal penetration depth (DERIVED)
equations.expression: delta = sqrt(a_w P/pi), P = 60/n_rpm ; contact temperature T_c = (e_w T_w + e_b T_b)/(e_w + e_b), e = sqrt(k rho c)
equations.variables: a_w wall diffusivity; e effusivity
equations.validity: Semi-infinite periodic conduction (standard result, not from a kiln paper)
equations.source: Derived; consistent with Herz (few mm) and Patisson (15 mm in refractory)

equations.name: Maxwell effective conductivity (bed or two-phase)
equations.expression: k_eff = k_g (2 k_g + k_s + 2 phi (k_s - k_g)) / (2 k_g + k_s - phi (k_s - k_g))
equations.variables: phi solid volume fraction; k_s solid; k_g gas
equations.validity: Dilute or dispersed; underestimates contact-dominated beds. Zehner-Schlunder is preferred for packed beds.
equations.source: wally models effective_thermal_conductivity (SimCem uses HT::conduction::maxwell)

key_sources.citation: Nafsun A.I., Herz F., Specht E., Scherer V., Wirtz S. (2014) The contact heat transfer in rotary kilns and the effect of material properties. HEFAT2014, Orlando
key_sources.why: Full text. Measured contact HTC for 6 materials at 1 and 6 rpm against 4 models (Wes, Tscheng, Schlunder-Mollekopf, Li). Gives the penetration and Schlunder equations. Primary validation data for the covered-wall term.

key_sources.citation: Suzuki T., Okazaki T., Yamamoto K., Nakata H., Fujita O. (2008) J. Thermal Sci. Technol. 3(3):523-531 and 532-539
key_sources.why: Full text. The only measured wall-to-waste U (22-55 W/m2K) and shell heat flux (11-16.5 kW/m2) for an externally heated (flue-gas jacket) SUS310S pyrolysis kiln with a plastic-rich feed. Part 2 gives the effect of lifters and rpm.

key_sources.citation: Patisson F., Lebas E., Hanrot F., Ablitzer D., Houzelot J.-L. (2000) Coal pyrolysis in a rotary kiln: Part II, Metall. Mater. Trans. B 31B:391-402
key_sources.why: Full text. Complete heat-transfer sub-model set for a pyrolysis kiln: Manitius radiation factors, convection, Tscheng wall-bed, regenerative wall (15 mm, ±75 °C), outside coefficients, emissivity 0.9.

key_sources.citation: Colin B. (2014) PhD thesis, Ecole des Mines d'Albi-Carmaux (tel-01162630)
key_sources.why: Compiles gas-wall, gas-solid, laminar, wall-bed (Wes, Lehmberg, Li) correlations and view factors. Validates Li's chi on an electrically heated pilot and gives chi(dp).

key_sources.citation: Thammavong P. (2010) PhD thesis, UPMC/CNAM (tel-05119895)
key_sources.why: Documents the factor-of-about-2000 spread of literature wall-solid HTCs, gives Tscheng and Wes rig parameters, and has measured h_sg of about 3-4 W/m2K in an electrically heated pilot.

key_sources.citation: Hared I.A. (2007) Optimisation d'un procede de pyrolyse en four tournant, INP Toulouse (tel-04619234)
key_sources.why: States the Tscheng & Watkinson gas correlations exactly and their observed parameter (in)dependence, in a pyrolysis-kiln context.

key_sources.citation: Lebas E. (1995) PhD thesis, INPL Nancy (coal pyrolysis in a rotary kiln); exact URL not recorded
key_sources.why: Gorog radiation locality, mean beam length, gray-gas error bound, emissivities of 0.9-1 for pyrolysing coal or char. Read in full text from a local copy (the linked HAL record is the companion paper).

key_sources.citation: Wade W.R. (1959) Measurements of total hemispherical emissivity of several stably oxidized metals and some refractory oxide coatings, NASA memo
key_sources.why: Emissivity of oxidised stainless (347: 0.87-0.91) and Ni alloys at 316-1093 °C, a proxy for an oxidised alloy kiln shell.

key_sources.citation: Beckmann M., Fontana A., Gehrmann H.-J. (2003) Mathematical modeling and experimental investigation of the pyrolysis of waste in rotary kilns, Sheffield
key_sources.why: Externally heated pilot kiln with PE plus sand, staged wall temperatures, and the statement that pyrolysis-gas radiation is non-gray.

key_sources.citation: SimCem kiln.hpp (Bannerman group) and wally/Kilnerys rotary_kiln.py with HtcTscheng1979 (local copies; repository URLs not recorded)
key_sources.why: Working code implementations of Li 2005, Tscheng 1979 and the gray-gas radiation network, with validity ranges in the docstrings. Directly portable to PyTorch.

key_sources.citation: Herz F. Hochschule Anhalt 'Rotary Drums' research brochure (2019); Herz, Mitov, Specht, Stanev (2012) IJHMT 55:7941-7948 and CES 82:312-318 (closed, not read)
key_sources.why: Group statements on contact-model spread (factor of 3), polydisperse validation, and regenerative wall depth of a few mm.

critical_numbers: Externally heated SUS310S kiln (ID 1 m, 25 mm wall): k_m-w 22 to 55 W/m2K at 555 °C wall, 27 to 55 at 630 °C (Suzuki 2008)
Shell heat flux measured: about 11 kW/m2 (555 °C wall), maximum 16.5 kW/m2 (630 °C wall), heating gas 700-800 °C (Suzuki 2008)
With lifters: 38.6 to 45.3 W/m2K (six 200 mm lifters, 2.7 rpm), 50.1 at 4.0 rpm
Contact HTC measured at F = 20 %: expanded clay 27-41 (1 rpm) and 36-54 (6 rpm); quartz sand 81-122 and 198-298; steel spheres 173-259 and 213-320 W/m2K (Nafsun 2014)
Li et al. chi = 0.096-0.198 (dp 157.5-1038 um); chi about 0.59 for 2 mm chips (Colin)
Wall-bed Tscheng: 11.6 (k_b/(R beta)) (n R^2 beta/a)^0.3; argument limit about 1e4 (exceeded for plastic beds: 5e4-5e5)
Gas convection in pyrolysis kilns about 2-10 W/m2K (measured 2.2-4.8; assumed 10)
Emissivities: oxidised steel shell 0.9; 347 SS oxidised 0.87-0.91; pyrolysing coal/char 0.9-1; models 0.8
Mean beam length L_m = 0.95 (D - H); gray-gas error under 20 % if eps_s, eps_w > 0.8
Regenerative depth: about 15 mm in refractory with surface swing up to 75 °C; derived 4-12 mm in a steel shell at 1-6 rpm
Outside: forced h 3-40 W/m2K (1-28 m/s), measured 17 W/m2K at 10.6 m/s; insulation loss about 0.2-0.4 kW/m2 (derived)
Contact time at 15 % fill: 18 s (1 rpm), 6 s (3 rpm), 3 s (6 rpm); half fill angle 54.2°
Literature wall-solid HTC spread: 0.08-185 W/m2K (factor about 2000); models differ by up to 3x on the same data
C_heat.notes:
I resumed after the usage-limit break. I reused the earlier downloads in the scratchpad (dl/, topicC_dl/) and added new reads in tc2/ (J-STAGE Suzuki papers, Beckmann papers, NASA NTRS, Polimeros). The calculation script is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Programacao/381db60a-cc64-54cc-aefe-1e483b5b217d/scratchpad/kilnB/htcalc.py. About 40 tool calls were used.

The short answer: the measured overall wall-to-waste coefficient for an externally heated kiln with plastic-rich waste is 22-55 W/m2K (Suzuki 2008), and the shell heat flux is 11-16.5 kW/m2.

**Spreads and conflicts**
- Covered-wall contact models disagree by up to about 3x on the same data (Herz), and literature compilations span 0.08-185 W/m2K (Debacq via Thammavong).
- In Nafsun's tests, Tscheng was too low for fine powders (animal powder 46 vs measured 65-98) but too high for steel spheres (326 vs 173-259). Wes overpredicts badly at 6 rpm, up to 1079 vs about 270. Li and Schlunder-Mollekopf fit best.
- The Tscheng wall-bed correlation has inconsistent secondary forms. wally gives (n R^2 beta/a)^0.3 with the length scale R beta. Patisson gives Go = omega alpha d^2/(2a). The two differ by a factor of 2 in the argument. Tscheng's stated limit of about 1e4 is far exceeded for low-diffusivity plastic beds.
- Colin prints the Tscheng gas-wall Re exponent as 0.535; Hared, SimCem and wally give 0.575.
- Patisson's natural-convection value of 0.26 W/m2K is printed as such and is implausibly low.
- Beckmann's '4.600 kJ/kg' reaction enthalpy is printed as such.
- Thammavong's own measured h_sp (4-51, with some negative balances) is unreliable.

**Not obtained (paywalled, anti-bot or download failed)**
- Herz et al. 2012 IJHMT/CES correlation constants.
- Schlunder-Mollekopf alpha_WP sub-formula and the exact denominator grouping.
- Gorog 1981 and 1982 originals; Agustini 2006 and Herz OvGU theses (Anubis); Tscheng 1978 UBC thesis (download returned HTML).
- Zhang et al. 2022 CEJ (DEM-CFD of plastic pyrolysis in a rotary furnace); HAL hal-04652254 (molten plastic heating).
- No measured emissivity was found for plastic flakes, PE melt or plastic char, and none for absorption by pyrolysis vapour or soot.
- No measured effective conductivity was found for a plastic-flake bed.
- No measured coefficient for a molten film on a kiln wall was found; the about 1000 W/m2K figure is second-hand and low-confidence.

**Modelling implications (synthesis)**
- **Wall and drive:** At a 450-650 °C wall, model the unlined steel shell as nearly isothermal around the circumference (effusivity about 9100 vs bed about 265). Use one lumped wall node per axial cell, with thermal mass and an axial conduction term. The rpm sensitivity enters through contact time (proportional to n^0.5 in penetration theory, n^0.3 in Tscheng). It saturates once the gas-film term (chi dp/kg) dominates, which happens for coarse flakes.
- **Covered-wall contact:** Use the series model 1/h = chi dp/kg + 1/h_pen.
  - Flakes, contact angle 2 gamma: k_b about 0.08-0.15, chi about 0.1-0.6.
  - Molten pool: k about 0.2, rho about 750, cp about 2600, no gas film.
  - Wall coated by a melt or char film: add k_m/delta.
- **Radiation:** Model radiation from the free wall to the bed chord with Manitius factors or the gray network. Use eps_w about 0.85-0.9, eps_bed about 0.9, and a nearly transparent N2 sweep. Pyrolysis vapours and soot are a non-gray gap, so run a sensitivity case with eps_g from 0 to 0.3.
- **Gas convection:** It is minor, about 2-10 W/m2K. Use the laminar Seghir-Ouali form or Tscheng clipped to its range.
- **Validation targets:**
  - Suzuki: lumped U 22-55 W/m2K, flux 11-16.5 kW/m2, and with lifters 38.6 to 50.1 W/m2K.
  - Nafsun Table 2: expanded clay is the closest analogue to a low-density plastic bed.

**KINTEK claim check**
- Uniform heating and better heat transfer with rotation are supported: penetration theory and the Nafsun, Suzuki and Ma data all show coefficients rising with rpm.
- The magnitude is modest: about +30 % for lifters and about +11 % going from 2.7 to 4 rpm (Suzuki).
- Static vs dynamic heating is supported by the very long conduction times of a static plastic bed (prior Topic H).
- Wall fouling by sticky plastic is a documented risk for externally heated kilns (patent; heat-carrier practice).

D_chem.topic: TOPIC D: plastic pyrolysis chemistry under rotary-kiln conditions (bed 400-650 °C, wall up to about 700 °C). Covers primary kinetics (HDPE/LDPE/PP/PS/PET/PVC and mixtures), isothermal conversion times, heat-up and melting properties, heat of pyrolysis and total energy from 25 °C, product distribution against temperature and vapour residence time (rotary kiln and similar), secondary vapour cracking schemes and gas composition, and contaminants (PVC to HCl, PET, paper). Ends with a recommended primary + secondary scheme for a 1D/3D kiln model.

findings.parameter: Westerhout 1997, Table 4: first-order kinetics (fitted at 70-90% conversion)
findings.units: k0 in s-1; E in kJ/mol; k(703 K) in s-1
findings.context: Isothermal TGA under N2: 400-450 °C for PE and PP, 365-400 °C for PS. Initial Mw: HDPE 125k, LDPE 350k, PP1 250k, PP2 427k, PS 280k. External h to the crucible = 45 ± 6 W/m2K. Runs with sample-to-gas dT > 2 °C were discarded, so no data above 450 °C (PE, PP) or 400 °C (PS). The authors warn that k0 and E are strongly correlated: PP1 and PP2 differ by 56 kJ/mol and 4 decades in k0 but have the same k at 703 K. Reactivity order: HDPE < LDPE < PP < PS
findings.source: Westerhout R.W.J., Waanders J., Kuipers J.A.M., van Swaaij W.P.M., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 36 (1997) 1955-1964, Table 4
findings.evidence: Table 4 and section 5.2 read from the PDF text

findings.parameter: Westerhout 1997, Table 5: random chain dissociation (RCD) model fitted over 10-90% conversion; Table 6: standard case
findings.value: HDPE k0 = 1.3e11, E = 207, k(703 K) = 0.5e-4. LDPE1 9.2e13 / 244 / 0.7e-4. LDPE2 3.5e12 / 225 / 0.7e-4. PP1 8.4e13 / 237 / 2.1e-4. PP2 3.7e10 / 192 / 2.0e-4. PS 1.3e14 / 219 / 69.4e-4. Standard case (Table 6): Nc = 20,000, Lc = 28 (longest chain that can evaporate), normal-bond k1 = 1.3e11 s-1 with E 207 kJ/mol, bond next to a side chain k3 = 8.4e13 s-1 with E 237 kJ/mol, T = 430 °C, beta-scission neglected
findings.units: k0 in s-1 (per bond); E in kJ/mol
findings.context: These are bond-breakage constants, not mass-loss constants. The RCD model fits the whole conversion curve; the first-order model fits only at high conversion. Predicted effect of initial Mw is negligible, and Westerhout also observed this. In the literature review, the Gaussian infinite-parallel-reactions model gives an average E of 208 kJ/mol for PE with A = 1e13 s-1
findings.source: Westerhout et al. 1997, Tables 5 and 6, section 5.3
findings.evidence: Tables 5 and 6 read in full text

findings.parameter: Westerhout 1997: kinetics of mixtures
findings.value: LDPE1/PP2 blends at 25, 50 and 75 wt% PE, pyrolysed at 425 °C, showed no significant change from the pure-polymer kinetics, so mixture kinetics are additive. The authors note that PE and PP rate constants differ by only about 2x at 400-450 °C, which would mask weak interactions
findings.context: Isothermal TGA; blends made in an extruder
findings.source: Westerhout et al. 1997, section 5.4 and abstract
findings.evidence: Section 5.4 text

findings.parameter: Independent reuse of the Westerhout first-order constants and their rates at 460 °C
findings.value: kLit used for the polymer to lumps step: HDPE 1.9e13 s-1 / 220 kJ/mol, LDPE 1.0e15 / 241, PP 3.2e15 / 244. Tabulated k at 460 °C: HDPE 4.02e-3, LDPE 6.76e-3, PP 1.32e-2 s-1
findings.context: Pilot tubular reactor; plastic dissolved in a carrier oil; 67 test runs
findings.source: Lechleitner A.E., Schubert T., Hofer W., Lehner M., 'Lumped Kinetic Modeling of Polypropylene and Polyethylene Co-Pyrolysis in Tubular Reactors', Processes 9 (2021) 34, Tables 3-4
findings.evidence: Tables 3 and 4 read

findings.parameter: Lechleitner 2021 four-lump liquid-phase cracking network (first-order, 6 irreversible reactions)
findings.value: Lumps by true boiling point: Gas (does not condense at 0 °C), Light liquids (IBP-350 °C), Spindle oil (350-410 °C), Residue/wax (410 °C+). Fitted k1..k6 as A [s-1] / E [kJ/mol]. PP: k1 2.0e2 / 80, k2 1.0e5 / 100, k3 5.0e14 / 249. LDPE: k2 1.6e47 / 700. HDPE: k2 1.0e47 / 700, k6 1.0e18 / 300. Carrier fluid: 4.1e15 / 270, 6.1e11 / 208, 4.7e14 / 269, 9.8e15 / 271, 1.8e15 / 271, 3.2e10 / 199. Rates at 460 °C: PP k1 3.99e-4, k2 7.51e-3, k3 8.28e-4; HDPE k2 1.34e-3, k6 4.21e-4 s-1. Mean reaction enthalpy 73.3 kJ/mol (printed with a decimal comma as '73,289 kJ/mol')
findings.context: Liquid phase at about 400-460 °C. The authors call the 700 kJ/mol paths unphysical (oil cracking is normally 50-500 kJ/mol), caused by low light-liquid yields. The text links the lowest E (80 kJ/mol) to wax to spindle oil. The other k-to-path assignments are in Fig. 2, which was not extractable
findings.source: Lechleitner et al., Processes 9 (2021) 34, Table 3, Table 4, section 3
findings.evidence: Table 3 and discussion read; Fig. 2 path map not readable as text

findings.parameter: Isoconversional Ea (Aboulkas 2010) and conflicting solid-state model assignments
findings.value: Aboulkas 2010: HDPE 238-247, LDPE 215-221, PP 179-188 kJ/mol, with R3 (contracting sphere) for PE and R2 (contracting cylinder) for PP. Das and Tiwari (TGA at 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C/min, 30-700 °C, Vyazovkin AIC) assign the opposite: R2 for LDPE/HDPE and R3 for PP
findings.context: Non-isothermal TGA under N2
findings.source: Aboulkas A., El harfi K., El Bouadili A., Energy Convers. Manage. 51 (2010) 1363 (taken from the previous round, abstract level). Das P., Tiwari P., 'Waste plastics: thermal degradation kinetics and lab scale pyrolysis', AIDIC/ISCRE25 extended abstract
findings.evidence: Aboulkas values from the abstract (earlier round). Das and Tiwari extended abstract read in full

findings.parameter: Spread among HDPE mechanisms and other HDPE Ea values
findings.value: Six single- and multi-step HDPE mechanisms disagree by up to a factor of 7 in transient pyrolysis at 650-823 K, although all were fitted to experiments. Isothermal TGA isoconversional Ea: 270-290 kJ/mol (Khedri). Lumped Ea for HDPE in a 2025 study: 222.97 kJ/mol
findings.context: Gascoin: 1 atm. Khedri: isothermal TGA of waste HDPE
findings.source: Gascoin N. et al., 'Kinetic Modelling of HDPE Pyrolysis: Part 1. Comparison of existing models', Polym. Degrad. Stab. (2012), HAL abstract. Khedri S., MSc thesis, Lakehead Univ. (2017), search summary
findings.evidence: HAL API abstract. The HAL full text sits behind an Anubis anti-bot wall, which was not bypassed

findings.parameter: Calibrated random-scission (L = 2) set from the earlier stirred-tank round, for comparison
findings.context: E from Aboulkas 2010 (PS from the literature band). A calibrated by us to consensus DTG peaks. Not an independent literature set
findings.source: Previous research round (scratchpad kin.py), reused
findings.evidence: Derived numerically and cross-checked: the Westerhout PS set gives Tpeak 411 °C and the HDPE set 474 °C at 10 K/min

findings.parameter: Isothermal time to 90% mass conversion (kinetic limit, no heat-transfer limit), at 420 / 450 / 475 / 500 / 550 °C
findings.context: First order: t90 = ln(10)/k. RS-L2: t90 = -ln(1 - sqrt(0.9))/k = 2.97/k. The two literature-anchored sets agree within 10-30% for HDPE in the bed range. Extrapolation above 450 °C goes beyond Westerhout's data window
findings.source: Calculated here from Westerhout 1997 Table 4 and the RS-L2 set
findings.evidence: Python calculation in this session

findings.parameter: Real semi-batch HDPE conversion against temperature (validation case for heat-transfer-limited conversion)
findings.value: 30 min at temperature, thermal: at 450 °C liquid 16.69 ± 1.74, gas 3.23 ± 1.69, unconverted solid 80.09 ± 0.22 wt%. At 500 °C liquid 89.30, gas 10.00, solid 0.7 ± 0.22. At 550 °C liquid 91.63, gas 8.37, solid 0.0. A fitted short-cut model needs about 73 min at 450 °C for full conversion
findings.context: Semi-batch reactor, N2 at 80 cm3/min, vapour residence 1.5-1.7 min. At 450 °C the measured time is about 5x the kinetic t90 (about 15 min), which shows heat-transfer and melt limits. Use this as a bulk-heating validation case
findings.source: Pires da Mata Costa L., 'Modeling plastic pyrolysis: from lumped approaches to detailed mechanistic and volatilization models', DSc thesis, COPPE/UFRJ (Oct 2025), Tables 3.2-3.3, section 3.4
findings.evidence: Tables 3.2 and 3.3 and the text read

findings.parameter: HDPE liquid composition against temperature (thermal; GC-MS area %) at 450 / 500 / 550 °C
findings.value: Paraffins 57.5 / 38.3 / 34.7. Olefins 36.1 / 54.5 / 61.7. Naphthenes 2.4 / 5.7 / 2.4. Aromatics 0.3 / 0.1 / 0. C1-C12 16.9 / 12.2 / 10.0. C13+ 83.1 / 92.5 / 90.0. For contrast, Y-zeolite catalytic runs at 500-550 °C give 48 % aromatics
findings.context: Same semi-batch set; vapour residence 1.5-1.7 min
findings.source: Pires da Mata Costa (2025), Table 3.4
findings.evidence: Table 3.4 read

findings.parameter: Semi-pilot rotary kiln, 500 °C: product yields of mixed plastics and MSW fractions
findings.value: Mixed plastics: pyrolysis oil 43 wt% (highest) and char 16 wt% (lowest). Wastepaper: char 30-40 wt%. Ternary and quaternary blends: up to 37 wt% oil and 18-28 wt% char, with less gas than pure biomass. Literature quoted in the paper: mixed MSW gives 38-56 wt% liquid and 17-25 wt% char
findings.context: Semi-batch rotary kiln at 2 rpm, heated at 20 °C/min to 500 °C and held 90 min, 1 atm, N2. Oil vessel at 200 °C followed by 3 condensers in series. TGA shows main devolatilisation at 230-550 °C. The gas yield of mixed plastics is not stated in the sentences read
findings.source: Bhatt M. et al., 'Co-pyrolysis of mixed municipal solid waste components in a semi-pilot scale rotary kiln...', RSC Advances (2026), doi:10.1039/d6ra02636b
findings.evidence: PMC full text (abstract and methods sentences extracted)

findings.parameter: Industrial rotary kiln pyrolysis: ConTherm plant at Hamm (waste-derived fuel)
findings.value: Kiln effective diameter 2.8 m, heated length 20 m, filling about 15%, mean solids residence in the heated zone about 90 min, process temperature about 500 °C, shell temperature about 750 °C. Capacity 100,000 t/a. Feed LHV 11-28 MJ/kg, moisture 5-50 wt%, ash 3-23 wt%, bulk density 60-250 kg/m3, particle size up to 200 mm. The DSD plastic residue has C 58-73 wt% and H 8-9 wt%
findings.context: Pyrolysis gas is fired directly in a power-plant boiler and the char is co-milled with lignite. Use these as a real kiln anchor: a 500 °C bed with a 750 °C shell
findings.source: DGEngineering, 'Hamm MW Pyrolysis Plant - Integrated Pyrolysis into Power Plant' (July 2009)
findings.evidence: Plant data sheet read

findings.parameter: Commercial Chinese rotary kiln plants for waste plastics or tyres (vendor-reported yields)
findings.value: Kingtiger (continuous, 50 t/d, near-horizontal kiln with catalyst): 45% fuel oil, 40% carbon black, 15% gas. Henan Doing (continuous, 100 t/d): oil 45-52%, carbon black 30%, gas 18-25%. Niutech (continuous, thermal-catalytic): oil 43-48%, carbon black 32-36%, gas 6-8%. Huayin (catalytic batch, 10 t): 45% crude oil, 30% carbon black, 10% gas
findings.context: Vendor claims compiled in a student report. The high 'carbon black' share includes fillers, ash and tyre-derived carbon; pure polyolefins leave almost no char
findings.source: Ma J., Zhong Q. (advisors Themelis N.J., Bourtsalas A.), 'Comparison of Chinese pyrolysis processes', Columbia University / WTERT
findings.evidence: Report text read; the numbers are manufacturer claims

findings.parameter: Proximate analysis of the polymers (fixes the char of clean feed)
findings.context: Compiled table in a review. Column order inferred from the table layout
findings.source: Shah H.H. et al., 'A review on gasification and pyrolysis of waste plastics', Front. Chem. 10 (2023) 960894
findings.evidence: Review table text extracted

findings.parameter: PP-rich waste (face masks plus nitrile gloves): products from 500 to 800 °C
findings.value: Condensable yield peaks at 76.9 wt% at 600 °C; gas rises to 31.0 wt% at 800 °C. H2, CH4 and ethylene dominate the gas. Condensable split at 600 °C: C4-C12 23.7, C13-C20 46.7, C21-C35 12.5, C35+ 17.1 %. Condensable is more than 90% aliphatic. Model-free kinetics: Ea 309.7 ± 2.4 kJ/mol, A 2.5 ± 3.4e25 s-1
findings.context: Heating at 100 °C/min, N2 at 100 mL/min. The feed is a mixture, so the very high Ea/A pair is an outlier for PP
findings.source: Baird R., Ocone R., Sanna A., Molecules 30 (2025) 3351, doi:10.3390/molecules30163351
findings.evidence: PMC abstract text extracted from the downloaded full text

findings.parameter: Vapour-phase secondary cracking of HDPE: temperature and vapour residence time (VRT)
findings.value: At 625 °C and VRT 1.4 s a wide range of gases and liquids form. At 675 °C and VRT 5.6 s the products are mostly hydrocarbon gases plus mono- and polyaromatics. For PE and PP at 550-600 °C and VRT 1.4-5.6 s, the products are mostly alkenes over a broad carbon range. Higher temperature and VRT raise the C2-C4 gas and aromatics. Kulas built a 10-reaction, 6-lump model (plastic, wax, heavy oil, light oil, gas, aromatics) fitted by least squares; its parameter values were not accessible
findings.context: Two-stage micropyrolysis reactor (TSMR) on a commercial micropyrolyser
findings.source: Gracida-Alvarez U. et al., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 57 (2018) 1912-1923. Kulas D.G., Zolghadr A., Shonnard D.R., ACS Sustain. Chem. Eng. 9 (2021) 14443-14450
findings.evidence: Michigan Tech Digital Commons abstracts (records 7803 and 15498); ACS full text not open

findings.parameter: Semi-detailed gas-phase model for PE volatiles (CRECK): structure, a sample rate constant and validation
findings.value: 2 liquid-phase species, 10 liquid-phase reactions, 155 gas species, 3558 gas reactions. Volatile surrogates: C2H4, C3H8, C3H6, C4H6, NC6H12, NC16H32 (diesel cut) and NC30H60 (wax). Example lumped initiation: NC16H32 => C3H5-A + C2H4 + 1.33 NC6H12 + NC3H7, k = 0.8e16 exp(-71000/RT); in CHEMKIN/CRECK units 71,000 cal/mol is about 297 kJ/mol (our reading of the units). At 700 °C, 1-5 isomerisation is about 2x faster than unzipping. H-abstraction by long radicals is about 10-100x slower than unimolecular decay. Validation 1 (Fu et al.): fixed bed at 500 °C, then a second stage at 700-1000 °C (D 0.4 cm, L 40 cm). Ethylene yield peaks at 40-50 wt% and then falls through condensation and dehydrogenation. Validation 2: drop tube with residence 3-4 s (short) and 17-26 s (long). In the condensed-phase model PE decomposes at about 475 °C. Even at a gas temperature above 900 °C, PE stays below 600 °C ('wet-bulb' behaviour)
findings.context: Open access (CC BY). The mechanism is on GitHub (CRECK). It underestimates C2H4 and C3H6 at high temperature for short residence, and CH4 for long residence
findings.source: Locaspi A., Pegurri A., Mehl M., Pelucchi M. et al., Faravelli T., 'A semi-detailed pyrolytic gas-phase kinetic model for the volatiles of polyethylene thermal degradation', Proc. Combust. Inst. 41 (2025) 105912
findings.evidence: Sections 2-4 read

findings.parameter: High-temperature HDPE/PP pyrolysis: gas composition against temperature (wall-side limit)
findings.value: At 700 and 800 °C ethylene is the main product; methane takes over at higher temperatures; acetylene matters at 900-1500 °C. H2 reaches 12.8 wt% at 1600 °C (HDPE contains about 14.2 wt% H). Liquid yield falls and its aromatic share rises as temperature increases
