findings.context: Lab reactor, 700-1600 °C, 1-4 bar, residence time 10 s at 1 bar, argon
findings.source: Pohl V.M., Fonzeu Monguen C.K., Heitlinger D.J., Lott P., Deutschmann O., React. Chem. Eng. (2026), doi:10.1039/d5re00442j
findings.evidence: Text sentences extracted; tables of exact yields at 700-800 °C not extracted

findings.parameter: Two-stage PE gasification: second stage at 800 °C
findings.value: Main gases are ethylene and methane. Optimum space time at 800 °C is 2.6 s; coking is below 1 wt%
findings.context: Two-stage thermal gasification of PE (Hokkaido University)
findings.source: 'Two-Stage Thermal Gasification of Polyethylene', Nippon Kagaku Kaishi (1999)
findings.evidence: Search-engine summary of the abstract

findings.parameter: Flash pyrolysis of HDPE at 1000-1500 K
findings.value: The usual diene / alkene / alkane triplet at each carbon number breaks down at these temperatures through secondary pyrolysis. Pressure up to 3.0 MPa changes the ethylene mass fraction by up to one order of magnitude
findings.context: Heating rates up to 20,000 K/s
findings.source: Gascoin N. et al., J. Anal. Appl. Pyrolysis (2013), HAL hal-00796085
findings.evidence: HAL API abstract

findings.parameter: Heat of pyrolysis by DSC and total heat of gasification from 25 °C
findings.value: Stoliarov and Walters: decomposition PE 920 ± 120, PP 1310 ± 70, PS 1000 ± 90 J/g. Melting: PE 218 ± 18, PP 80 ± 4 J/g. Total from 25 °C: PE 2510 ± 250, PP 2540 ± 190, PS 1800 ± 160 J/g. Older compiled values (Frederick and Mentzer 1975): PE 670, PP 630, PS 820 J/g. Isothermal DSC of waste HDPE at 400-430 °C: 1375 ± 233 kJ/kg (Khedri 2017)
findings.context: Open-pan DSC under N2 (vaporisation included). Spread for HDPE: 670 to 1375 kJ/kg. Gascoin's DSC heat could not be read (HAL anti-bot wall, not bypassed)
findings.source: Stoliarov S.I., Walters R.N., Polym. Degrad. Stab. 93 (2008) 422, and FAA DOT/FAA/AR-TN07/62. Khedri S., MSc thesis, Lakehead Univ. 2017
findings.evidence: Stoliarov values from the previous round (search-engine extract; FAA PDF blocked again by an edge error). Khedri from the thesis abstract

findings.parameter: Total energy to take each polymer from 25 °C to fully converted at 480 °C
findings.value: HDPE about 2.28, LDPE about 2.22, PP about 2.49, PS about 1.87 MJ/kg. Stoliarov's measured totals (PE 2.51, PP 2.54, PS 1.80 MJ/kg) agree within about 10%
findings.source: Derived here; property ranges from the rows below and Stoliarov and Walters
findings.evidence: Arithmetic in this session

findings.parameter: Solid and melt properties for a heat-up/melting model
findings.value: HDPE: melting 125-135 °C, melting enthalpy 293 J/g (probably the 100%-crystalline reference), cp 1.8-2.7 J/gK, k 0.33-0.53 W/mK, density 0.94-0.96 g/cm3 (NETZSCH). A PMC table gives HDPE 950 kg/m3, 2300 J/kgK, 0.45 W/mK and LDPE 920 kg/m3, 3400 J/kgK, 0.34 W/mK. A materials database gives LDPE 2300 J/kgK, 0.36 W/mK, and PS 1250-1400 J/kgK, 0.14-0.22 W/mK. Hot-wire measurements of k and cp for HDPE, LDPE, PP, PS and HIPS up to Tm + 50 °C exist only as figures
findings.context: LDPE cp disagrees between sources (2300 vs 3400 J/kgK). Use measured DSC melting heats for real crystallinity (PE 218, PP 80 J/g)
findings.source: NETZSCH PE-HD datasheet; PMC11336857 Table 3; MakeItFrom; Polímeros (2005) hot-wire study (SciELO)
findings.evidence: Search-engine summaries. The NETZSCH page is JavaScript-rendered and the Polímeros values are only in figures

findings.parameter: Bulk density of feed forms
findings.value: Washed PET bottle flake 250 kg/m3 (400 in parentheses on the datasheet). Post-consumer HDPE regrind 320 kg/m3 (ISO 60). Post-industrial HDPE pipe regrind about 500 kg/m3. PP regrind 300-400 kg/m3. Virgin PET pellets 50 lb/ft3 (about 800 kg/m3); PET sheet regrind 10 lb/ft3 (about 160 kg/m3). RDF or plastic-residue fluff at Hamm: 60-250 kg/m3. Rotary kiln tracer study: plastic pellets 610 kg/m3 bulk, 978 kg/m3 apparent, porosity 0.38, angle of repose 45°
findings.context: ISO 60 is the standard method. Film and fluff are 3-5x less dense than flakes or pellets, which sets the kiln fill degree
findings.source: Plasgran TDS (Knowde); plasticker Recybase datasheets; Conair table; DGEngineering Hamm 2009; Jaworski T. et al., Sensors 23 (2023) 6526
findings.evidence: Hamm and Jaworski read in full text; the vendor datasheets are search summaries

findings.parameter: PVC two-stage pyrolysis kinetics (contaminant, the HCl source)
findings.value: Stage I (dehydrochlorination, 490-675 K): Ea 75 kJ/mol, A 1.81e6 min-1, P2 model. Stage II (dechlorinated residue, 675-825 K): Ea 140 kJ/mol, A 4.84e9 min-1, F3 model. Literature cited there: stage I 523-623 K and stage II 623-798 K; at high heating rate stage I Ea 48.6 / 48.1 / 49.8 kJ/mol (FWO / KAS / Friedman); other pairs 190 / 250 kJ/mol. NREL (Wu et al. 2024): apparent E 116.7 kJ/mol (autocatalytic dehydrochlorination, HCl and benzene the main products) and 230.6 kJ/mol (residue). Other values: 133.8 kJ/mol with near-complete dechlorination by 340 °C, and 119.8 ± 12.4 kJ/mol
findings.context: TGA at 5, 10 and 20 K/min (Polymers 2021). Stage-I Ea spans about 49-190 kJ/mol across methods. Theoretical HCl = 36.46/62.50 = 58.3 wt% of PVC (stoichiometry). PVC fixed carbon is 5-6 wt%
findings.source: 'Pyrolytic Behavior of Polyvinyl Chloride: Kinetics, Mechanisms, Thermodynamics, and Artificial Neural Network Application', Polymers (2021), PMC8706959 (authors not checked here). Wu et al., ACS Sustain. Chem. Eng. 2024 (NREL record; AIChE 2022 abstract)
findings.evidence: PMC abstract and introduction read. NREL values from search summaries

findings.parameter: PET and paper/cellulose co-feed behaviour
findings.value: PET: Ea 204-220 kJ/mol; DTG peak 680 K at 2 K/min; about 80% mass loss in the main step with about 20% residue (Dubdub and Al-Yaari 2023). Volatiles are oxygenated: CO, CO2, acetaldehyde, benzoic acid and terephthalic acid; the last two sublime and foul condensers (earlier round, unverified). Paper: in the 500 °C rotary kiln, wastepaper leaves 30-40 wt% char. Paper-mill waste char falls from about 48 wt% at 450 °C to 24 wt% at 650 °C, with CO, CO2, CH4 and H2 from decarboxylation and decarbonylation. Biomass oils carry 15-50 wt% water and 35-40 wt% O (HHV 15-26 MJ/kg) against 29-43 MJ/kg for plastic oil
findings.context: PET, PVC and paper move O and Cl into the oil and gas; the oil phase separates into an aqueous phase
findings.source: Dubdub I., Al-Yaari M., Polymers 15 (2023) 3010. Bhatt M. et al., RSC Adv. (2026) PMC13329883. Bhatt M. et al., RSC Adv. (2026) doi:10.1039/d5ra08655h, PMC12927709
findings.evidence: Paper data from PMC full text; PET from the earlier round (secondary)

findings.parameter: Other lumped/detailed polyolefin models found but not readable here
findings.value: Al-Salem and Lettieri 2010 (HDPE; lumps C1-C4 gas, C5-C10 non-aromatic liquid, aromatics, C11+ wax, char). Locaspi et al., Waste Manage. 156 (2023) 107-117 (semi-detailed; liquid-phase 74 species for PE, 126 for PP). Reduced-order condensed-phase models for PE, PP and PS (Chem. Eng. J. 2024, multi-step fully lumped). Ranzi et al. 1997; Levine and Broadbelt 2009; Westerhout 1998 PhD thesis (Twente); Kulas 2021; Mastalski 2023 UMN thesis. Westerhout 1998 is a thesis record only; Ding et al. could not be identified
findings.context: Paywalled, embargoed or not located. Locaspi 2023 SI read: HMW functional groups at NC = 21; LLMW C15, C21, C30, C39. Leaving out evaporation of C30-C39 shifts the mass-loss curve about +10 °C
findings.source: Locaspi A., Pelucchi M., Mehl M., Faravelli T., Waste Manage. 156 (2023) 107, Supplementary Material
findings.evidence: SI read; main texts restricted

findings.parameter: Rough vapour residence time in an industrial kiln freeboard
findings.value: About 20-35 s at Hamm scale
findings.context: Freeboard about 105 m3 (D 2.8 m, L 20 m, 85% free). Assumed: about 12.5 t/h feed (100,000 t/a over 8000 h), about 70% volatiles, mean M about 50 g/mol, 500 °C; steam from 20% feed moisture lowers it to about 19 s. Tens of seconds at 500-550 °C makes wax cracking marginal in the bulk freeboard, but vapour in contact with a 650-700 °C wall cracks within seconds
findings.source: Derived here from the Hamm plant data
findings.evidence: Arithmetic with stated assumptions

findings.parameter: RECOMMENDED primary + secondary scheme for the kiln model (summary; full list in notes)
findings.value: Bed (melt): HDPE, LDPE, PP and PS use random scission L = 2 or the Westerhout first-order set (HDPE t90 about 15 min at 450 °C for both). PET first order (E 210, A 2.59e13 s-1, char 0.15). PVC two-stage (75 kJ/mol, A 3.0e4 s-1, P2, gives 0.583 HCl; then 140 kJ/mol, A 8.1e7 s-1, F3). Volatile split at 500-550 °C for polyolefins: G 0.10 / O(C5-C20) 0.55 / W(C21+) 0.35. Freeboard: W -> O with k_W = 3 k_O; O -> (1 - phi_A) G + phi_A A. Option B (preferred): k_O = 1.0e16 exp(-300 kJ/mol / RT). Option A: k_O = 1.3e12 exp(-230 / RT)
findings.context: Option B is consistent with no gas rise between 500 and 550 °C at about 96 s VRT (Pires), mostly gas at 675 °C and 5.6 s (Gracida-Alvarez), and the CRECK allylic initiation (0.8e16, 297 kJ/mol). Option A overpredicts gas at 550 °C
findings.source: Derived here from the sources above
findings.evidence: Consistency checks computed in this session

equations.name: Westerhout power-law (first-order) model
equations.expression: dxi/dt = k0 exp(-Eact/RT) (1 - xi)^n, with n = 1 at high conversion
equations.variables: xi = mass conversion; k0 = pre-exponential factor [s-1]; Eact [kJ/mol]; T [K]
equations.validity: Isothermal TGA at 400-450 °C (PE, PP) and 365-400 °C (PS); fitted at 70-90% conversion
equations.source: Westerhout et al. 1997, eq 2 and Table 4

equations.name: Random scission with L = 2 (CFD sink form)
equations.expression: dx/dt = k(1 - x); alpha = x^2; dY_P/dt = -[2 k x/(1 + x)] Y_P; general L: alpha = 1 - (1 - x)^(L-1) [1 + (L - 1) x]
equations.variables: x = fraction of bonds broken; alpha = mass conversion; Y_P = polymer mass fraction; k = A exp(-E/RT)
equations.validity: DPn0 >> L; TGA range about 350-550 °C
equations.source: Sanchez-Jimenez et al., J. Phys. Chem. A 114 (2010); Westerhout RCD concept

equations.name: Isothermal time to 90% conversion
equations.expression: First order: t90 = ln(10)/k. RS-L2: t90 = -ln(1 - sqrt(0.9))/k = 2.97/k
equations.variables: k in s-1 at bed temperature
equations.validity: Kinetic limit only; real kilns are heat-transfer limited (450 °C semi-batch needed about 73 min against a kinetic t90 of about 15 min)
equations.source: Derived

equations.name: Four-lump liquid-phase cracking network (TBP lumps)
equations.expression: dw_j/dt = sum_i k_ij w_i - sum_m k_jm w_j, with k = A exp(-EA/RT) and first-order irreversible steps among Residue (410 °C+), Spindle oil (350-410 °C), Light liquids (IBP-350 °C) and Gas
equations.variables: w = lump mass fractions; 6 rate constants k1..k6
equations.validity: Tubular liquid-phase reactor at about 400-460 °C
equations.source: Lechleitner et al., Processes 9 (2021) 34, eq 1 and Table 3

equations.name: Recommended lumped freeboard secondary cracking
equations.expression: dW/dt = -k_W W; dO/dt = k_W W - k_O O; dG/dt = (1 - phi_A) k_O O; dA/dt = phi_A k_O O. Option B: k_O = 1.0e16 exp(-300000/RT) s-1, k_W = 3 k_O. Option A: k_O = 1.3e12 exp(-230000/RT), k_W = 3.9e12 exp(-230000/RT). phi_A = 0 at T <= 600 °C, rising linearly to about 0.3 at 700 °C (calibration knob)
equations.variables: W = wax (C21+), O = oil (C5-C20), G = gas (C1-C4), A = aromatics (mass concentrations in the vapour); R = 8.314 J/molK
equations.validity: Dilute vapour at 1 atm, 450-750 °C. Unverified: calibrate against one TSMR / two-stage dataset
equations.source: Derived here; anchors Pires 2025, Gracida-Alvarez 2018, Locaspi 2025 (PCI)

equations.name: CRECK lumped initiation of a diesel-cut surrogate
equations.variables: E in cal/mol (CHEMKIN convention, about 297 kJ/mol); k in s-1
equations.validity: Gas-phase pyrolysis at about 600-1000 °C, 1 atm
equations.source: Locaspi et al., Proc. Combust. Inst. 41 (2025) 105912

equations.name: Degrading polymer particle energy balance (wet-bulb form)
equations.expression: (sum_i w_i cp,L,i) dT_L/dt = a [h (T_ext - T_L) + sigma eps (T_ext^4 - T_L^4)] - sum_j r_L,j dh_r,j
equations.variables: w_i = mass fractions; cp,L = liquid cp; a = surface/volume; eps = polymer emissivity; T_ext = gas temperature; r_L,j and dh_r,j = rates and enthalpies of the liquid reactions
equations.validity: Lab reactors. Predicts T_PE < 600 °C even for T_ext > 900 °C. The convective term is inferred from the variable list
equations.source: Locaspi et al. 2025, eq 1

equations.name: PVC two-stage kinetics
equations.expression: Stage I: da1/dt = A1 exp(-E1/RT) 2 a1^(1/2) (P2), E1 = 75 kJ/mol, A1 = 1.81e6 min-1, giving HCl 0.583 kg per kg PVC. Stage II: da2/dt = A2 exp(-E2/RT) (1 - a2)^3 (F3), E2 = 140 kJ/mol, A2 = 4.84e9 min-1
equations.variables: a = stage conversion; T [K]
equations.validity: TGA at 5-20 K/min, 490-825 K. Stage-I E ranges 49-190 kJ/mol in the literature
equations.source: Polymers 2021, PMC8706959; HCl stoichiometry derived

equations.name: Total conversion energy from 25 °C
equations.expression: Q = cp,s (Tm - T0) + dHf + cp,l (Tr - Tm) + dH_pyr (+ product superheat)
equations.variables: cp,s and cp,l = solid and melt heat capacity; dHf = measured melting enthalpy; dH_pyr = DSC heat of decomposition
equations.validity: Gives about 1.9-2.5 MJ/kg for 480 °C; Stoliarov measured 1.8-2.54 MJ/kg
equations.source: Derived; Stoliarov and Walters 2008

key_sources.citation: Westerhout R.W.J., Waanders J., Kuipers J.A.M., van Swaaij W.P.M., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 36 (1997) 1955-1964
key_sources.why: Read in full: first-order and RCD kinetics for HDPE/LDPE/PP/PS (Tables 4-6) and proof that blends follow additive kinetics

key_sources.citation: Locaspi A. et al., Faravelli T., Proc. Combust. Inst. 41 (2025) 105912 (open access)
key_sources.why: Semi-detailed gas-phase secondary cracking of PE volatiles (CRECK). Two-stage and drop-tube validation; ethylene peaks at 40-50 wt%; polymer stays below 600 °C at high wall temperature

key_sources.citation: Pires da Mata Costa L., DSc thesis, COPPE/UFRJ (2025)
key_sources.why: Measured HDPE yields and liquid PIONA / carbon-number split at 450-550 °C with a known vapour residence; 73 min needed at 450 °C

key_sources.citation: Lechleitner A.E. et al., Processes 9 (2021) 34
key_sources.why: Four-lump TBP cracking network with fitted A/E for PP, LDPE and HDPE; reuses the Westerhout constants independently

key_sources.citation: Bhatt M. et al., RSC Advances (2026), semi-pilot rotary kiln co-pyrolysis
key_sources.why: Only rotary kiln dataset found with mixed plastics at 500 °C: oil 43 wt%, char 16 wt%; wastepaper char 30-40 wt%

key_sources.citation: DGEngineering, Hamm ConTherm rotary kiln pyrolysis plant (2009)
key_sources.why: Industrial kiln conditions: 500 °C process, 750 °C shell, 90 min, 15% fill, feed bulk density 60-250 kg/m3

key_sources.citation: Pohl V.M. et al., Deutschmann O., React. Chem. Eng. (2026) d5re00442j
key_sources.why: Gas composition against temperature for HDPE/PP at 700-1600 °C (wall-side limit)

key_sources.citation: Pyrolytic Behavior of PVC: Kinetics, Mechanisms, Thermodynamics and ANN, Polymers (2021)
key_sources.why: Two-stage PVC kinetics plus a literature spread for dehydrochlorination Ea

key_sources.citation: Gracida-Alvarez U. et al., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 57 (2018) 1912; Kulas D.G. et al., ACS Sustain. Chem. Eng. 9 (2021) 14443
key_sources.why: Effect of temperature and vapour residence time on secondary cracking (550-675 °C, 1.4-5.6 s); 6-lump scheme (abstract only)

key_sources.citation: Ma J., Zhong Q., Comparison of Chinese pyrolysis processes (Columbia/WTERT)
key_sources.why: Vendor oil / carbon-black / gas yields from commercial rotary kiln plastic pyrolysis plants

critical_numbers: Westerhout first order (70-90% conv.): HDPE 1.9e13 s-1 / 220 kJ/mol; LDPE 1.0e15 / 241; PP 3.2e15 / 244; PS 3.3e13 / 204
Westerhout RCD: HDPE 1.3e11 / 207; PP1 8.4e13 / 237; PS 1.3e14 / 219 (per bond, s-1 / kJ/mol); Lc = 28 at 430 °C
Westerhout LDPE/PP blends at 425 °C: no interaction (additive)
HDPE t90 (kinetic) = 77 / 15.7 / 4.6 / 1.5 / 0.19 min at 420 / 450 / 475 / 500 / 550 °C (Westerhout first order)
HDPE semi-batch, 30 min: 80% unconverted at 450 °C; at 500 °C liquid 89.3 / gas 10.0 wt%; at 550 °C 91.6 / 8.4 wt%; VRT 1.5-1.7 min
HDPE oil olefin share 36 to 62 area% from 450 to 550 °C; aromatics at most 0.3%; C13+ 83-92%
Rotary kiln at 500 °C (semi-pilot): mixed plastics oil 43 wt%, char 16 wt%; paper char 30-40 wt%
Hamm industrial kiln: 500 °C process, 750 °C shell, 90 min solids residence, 15% fill, D 2.8 m x L 20 m
Chinese rotary kiln plants (claims): oil 43-52%, carbon black 30-40%, gas 6-25%
Second stage at 700-1000 °C: ethylene peaks at 40-50 wt%; at 700-800 °C ethylene is the main gas; CH4 dominates above
PE particle stays below 600 °C even at a gas temperature above 900 °C (wet-bulb)
Heat of decomposition: PE 920 ± 120, PP 1310 ± 70, PS 1000 ± 90 kJ/kg (spread for HDPE 670-1375)
Total heat from 25 °C: PE 2.51, PP 2.54, PS 1.80 MJ/kg (DSC); derived 1.9-2.5 MJ/kg
PVC: stage I 75 kJ/mol (490-675 K), stage II 140 kJ/mol (675-825 K); HCl 58.3 wt% of PVC; stage-I Ea spread 49-190

D_chem.notes:
I picked up the earlier round's work and the files already in the scratchpad, then added new open full texts: Westerhout 1997, Lechleitner 2021, Pires 2025, Locaspi 2025 (PCI), the KIT 2026 paper, the PVC paper (Polymers 2021), the Bhatt rotary kiln paper, the Hamm plant sheet and the WTERT report. Full texts I could not read: HAL (Gascoin) sits behind an Anubis anti-bot challenge, which I did not bypass. The FAA Stoliarov report returned an edge error. The Polimi Elsevier versions are restricted, as are ACS (Kulas, Gracida-Alvarez) and Elsevier (Al-Salem and Lettieri 2010, Ranzi 1997, Levine and Broadbelt 2009, Mastral 2002, Williams 1999). I could not identify 'Ding et al.'. mdpi-res.com serves MDPI PDFs that mdpi.com blocks. Working files are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Programacao/381db60a-cc64-54cc-aefe-1e483b5b217d/scratchpad/tD2 and the fetch script is tDs/get.sh.

RECOMMENDED SCHEME (1D/3D kiln).

(1) PRIMARY, in the bed or melt:
- HDPE, LDPE, PP and PS: random scission with L = 2, using the calibrated set (HDPE 238 kJ/mol / 5.2e14; LDPE 215 / 1.92e13; PP 179 / 6.98e10; PS 180 / 4.1e11). As a literature-only alternative, use Westerhout's first-order set (HDPE 1.9e13 / 220; LDPE 1.0e15 / 241; PP 3.2e15 / 244; PS 3.3e13 / 204). Both give HDPE t90 of about 15 min at 450 °C and about 1.2-1.5 min at 500 °C. Treat blends as additive (Westerhout); an optional PS-to-PE acceleration factor exp(gamma w_PS) with gamma 0-1 can be added.
- PET: first order, E 210 kJ/mol, A 2.59e13 s-1. Char 0.15 (0.10-0.20); volatiles are oxygenated and include sublimates.
- PVC: stage I 75 kJ/mol, A 3.0e4 s-1, P2 model, releasing 0.583 kg HCl per kg PVC. Stage II 140 kJ/mol, A 8.1e7 s-1, F3 model, releasing aromatics/benzene and leaving about 0.06 char.
- Paper/cellulose: treat it as biomass. About 0.3-0.4 char at 500 °C in a kiln, with water, CO, CO2, CH4 and H2.
- Primary volatile split for polyolefins at 450-550 °C (calibration knob): G 0.10, O 0.55, W 0.35. This rests on Pires (gas 8-10 wt%, C13+ about 90% of the liquid) and Baird (at 600 °C: C4-C12 24, C13-C20 47, C21+ 30% of the condensable). PS gives mostly styrene (about 0.65, unverified).

(2) ENERGY:
- Melting enthalpy (DSC): PE 218 J/g, PP 80 J/g; PS has none (Tg about 100 °C).
- Heat of decomposition: PE 0.92, PP 1.31, PS 1.0 MJ/kg; PET about 0.3-0.5 (unverified); PVC dehydrochlorination about 0.3-0.5 (not found; unverified).
- Total from 25 °C is about 1.8-2.5 MJ/kg.
- Under a 700-750 °C shell the bed sits near 450-500 °C because pyrolysis is endothermic (Hamm runs a 500 °C process under a 750 °C shell; Locaspi reports polymer < 600 °C).

(3) SECONDARY, in the freeboard gas: W -> O -> (1 - phi_A) G + phi_A A, first order, with k_W = 3 k_O.
- Preferred Option B: k_O = 1.0e16 exp(-300 kJ/mol / RT). It is consistent with three anchors: no gas increase between 500 and 550 °C at about 96 s VRT (Pires); mostly gas plus aromatics at 675 °C / 5.6 s (Gracida-Alvarez); and the CRECK allylic-initiation constant (0.8e16, about 297 kJ/mol).
- Option A from the earlier round (1.3e12 exp(-230 / RT)) predicts 27% oil-to-gas at 550 °C / 96 s, which contradicts Pires.
- Gas speciation lumps by temperature:
  - Up to 550 °C: C3-C4 olefins with some C2H4 and little CH4/H2 (qualitative; Kulas: mostly alkenes).
  - 650-800 °C: C2H4 dominant, rising toward 40-50 wt% of products, with CH4 increasing.
  - Above 850 °C: CH4, H2, C2H2 and soot. Coke stays below 1 wt% at 800 °C / 2.6 s.
- For detailed speciation, couple the open CRECK PE gas mechanism (155 species) in post-processing.

(4) KILN-SPECIFIC USE: Bulk freeboard residence is tens of seconds at about 500-550 °C, so wax cracking stays modest. Near-wall vapour at 650-700 °C cracks in seconds (k_O 0.1-0.8 s-1), which is the mechanism behind the KINTEK claim that fast vapour removal reduces secondary cracking. Report the oil/gas ratio against wall temperature and gas sweep rate.

SPREADS AND CAVEATS:
- HDPE Ea ranges 207-290 kJ/mol and mechanisms disagree by up to 7x (Gascoin).
- The R2/R3 model assignment is reversed between Aboulkas and Das and Tiwari.
- PVC stage-I Ea ranges 49-190 kJ/mol.
- HDPE heat of decomposition ranges 670-1375 kJ/kg.
- LDPE cp is quoted as 2300 or 3400 J/kgK.
- Industrial 'carbon black' yields of 30-40% reflect fillers, ash and tyres, not polyolefin chemistry; clean polyolefins have fixed carbon of about 0-1.2 wt%.
- The secondary-cracking A and E values are calibrated by us, not literature values; present them as such and calibrate against the Kulas or Gracida-Alvarez TSMR data if the full text becomes available.

E_model.topic: TOPIC E: gas phase and freeboard, plus modelling approaches for rotary kiln pyrolysis of plastic waste. Covers sweep gas, vapour residence time, published kiln models, feasibility on one T4 GPU in Colab, and a recommended architecture for a validated demonstrator.

findings.parameter: Benchmark lab rotary furnace for plastic pyrolysis (Zhang et al. 2020 FPT 206:106455 experiments; Zhang et al. 2022 CEJ 445:136686 CFD-DEM): geometry and operating point
findings.value: Drum ID 300 mm, width 65 mm. Wall 773 K. 6 rpm. N2 sweep 350 ± 10 mL/min. Particles injected at 303 K (LDPE, d = 2.5 mm, 2000 particles/s for 1 s). Validation paper ran 300 s of physical time.
findings.context: These are the setup values the Lund thesis copied from Zhang et al. to rebuild the case in Star-CCM+. Both Zhang papers are paywalled, so the numbers are second-hand.
findings.source: Belcher E.C. (2026) MSc thesis, Lund University, 'CFD-DEM simulation for Advanced Chemical Recycling of Mixed Plastic Waste', Sect. 4.1
findings.evidence: Thesis Sect. 4.1: 'internal drum diameter was set to 300 mm and width to 65 mm'; '773 K ... wall relative rotation of 6 rpm'; 'volume flow rate of 350 ± 10 ml/min given by Zhang et al. [77]'

findings.parameter: Zhang et al. 2022 CEJ: CFD-DEM findings without a reaction model (heat carrier loading, rotation speed, volatile residence time)
findings.value: Adding granular heat carriers greatly increases the heating rate of plastic particles. Higher heat-carrier loading also increases the residence time of pyrolysis volatiles. Faster rotation raises particle translational and angular velocities, but the heat-transfer gain is 'not obvious', which matches the small change in experimental product yields.
findings.context: This is the only peer-reviewed CFD-DEM study found of a plastic-waste rotary furnace. Authors: Zhang M., Zhang Y., Ma D., Li A., Fu W., Ji G., Dong J. No pyrolysis reaction model was included.
findings.source: Zhang M. et al. (2022) Chem. Eng. J. 445:136686, doi:10.1016/j.cej.2022.136686 (abstract from RMIT figshare record)
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'The increase in the heat carrier loading also increased the residence time of the pyrolysis volatiles... With the acceleration of the rolling speed... the improvement of heat transfer efficiency is not obvious.'

findings.parameter: Commercial CFD-DEM cost for this benchmark (Star-CCM+ 2506)
findings.value: About 2000 particles. Drum meshes of 66,324, 113,503 and 448,130 cells (base size 7.5, 5 and 2.5 mm) took 21.6, 32.5 and 46.2 h of solver time for 15 s of physical time, on 64 cores of one node.
findings.context: Star-CCM+ recommends about 1 core per 1500 DEM particles, and the run was only stable on a single node. Radiation was omitted. Time step was 0.005–0.015 s while particles fell and 0.25–0.75 s while they rolled (implicit unsteady solver, SIMPLE).
findings.source: Belcher (2026) Lund MSc thesis, Table 5.1 and Sect. 6
findings.evidence: Table 5.1: 'Total solver elapsed time 21.6 hours 32.5 hours 46.2 hours'; 'number of DEM particles by 1500'; 'physical time simulated for the mesh sensitivity was set to 15 s'

findings.parameter: Lund CFD-DEM: accuracy problems and lessons
findings.value: At 100 s the mean particle temperature was about 540 K (thesis case 1.0) against about 600 K in Zhang 2022, a 60 K gap. One-way coupling heated particles 'unreasonably fast', so two-way thermal coupling is required. The default limit of 20,000 DEM sub-steps was hit for all particles, and cutting it to 1000 gave 'completely inaccurate' results.
findings.context: These are pitfalls to avoid in our own solver. The freeboard gas must lose the heat the particles gain, and the contact time step must be properly resolved.
findings.source: Belcher (2026) Lund MSc thesis, Sect. 6 Discussion
findings.evidence: 'At time step 100 s, the average particle temperature measured approximately 540 K for case 1.0 and 600 K for the validation paper'; 'one-way coupling heating the particles unreasonably fast'

findings.parameter: Vapour residence time vs N2 flow and HDPE wax yield (fixed bed, Abdy et al. 2023, J. Cleaner Prod. 405)
findings.value: Vapour residence time (VRT) at 2 / 4 L/min N2: 3.76 / 1.88 s at 450 °C, 3.52 / 1.76 s at 500 °C, 3.30 / 1.65 s at 550 °C. Wax yield was 75.73–79.46 wt% at 450 °C, 91.87 wt% maximum at 500 °C with 4 L/min (1.76 s), and 86.53–87.86 wt% at 550 °C.
findings.context: Reactor tube 50.8 mm ID × 150 mm. 25 g HDPE plus 20 g metal balls. Condenser at 5 °C. VRT is computed from the N2 flow only (ideal gas), and I reproduced it: V = 3.04e-4 m3 gives 1.73 s at 500 °C and 4 L/min. Nitrogen was not preheated, which cooled the bed at 450 °C. The authors say temperature affected yields more than VRT.
findings.source: Abdy C., Zhang Y., Wang J. et al. (2023) 'Investigation of high density polyethylene pyrolyzed wax for asphalt binder modification', J. Cleaner Production 405 (Aston AAM), Table 1 and Sect. 3.1
findings.evidence: Table 1 lists VRT values; text: 'wax yield increases with temperature from 75.73-79.46 wt% at 450 °C to 86.53-87.86 wt% at 550 °C... 91.87 wt% at 500 °C'

findings.parameter: Gas-phase secondary cracking at short residence times (polyolefin vapours)
findings.value: Less than 30% compositional change at 750 °C within a gas residence time of 4 s (van Wyk et al. 2026, Fuel 407:137561). Li et al. therefore neglected gas-phase reactions at about 500 °C with 2–4 s gas residence time.
findings.context: Fluidized bed data. In a rotary kiln the vapour residence time is minutes (see the derived estimate below), so gas-phase cracking cannot be dismissed by the same argument unless the freeboard is kept cool.
findings.source: Li M., Zhang F., et al. (2026) Particuology 115:214–227, 'Numerical simulation of plastic pyrolysis in fluidized bed reactors under continuous and batch-wise feeding', Sect. 2.1 (citing van Wyk et al. 2026)
findings.evidence: 'neglected here because the gas residence time is much shorter than the characteristic timescale of gas-phase reactions at around 500 °C (for reference, less than a 30 % compositional change occurs at 750 °C within a gas residence time of 4 s (van Wyk et al., 2026))'

findings.parameter: Five-lump PP pyrolysis kinetics (Lechleitner et al. 2020, as used by Li et al. 2026)
findings.value: PP→Wax: A = 3.2e15 1/s, Ea = 244 kJ/mol. W→HF: A = 2.0e2, Ea = 80. W→LF: A = 1.0e5, Ea = 100. W→G: A = 5.0e14, Ea = 249. Overall apparent enthalpy 542 kJ/kg (DSC, Netsch et al. 2024). At 505 °C the model gives LF 67.4, G 29.6 and HF 3 wt%.
findings.context: The wax intermediate stays in the particle (melt) phase, and HF/LF/G are released to the gas at once. This gives a ready wax→oil→gas lumping for the melt pool in the kiln. My derived rate constants at 500 °C: PP→W 0.105 1/s, W→LF 0.0175 1/s, W→G 0.0075 1/s, W→HF 7.9e-4 1/s.
findings.source: Li et al. (2026) Particuology 115, Table 2; original Lechleitner A.E. et al. (2020) Processes 9(1):34

findings.parameter: Validity of the lumped (Lagrangian) particle temperature for plastic pyrolysis
findings.value: Applicable only for particle diameter below 2 mm. Above 4 mm the core and surface differ by more than 10 K and lumped models predict much slower conversion than particle-resolved ones.
findings.context: Particle-resolved simulation of an HDPE particle in hot N2. Kiln feed (flakes, pellets of 3–10 mm) therefore needs a 1D internal conduction or shrinking-core model per parcel, or at least a Biot-number correction.
findings.source: Zhang F., Tavakkol S., Galeazzo F.C.C., et al. 'Particle-resolved simulation of the pyrolysis process of a single plastic particle' (Heat and Mass Transfer, 2025), KITopen
findings.evidence: 'For particle diameters larger than 4 mm, distinct temperature gradients... more than 10 K'; 'the Lagrangian approach... is only applicable for particle diameters smaller than 2 mm'

findings.parameter: Cost of 3D Euler-Lagrange simulation of a plastic-pyrolysis reactor (KIT, OpenFOAM-based)
findings.value: Simulating the full 3D fluidized bed for only a few seconds of flow can take about one day (Zhang et al. 2024). The authors fell back to a single-cell-layer quasi-2D slice with 4 mm cubic cells and about 480,000 sand particles at 4 particles per parcel.
findings.context: This is independent evidence that 3D CFD-DEM of a full pyrolysis reactor is far beyond a 10–60 min Colab budget. Slicing and parcels are the standard workaround.
findings.source: Li et al. (2026) Particuology 115, Sect. 3.1
findings.evidence: 'simulating the full three-dimensional FBR for only a few seconds of fluid-dynamic behavior can require about one day of simulation time (Zhang et al., 2024)'; 'single-cell-layer thin slice'

findings.parameter: Barr 1986 pilot kiln (basis of Barr, Brimacombe & Watkinson 1989 Metall. Trans. B, Parts I and II): size and heat-transfer results
findings.value: 0.406 m ID × 5.5 m refractory-lined, natural-gas-fired pilot kiln, 23 trials, bed in rolling mode. Covered wall→covered bed heat transfer was below 30% of the freeboard→exposed bed rate (instrumented section 1.32–5.0 m). Freeboard gas→surface radiative coefficient 15–55 W/m2K for gas at 800–1800 K (10% excess air), about 3× higher for a 4 m ID prototype. Freeboard convection about 2–3 W/m2K at Re ≈ 2000 (under 10% of wall flux above 700 K).
findings.context: The 1989 papers (doi 10.1007/BF02696991 and 10.1007/BF02696992, 'Part II. Development of the cross-section model') are closed access. Content was read from Barr's 1986 UBC PhD thesis full text through the UBC Open Collections API. Barr's model is a 1D axial model with a cross-section (refractory plus bed) finite-difference sub-model.
findings.source: Barr P.V. (1986) 'Heat transfer processes in rotary kilns', PhD thesis, UBC
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'Q_cw→cb, was < 30% of the rate to exposed bed surface'; 'radiative heat transfer ... range from 15 → 55 W/m²K for gas temperatures from 800 → 1800 K'; body: 'At Re = 2000, representative of the pilot kiln trials, values of h ~ 2-3 W/m²K'

findings.parameter: Boateng 1993 quasi-3D kiln model (basis of Boateng & Barr 1996 IJHMT 39(10):2131–2147)
findings.value: A 2D transverse-plane bed model (active-layer granular flow reduced to Prandtl boundary-layer equations, plus advection–conduction energy) embedded in a 1D axial plug-flow kiln model. Validated on the 0.41 m × 5.5 m pilot kiln. The bed is turned over about 3 times per revolution, so transverse Péclet numbers are large and advection dominates conduction. A stationary kiln shows radial bed gradients that the model reproduces.
findings.context: This is the reference for the 'static heating (hot charred wall layer, cool centre) vs dynamic agitation' claim on the KINTEK page. The rotation-off vs rotation-on comparison is a validated, physically grounded demo case.
findings.source: Boateng A.A. (1993) 'Rotary kiln transport phenomena: a study of the bed motion and heat transfer', PhD thesis, UBC
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'a quasi-three-dimensional rotary kiln model'; 'bed material is turned over about three times per kiln revolution, the Peclet numbers... ensure the predominance of advective heat transfer'; 'For a stationary kiln (no rotation), measured thermal gradients in the radial direction of the bed are in agreement with model predictions'

findings.parameter: Transverse bed-motion validation data for POLYETHYLENE PELLETS (Boateng 1993, Table 4.2; 0.96 m ID drum, optical-fibre probes)
findings.value: PE pellets: dp 3.63 mm, 960 kg/m3, static angle of repose 25°, restitution coefficients 0.85 and 0.7 (Table 4.1). At 3.3% fill (H 7.5 cm, chord 50 cm), 2.05→5.22 rpm: normalized surface velocity 2.47→1.70, active layer depth 28.6→37.8% of bed depth, shear rate 12.2→17.0 1/s. At 8.5% fill (H 13.5 cm), 1.88→5.08 rpm: 4.17→2.59, 27.0→31.1%, 10.3→13.8 1/s. At 15% fill (H 20 cm), 2.14→5.11 rpm: 4.27→3.19, 23.6→27.4%, 8.6→14.2 1/s. At 29% fill (H 32 cm), 0.92→5.15 rpm: 7.50→4.49, 14.3→18.6%, 6.6→17.5 1/s.
findings.context: This is the best validation target for a transverse granular model in a plastics kiln because it uses the actual material class. Normalized surface velocity = surface velocity / (ωR). Columns were read from the extracted thesis text; the '%' unit of active layer depth is inferred from the column header.
findings.source: Boateng (1993) UBC PhD thesis, Tables 4.1 and 4.2
findings.evidence: 'Table 4.2. Data on Flow Characteristics for Polyethylene Pellets ... 3.3 2.054 10.349 2.474 28.571 12.173 (H = 7.5 cm, 2L = 50.0 cm) ...'

findings.parameter: Covered wall to bed heat transfer coefficient (typical estimate)
findings.value: 50–100 W/m2K, the typical 'guess-estimated' range from Gorog et al. 1982. Penetration (surface-renewal) models of Wes et al. 1976 compute h from the unsteady conduction of an effective (k·rho·cp) continuum over the wall contact time.
findings.context: This is a boundary condition for the bed-wall contact. Barr (1986) found the coefficient much lower in refractory-lined kilns than in unlined metal drums.
findings.source: Boateng (1993) UBC PhD thesis, Sect. 2.5.2
findings.evidence: 'Typical guess-estimated values for wall-solid heat transfer coefficient lie within the range of 50-100 W/m2K (Gorog et al., 1982). One of the earlier surface renewal-penetration models was that of Wes et al. (1976).'

findings.parameter: Flighted kiln minimal heat-transfer model (gas, bed, curtain, wall): nominal coefficients
findings.value: hbg = 102.83, hcg = 112.80, hgw = 35.23 and hsw = 242.96 W/m2K. Exchange lengths per unit axial length: lbg 2.320 m, lcg 9.71 m, lgw 3.55 m, lsw 1.79 m. Curtain fraction αcg = 3%, ds = 5 mm, ṁs = 33.98 kg/s, ṁg = 3.74 kg/s, ρg = 0.84 kg/m3, μg = 3.59e-5 Pa s, cp,s 830 and cp,g 1100 J/kgK.
findings.context: Industrial asphalt-plant flighted kiln (Piton et al. correlations). The curtain has about 4× the bed exchange length, so lifters mainly add gas–solid contact area. Without radiation the temperature profiles are exponential; with radiation they are stretched exponentials. The model is analytical, which makes it a good 1D verification case.
findings.source: Le Guen L., Piton M., Hénaut Q., Huchet F., Richard P. (2017) 'Heat convection and radiation in flighted rotary kilns: a minimal model', Can. J. Chem. Eng. (arXiv:1612.05762)

findings.parameter: DEM wall-to-particle conduction validation (Chaudhuri, Muzzio, Tomassone; CES 61:6348–6360, 2006, and InTech 2011 chapter)
findings.value: Experimental calciner 6 in ID × 3 in long aluminium tube, 20–50% fill, 10 thermocouples. Alumina (200 μm powder; ks 35 W/mK, cp 875 J/kgK) and silica (ks 14 W/mK, cp 740 J/kgK) at 10, 20 and 30 rpm with the wall at 100 °C. Rotation speed has a minimal effect on bed heating in the experiments. DEM runs: 20,000 particles of 1 mm in a 6 in × 0.6 in slice, wall at 1298 K. Simulations ran 12 s against 1200 s of experiment, reconciled by a length-scale-squared time-scaling argument.
findings.context: The DEM ignores interstitial gas, so conduction is solid–solid only, with a Hertzian contact conductance. Spread between sources: Chaudhuri's 2005 DEM abstract says rotation speed increases heat transfer and uniformity, but the 2006 experiments and the 2011 chapter find a minimal speed effect. Zhang 2022 also says the speed effect on heat transfer is 'not obvious'.
findings.source: Chaudhuri B., Muzzio F.J., Tomassone M.S. (2011) 'Experimentally Validated Numerical Modeling of Heat Transfer in Granular Flow in Rotating Vessels', InTech, doi:10.5772/13536; original CES 2006 doi:10.1016/j.ces.2006.05.034
findings.evidence: 'Alumina and silica powders are heated at varying vessel speed of 10, 20 and 30 rpm... The average bed temperatures for all the cases follow nearly identical trends'; 'each of our simulation runs was performed for only 12 seconds'

findings.parameter: DEM-CFD heat-transfer regime in a rotary kiln (Shi and McCarthy, AIChE 2005, paper 209h)
findings.value: At low particle conductivity, gas–solid conduction (through the gas gap) dominates. At high particle conductivity, solid–solid conduction dominates.
findings.context: Plastic particles (k ≈ 0.2–0.5 W/mK) sit in the low-conductivity regime, so a DEM heat model for plastics needs a gas-gap (particle–fluid–particle / particle–fluid–wall) conductance, not just the Hertzian contact term.
findings.source: Shi D., McCarthy J.J. (2005) AIChE Annual Meeting paper 209h, 'Numerical Simulation of Heat Transfer in a Rotary Kiln'
findings.evidence: 'At low particle conductivities, the heat transfer is dominated by gas-solid conduction; however, at higher particle conductivities solid-solid conduction plays the dominant role.'

findings.parameter: Granular heating-time regimes in rotary drums (Emady et al. 2016, CES, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2016.05.022)
findings.value: Three time scales: bed heating time τ, particle thermal time constant τp and wall contact time τc. τ/τc collapses onto a single curve of ϕ = τp/τc with three regimes. At low ϕ, conduction dominates and the bed heats as a solid body. At high ϕ, granular convection dominates and the bed heats nearly uniformly but slowly. In between, the bed has a cool core with warm outer layers.
findings.context: This gives a priori bed heating time scales for verifying a continuum bed model. Not read in full; the summary comes from search snippets and AIChE abstracts.
findings.source: Emady H.N., Anderson K.V., Borghard W.G., Muzzio F.J., Glasser B.J., Cuitiño A.M. (2016) Chem. Eng. Sci. 'Prediction of conductive heating time scales of particles in a rotary drum'
findings.evidence: Search-result summary of the abstract: 'results fall onto a monotonic curve of τ/τc versus ϕ (τp/τc), with three heating regimes'

findings.parameter: Two-fluid (Eulerian-granular, KTGF) model of a rotary kiln cross-section (Yin et al. 2016, Powder Technol. 287)
findings.value: 2D cross-section, two-fluid model with kinetic theory of granular flow and several heat-transfer models, validated against available data. Highest temperature at the bed surface. The temperature gradient in the bed is lower than in the kiln wall. Main controls are the initial gas temperature and the rotation speed.
findings.context: This shows a continuum (Eulerian) bed model is viable for 2D kiln slices, a cheaper alternative to DEM.
findings.source: Yin et al. (2016) Powder Technology 287 (abstract on Dalian Univ. of Technology faculty page)
findings.evidence: 'A two-fluid approach and diverse heat transfer models are applied to a two-dimensional cross-section of a rotary kiln coupled with granular flow kinetic theory... The highest temperature is found at the bed surface'

findings.parameter: CFD + bed model for rotary cement kilns (Mujumdar & Ranade 2008, APJChE 3:106–118; RoCKS, CES 62:2590–2607, 2007)
findings.value: Separate but coupled models for the bed (solids as a pseudo-fluid, clinker reactions, coating) and the freeboard (swirling burner flow, coal and volatile combustion, radiation). They exchange mass and energy through a common interface (CO2 from bed calcination becomes a freeboard source). RoCKS: three coupled kiln sub-models, pseudo-homogeneous bed, melting and coating, solved iteratively. The 1D model paper (CHERD 84:165, 2006, doi:10.1205/cherd.04193) is closed and was not read.
findings.context: This is the template for interface coupling between bed and freeboard. Spread in the literature: Mujumdar's 1D papers resolve the bed axially, while the 2008 CFD paper treats the bed as a pseudo-fluid CFD zone.
findings.source: Mujumdar K.S., Ranade V.V. (2008) 'CFD modeling of rotary cement kilns', Asia-Pac. J. Chem. Eng.; Mujumdar et al. (2007) RoCKS, Chem. Eng. Sci.
findings.evidence: 'Separate but coupled computational models were developed for the bed and the freeboard regions... The developed bed and freeboard models were coupled by mass and energy communication through common interface.'

findings.parameter: Waste-pyrolysis kiln model with CFD freeboard (Marias et al. 2005, CES 60(16):4609–4622; Marias 2003, Comput. Chem. Eng. 27:813–825)
findings.value: Pechiney pilot plant: 1 kg/h, electrically heated. Three sub-models: (1) bed of plate-shaped particles in plug flow with first-order coating pyrolysis; (2) kiln wall with 1D axial energy balance (axial conduction, exchange with bed and gas, convection and radiation, heater input); (3) freeboard CFD in Fluent with homogeneous oxidation and radiation. They were coupled by an iterative algorithm in dedicated software and validated first on an inert bed (axial temperature profile).
findings.context: This is the closest published architecture to the recommended demonstrator: 1D bed + 1D shell + 3D CFD freeboard, coupled iteratively. The 2003 incinerator paper (doi:10.1016/S0098-1354(02)00268-5) is closed.
findings.source: Marias F. personal research page, 'Pyrolysis of Aluminium Waste' (Univ. Pau)
findings.evidence: 'a pilot plant (1 kg/h)'; 'three sub-models: 1) a model for the moving bed of solids, 2) a model for the kiln itself and 3) a model for the gas phase'; 'relying on the use of CFD and more precisely on the use of Fluent'; 'an interative algorithm had been implemented'

findings.parameter: 1D pyrolysis kiln model with Saeman granular flow, validated on a pilot plant (Babler et al. 2017, Applied Energy 207:123–133)
findings.value: Mass and energy conservation with a two-step pyrolysis mechanism (biomass → gas, char and tar, then further reactions), conduction, convection and radiation, and Saeman bed flow. Nine pilot trials at different feed rates and heat supplies. Agreement is good at moderate heat supply but deviates at high heat supply. Rotation speed controls both heat transfer and granular flow, which interact strongly. Heat losses are important.
findings.context: This is the modern reference for a validated 1D axial model of an indirectly heated pyrolysis kiln.
findings.source: Babler M.U., Phounglamcheik A., Amovic M., Ljunggren R., Engvall K. (2017) Appl. Energy 207:123–133, doi:10.1016/j.apenergy.2017.06.034 (abstract on IDEAS/RePEc)
findings.evidence: 'the granular flow model is described by the well known Saeman model... In total 9 pilot plant trials... a strong interplay between heat transfer and granular flow which both are controlled by the kiln rotation speed'

findings.parameter: Fantozzi/Bidini (Perugia) rotary kiln slow pyrolysis, Parts I–II (J. Eng. Gas Turbines Power 129, 2007)
findings.value: Micro-scale, electrically heated rotary kiln with a tar scrubber and a syngas combustion chamber. Part I gives theoretical and experimental relations between residence time and flow rate (the 'working envelope') as a function of bulk density, moisture and heater power. The feed screw is mechanically linked to the kiln, so feed rate and residence time are coupled. Part II adds product yields (syngas, tar, char) to the energy balance at fixed rpm.
findings.context: Not read in full (doi:10.1115/1.2720521 is closed). Use only as a modelling precedent for energy balances.
findings.source: Fantozzi F., Colantoni S., Bartocci P., Desideri U. (2007) Rotary kiln slow pyrolysis..., Part I, J. Eng. Gas Turbines Power 129:901–907 (UniPG record and search snippets)
findings.evidence: Search snippet: 'theoretical and experimental calculation of the relationships between Residence Time and Flow Rate used to determine the working envelope of the reactor'

findings.parameter: Granular regime vs Froude number in a rotating drum (Chrono::GPU validation)
findings.value: Fr = ω²R/g. Rolling at Fr = 1e-4 to 1e-3, cascading (S-shaped surface) at 0.01, cataracting at 0.5, centrifuging at 1.5. Benchmark: 60 mm drum, 5 mm deep, half full, particles 0.54 mm.
findings.context: For the lab benchmark (D = 0.30 m, 6 rpm) I derive Fr ≈ 0.006, i.e. rolling to cascading, before lifters are added. Lifters then create the falling curtain independently of Fr.
findings.source: Fang L., Zhang R., Vanden Heuvel C., Serban R., Negrut D. (2021) 'Chrono::GPU: an open-source simulation package for granular dynamics using DEM', Processes 9:1813, Sect. 4.2.4
findings.evidence: 'When Fr = 1 × 10−4 and 1 × 10−3... rolling regime. When Fr = 0.01, a cascading regime sets in... At Fr = 0.5... cataracting... at Fr = 1.5, centrifuging'

findings.parameter: GPU DEM throughput (Chrono::GPU, single GPU)
findings.value: Linear scaling up to 123 million particles on an A100. A100 is more than 2× faster than V100. Rule of thumb: well under 1 h per 1 million particles per 1 s of simulated time at 1e5 steps, i.e. at least 2.8e7 particle-steps/s. Mixer time steps took 0.0031, 0.0096 and 0.065 s on the A100 at the three resolutions tested.
findings.context: Monodisperse spheres with full contact history and mesh interaction, dt = 1e-5 s. Other literature cited there: a 2.8 million particle system on a GTX 1080Ti took about 0.03 s per step (about 9e7 particle-steps/s with simplifications).
findings.source: Fang et al. (2021) Processes 9:1813, Sect. 5 and Fig. 15–16
findings.evidence: 'on A100 with the current Chrono::GPU implementation, a fully resolved DEM simulation... takes well below 1 h per 1 million particles and 1 s of simulation time (more precisely, 1 × 10^5 simulation steps)'

findings.parameter: Quasi-real-time GPU DEM of an industrial rotating drum (Xu et al. 2011, Particuology 9:446–450)
findings.value: Simplified DEM (no tangential contact force, no particle rotation): about 8000 particles in real time on one CPU. Industrial-scale drum on more than 200 GPUs, 10-domain decomposition, at about 1/11 of real time.
findings.context: Simplified physics. It shows that real time at industrial scale needs a GPU cluster, not one T4.
findings.source: Xu J., Qi H., Fang X., Lu L., Ge W., Wang X., et al., Li J. (2011) Particuology 9:446–450, doi:10.1016/j.partic.2011.01.003 (abstract via Semantic Scholar)
findings.evidence: 'A single CPU is used first to simulate a small model system with about 8000 particles in real-time... more than 200 GPUs... The overall speed is about 1/11 of the real-time.'

findings.parameter: NVIDIA T4 specifications
findings.value: FP32 8.1 TFLOPS, FP16 mixed 65 TFLOPS, 2560 CUDA cores, 320 Tensor cores, 16 GB GDDR6, bandwidth 320+ GB/s, 70 W
findings.context: DEM and CFD stencil codes are memory-bandwidth bound. T4 bandwidth is about 0.21× the A100-40GB figure of 1555 GB/s (A100 value from background knowledge, not read here).
findings.source: NVIDIA T4 product page
findings.evidence: 'Single Precision Performance (FP32) 8.1 TFLOPS ... Memory Capacity 16 GB GDDR6 Bandwidth 320+ GB/s Power 70 watts'

findings.parameter: DERIVED ESTIMATE: DEM throughput and budget on one T4
findings.value: About 5.7e6 particle-steps/s for an optimized CUDA-class DEM (A100 Chrono rate × 320/1555 bandwidth ratio), uncertain by about 2–3×. A pure-PyTorch tensor DEM is probably 3–10× slower (my judgement, unverified). A 30 min run therefore gives about 1e10 particle-steps at best. Example: a 34k-particle slice (D 0.3 m, 65 mm, 10% fill, d = 2.5 mm) for about 3e5 steps at dt about 5e-5 s (soft contact, E about 1e6 Pa) is only about 15 s, or about 1.5 rev at 6 rpm.
findings.context: Derived by me from the Chrono and NVIDIA numbers above. Particle counts are derived too: 3.4e4 for the lab slice, 6.5e4 for a 0.3 m × 1 m kiln with 5 mm particles, and 5.2e6 for a 2 m × 12 m kiln with 10 mm particles at 12% fill. Bed heat-up needs 300 s or more (the Zhang validation ran 300 s), so a coupled DEM simulation over the whole heat-up is not feasible. DEM should calibrate the transverse kinematics over a few revolutions, and continuum or parcel models should carry the heat and chemistry.
findings.source: Derived (this work) from Fang et al. 2021 and the NVIDIA T4 page
findings.evidence: Arithmetic: 1e6×1e5/3600 = 2.78e7; × 320/1555 = 5.7e6 particle-steps/s; dt ≈ 0.1π√(m/k) with k ≈ E·R

findings.parameter: DERIVED ESTIMATE: freeboard gas dynamics in the lab benchmark (D 0.30 m × 65 mm, 773 K, 6 rpm, N2 350 mL/min)
findings.value: N2 at 773 K: μ ≈ 3.4e-5 Pa s, ρ ≈ 0.44 kg/m3, ν ≈ 7.8e-5 m2/s. Hot-gas flow ≈ 1.5e-5 m3/s, so empty-drum mean gas residence time V/Q ≈ 300 s. Wall speed 0.094 m/s, giving Re_ω = D²ω/(2ν) ≈ 365. Grashof for ΔT = 100 K is about 6e6.
findings.context: My calculation. The sweep flow carries almost no momentum (Re of order 1), so the lab freeboard is laminar mixed convection driven by wall rotation and buoyancy. That explains why the CEJ study reports volatile residence time as a key output.
findings.source: Derived (this work) from the Lund thesis setup values and ideal-gas/Sutherland properties

findings.parameter: DERIVED ESTIMATE: vapour residence time in an industrial-size plastic pyrolysis kiln
findings.value: Example: 1 t/h feed, 85% condensable vapour, D = 2 m, L = 12 m, 12% fill, 450 °C. Outlet vapour flow is 0.047–0.28 m3/s for mean molar mass 0.30–0.05 kg/mol, and freeboard V/Q_out is 120–710 s (355 s at 0.15 kg/mol). Outlet velocity ≈ 0.03 m/s, Re_D ≈ 1e4, Gr(ΔT = 100 K) ≈ 2e9. A 50 Nm3/h N2 sweep adds only about 0.04 m3/s.
findings.context: My calculation with stated assumptions. Kiln vapour residence time is minutes, against 1–4 s in fixed or fluidized beds. Freeboard temperature therefore controls secondary cracking, and 'fast vapour removal' in practice means short hot-path length and a cooler freeboard, not high gas velocity. This should be shown with a mean-age-of-gas field.
findings.source: Derived (this work); for comparison see Abdy et al. 2023 and Li et al. 2026

findings.parameter: DERIVED ESTIMATE: linearized surface radiation coefficient in an indirectly heated kiln freeboard
findings.value: h_rad ≈ 4εσT³ ≈ 84 W/m2K at T = 773 K and ε = 0.8
findings.context: My calculation. Wall-to-bed and wall-to-curtain surface radiation is comparable to or larger than covered-wall contact (50–100 W/m2K) and far larger than gas convection (2–35 W/m2K). N2 with hydrocarbon vapour at 400–550 °C is only weakly participating, so radiation is mostly surface to surface.
findings.source: Derived (this work); compare Barr 1986 (radiative coefficients 15–55 W/m2K for combustion gas) and Le Guen et al. 2017

findings.parameter: Wax fouling and condensation at cold ends (plastic pyrolysis vapour lines)
findings.value: Heavy waxy components and tar deposit on surfaces, especially the cooling surfaces of condensers and heat exchangers. They first insulate and reduce heat transfer, then block flow. A pilot fluidized-bed system (KNU, 100 kg/day) had no reactor blockage but clogging in condensers and pipelines during low-temperature operation, attributed to the product oil's pour point. A rotary-kiln patent places the vapour outlet pipe at the discharge end; temperatures are not given.
findings.context: No quantitative kiln freeboard or duct temperature specification was found. A demonstrator should map the dew point and pour point of the heavy lump (Riazi cut) against wall temperature to flag deposition risk.
findings.source: US patent 11969689 'Method for processing plastic waste pyrolysis gas'; US11988382 'Rotary kiln for the evaporation of thermoplastic waste'; KNU CFB pilot (search snippets)
findings.evidence: 'The waxy components and tar are especially problematic on cooling surfaces of heat exchangers used in condensing the reaction mixture'; 'The deposits will eventually clog the heat exchanger'

findings.parameter: Vapour residence time and product slate (general trend)
findings.value: Low temperature (400–500 °C) with short VRT (under 1 s) favours wax. High temperature (above 700 °C) with short VRT favours gas. Longer VRT cracks wax to oil and then to gas. HDPE at 600 °C showed lower wax and roughly constant non-condensable gas as VRT increased.
findings.context: Conference poster, read via search snippet only. Its direction is consistent with Abdy 2023, but magnitudes are not transferable to kilns.
findings.source: Aftab S. et al., tcbiomass 2024 poster (GTI Energy)
findings.evidence: Search snippet: 'a low pyrolysis temperature (400-500 °C) and short VRT (<1 s) favors waxes, and a high pyrolysis temperature (>700 °C) and short vapor residence time favors gas'

findings.parameter: Flighted drum particle motion: DEM vs particle-tracking validation data
findings.value: Four rectangular flights at 10, 20 and 30 rpm and 10, 15 and 20% fill, with good PTV–DEM (LIGGGHTS) agreement (Powder Technol. 2020). A follow-up with 1, 4, 8 or 12 flights found that 8 and 12 flights give a larger, more stable dilute-phase (curtain) fraction, and that literature (geometric) flight models deviate significantly. Karali, Herz & Specht studied optimum loading in a 500 mm × 150 mm drum at 1–5 rpm with flight length ratios 0.375 and 0.75.
findings.context: Use these as validation data for the lifter/curtain sub-model. Abstracts only.
findings.source: Zhang L., Jiang Z., Weigler F., Herz F., Mellmann J., Tsotsas E. (2020) Powder Technol.; Zhang et al. (2020) Particuology; Karali, Herz, Specht (2015) UK PTF
findings.evidence: 'The FRD is operated by varying the drum rotating speed (10, 20, and 30 rpm) and filling degree (10, 15, and 20%). Good agreements are observed between the PTV measurements and DEM simulations.'

findings.parameter: Melting and agglomeration models for plastic pyrolysis particles
findings.value: No published DEM or CFD model of molten-plastic coating or agglomeration specifically in a rotary kiln was found. The nearest is a liquid-bridge model in NETL MFiX (fluidized bed), where the molten plastic layer's mass, volume and species evolve with pyrolysis, and coating causes agglomeration and defluidization. Earlier liquid-bridge models mishandled capillary forces between unlike particles and the changed collision properties of coated particles.
findings.context: This is a modelling gap. For the demonstrator, a stickiness/coating indicator (melt fraction × contact) is defensible, but a validated agglomeration model is not available.
findings.source: AIChE 2024 Annual Meeting paper 340a, 'Development of a liquid bridge model for particle agglomeration and defluidization in plastic pyrolysis' (abstract)
findings.evidence: Search summary: 'liquid bridge model in NETL's open-source MFiX solver, where the molten plastic layer's mass, volume, and species evolve as pyrolysis proceeds'

findings.parameter: Komossa et al. DEM vs experiment for indirectly heated rotary drums
findings.value: Citations confirmed: 'Transversal bed motion in rotating drums using spherical particles: comparison of experiments with DEM simulations', Powder Technol. 264 (2014) 96–104; 'Heat transfer in indirect heated rotary drums filled with monodisperse spheres: comparison of experiments with DEM simulations', Powder Technol. 286 (2015) 722–731, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2015.07.022
findings.context: Abstracts and numbers were not accessible (closed; Semantic Scholar has no abstract). They are listed only as validation candidates.
findings.source: Fang et al. 2021 reference list (ref. 75); Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall metadata
findings.evidence: Chrono paper ref. 75: 'Komossa, H.; Wirtz, S.; Scherer, V.; Herz, F.; Specht, E. Transversal bed motion in rotating drums using spherical particles: Comparison of experiments with DEM simulations. Powder Technol. 2014, 264, 96–104.'

findings.parameter: 'Liu, Dai & Li' CFD-DEM of PE pyrolysis in a kiln
findings.value: Not found
findings.context: Several searches found no such paper. The closest matches are Zhang M. et al. 2022 CEJ (CFD-DEM of a plastic rotary furnace, no reaction), Belcher 2026 (Lund/Tetra Pak, Star-CCM+), and KIT work by Zhang F., Dai X., Li M. et al. 2026 on conical spouted and fluidized beds, not kilns. The citation in the brief may conflate these and should be checked before use.
findings.source: Search results (this work)
findings.evidence: KIT ref. list: 'Zhang, F., Dai, X., Li, M., Tavakkol, S., & Stapf, D. (2026). Numerical analysis of hydrodynamics in conical spouted bed reactors. Physics of Fluids 38(5) 053333'

equations.name: 1D axial energy balances: solid, gas and insulated wall (flighted kiln minimal model)
equations.expression: ṁs cp,s dTs/dz = (hbg lbg + hcg lcg)(Tg−Ts) + Egs(lbg+lcg)(Tg⁴−Ts⁴) + hsw lsw (Tw−Ts) + Esw(lbg+lcg)(Tw⁴−Ts⁴);  ṁg cp,g dTg/dz = (hbg lbg + hcg lcg)(Ts−Tg) + Egs(lbg+lcg)(Ts⁴−Tg⁴) + hgw lgw (Tw−Tg) + Egw lgw (Tw⁴−Tg⁴);  wall: hsw lsw (Ts−Tw) + Esw(lbg+lcg)(Ts⁴−Tw⁴) + hgw lgw (Tg−Tw) + Egw lgw (Tg⁴−Tw⁴) = 0
equations.variables: Subscripts: s solid, g gas, w wall, b bed, c curtain. lij = dSij/dz is the exchange length per unit kiln length. Eij = σεij. For an externally heated kiln, replace the insulated-wall condition with a shell energy balance that includes the heater flux.
equations.validity: Steady state, temperatures uniform over each cross-section, no bed conduction. Without radiation, the temperatures relax exponentially over a length Λ = E/(I+1)·1/(A+B+CD/(D+C)), with A = hcg lcg, B = hbg lbg, C = hsw lsw, D = hgw lgw, E = ṁg cp,g (Eq. 9).
equations.source: Le Guen et al. (2017) Can. J. Chem. Eng., Eqs. 2–4 and 9 (arXiv:1612.05762)

equations.name: Gas-to-bed, gas-to-curtain, gas-to-wall and bed-to-wall coefficients (Piton et al. correlations, as compiled by Le Guen et al.)
equations.expression: hbg = Hbg(σbg ṁg/Ag)^ηbg with Hbg = 0.4 W/m2K, σbg = 3600 kg⁻¹m²s, ηbg = 0.62;  hcg = (ks/ds)[2 + Acg Re_p^a + Bcg Re_p^b Pr^c] (Re_p < 200: A = 0, B = 0.6, b = 1/3, c = 1/3; 200–1500: A = 0.5, a = 0, B = 0.02, b = 0.8; > 1500: A = 4.5e-5, a = 1.8, B = 0);  hgw = (kg/Dh)(0.02 Re^0.93 + 8.5e-6 Re_ω^1.45), Dh = Dt(2π−εB+sin εB)/(2π−εB−sin εB), Re = DD vg/νg, Re_ω = DD² ω/(2νg);  hsw = 11.6 (ks/(εB DD)) (ω εB DD²/(2 as))^0.3
equations.variables: Ag: hot-gas cross-section. Re_p = vg ds/νg. as = ks/(ρs cp,s) is solid thermal diffusivity. εB is the bed half-angle from αB Ft = (εB − sin εB cos εB)/π. ks is written as printed in Table II; the standard Ranz–Marshall form uses gas conductivity.
equations.validity: hbg validity range 50–100 W/m2K; hgw for 1100 < Re_ω < 58000 and 0 < Re < 30000; hsw for ω in 3.5–10 rad/s. The lab benchmark has Re_ω ≈ 365 and Re of order 1, which is outside the hgw range, so resolve the freeboard by CFD there.
equations.source: Le Guen et al. (2017), Tables I–V (arXiv:1612.05762), citing Piton et al.

equations.name: Curtain (dilute-phase) solids fraction
equations.expression: αcg = (2/3)(dN/dz) ds³ / (DD² Ft)
equations.variables: dN/dz: grains in the curtain per unit length; ds: grain diameter; DD: drum diameter; Ft: kiln volume fraction of solids
equations.validity: Monodisperse spheres; dilute curtain
equations.source: Le Guen et al. (2017), Eq. 1

equations.name: DEM contact conduction (Hertzian contact conductance)
equations.expression: Qij = Hc (Tj − Ti);  Hc = 2 kS [3 FN r* / (4 E*)]^(1/3);  dTi/dt = Σj Qij / (ρi ci Vi)
equations.variables: kS: solid conductivity; FN: normal contact force; r*: geometric mean radius; E*: effective Young's modulus
equations.validity: Interstitial gas neglected; constant properties; lumped particles (Bi << 1); requires (kS a)/(kf r) >> 1 (O'Brien 1977). Not valid for plastics in gas, where the gas-gap path dominates (Shi & McCarthy 2005), so add a particle–fluid–particle term. A softened Young's modulus E* inflates Hc, so correct it if contact stiffness is reduced for speed.
equations.source: Chaudhuri, Muzzio & Tomassone (2011) InTech chapter, Eqs. 3–5 (same model as CES 2006)

equations.name: Drum flow-regime Froude number
equations.expression: Fr = ω² R / g
equations.variables: ω: angular speed (rad/s); R: drum radius
equations.validity: Regimes seen in simulations: rolling at Fr 1e-4–1e-3, cascading at about 0.01, cataracting at about 0.5, centrifuging at about 1.5 (no lifters)
equations.source: Fang et al. (2021) Chrono::GPU, Processes 9:1813, Eq. 17

equations.name: Gas species transport with devolatilization source (Euler–Lagrange pyrolysis)
equations.expression: ∂ρg/∂t + ∇·(ρg Ug) = Sρ;  ∂(ρg Ug)/∂t + ∇·(ρg Ug Ug) = −∇p + ρg g + ∇·τ + SU;  ∂(ρg Yi)/∂t + ∇·(ρg Ug Yi) − ∇·(ρg D ∇Yi) = SiY + ri,g
equations.variables: Sρ, SiY: mass sources from particle devolatilization; SU: momentum exchange; ri,g: gas-phase reaction rate (neglected by Li et al. at about 500 °C and 2–4 s)
equations.validity: Point-particle approximation (ε ≈ 1). In a kiln freeboard the bed is a boundary, so apply Sρ as a surface flux on the bed free surface and as volumetric sources in the curtain.
equations.source: Li et al. (2026) Particuology 115:214–227, Eqs. 1, 2, 4

equations.name: Five-lump wax kinetics (PP)
equations.expression: dYPP/dt = −k0 YPP;  dYW/dt = k0 YPP − (k1+k2+k3) YW;  dYHF/dt = k1 YW; dYLF/dt = k2 YW; dYG/dt = k3 YW;  ki = Ai exp(−Ea,i/RT)
equations.validity: PP, fitted on tubular reactors (Lechleitner 2020) and used up to about 550 °C. For PE, swap in the team's RS-L2 primary step and keep the wax→lump split as a hypothesis to be calibrated.
equations.source: Li et al. (2026), Table 2 (from Lechleitner et al. 2020, Processes 9:34)

equations.name: Vapour residence time from carrier flow (ideal gas)
equations.expression: τv = Vreactor / [Q_N2,ref · (T/Tref) · (pref/p)]
equations.variables: Vreactor: free volume; Q_N2,ref: N2 flow at room conditions
equations.validity: Ignores the pyrolysis vapour's own volume flow and dead zones. In kilns, where vapour flow exceeds the sweep, use a local mean-age-of-gas field instead.
equations.source: Abdy et al. (2023), Table 1 footnote; I reproduced 1.73 s for 500 °C, 4 L/min, V = 3.04e-4 m3

equations.name: Mean age of gas (local vapour residence time field)
equations.expression: ∂(ρ a)/∂t + ∇·(ρ u a) = ∇·(ρ D ∇a) + ρ  (a = 0 at the N2 inlet). For vapour released at the bed: transport a vapour-weighted age, ∂(ρYv av)/∂t + ∇·(ρ u Yv av) − ∇·(ρD∇(Yv av)) = ρ Yv + S_v·0
equations.variables: a: local mean age (s); Yv: vapour mass fraction; S_v: vapour source (born with age 0)
equations.validity: Standard passive-scalar residence-time method. The form is from background knowledge and was not read from a source in this session, so verify against a ventilation-CFD reference before citing.
equations.source: Background knowledge (standard CFD residence-time technique); not verified in this session

equations.name: Kramers–Croockewit / Saeman axial bed-depth equation (axial transport)
equations.expression: dh/dz = −tan β / cos θ + (3 qv tan θ)/(4π n R³) · [2h/R − (h/R)²]^(−3/2)
equations.variables: h: bed depth at the chord centre; z: axial coordinate from the discharge end; β: kiln inclination; θ: dynamic angle of repose; qv: volumetric solids flow; n: rotation rate (rev/s); R: kiln radius
equations.validity: Rolling bed, free-flowing solids, no lifters. Melting or sticky plastic invalidates it. The equation form is from background knowledge: the Kramers & Crockewit 1952 citation (Chem. Eng. Sci. 1(6), 259) is confirmed in Boateng 1993's reference list, and Babler 2017 confirms use of the Saeman model, but the formula was not read in this session.
equations.source: Kramers H., Crockewit P. (1952) Chem. Eng. Sci. 1:259 (citation via Boateng 1993); Saeman (1951) as used by Babler et al. 2017

equations.name: Penetration (surface-renewal) model for covered wall to bed heat transfer
equations.expression: h ≈ 2 √[(k ρ cp)eff / (π tc)], tc = (2εB)/ω (contact time of bed with the covered wall); combine in series with a contact resistance: 1/h = 1/hcontact + 1/hpen
equations.variables: (kρcp)eff: effective bed thermal effusivity squared; εB: bed half-angle; ω: angular speed
equations.validity: Continuum bed over the contact time. Boateng 1993 attributes the approach to Wes et al. 1976, but the extracted equation text was garbled, so the standard form here is from background knowledge. It overestimates h without the contact resistance term.
equations.source: Boateng (1993) Sect. 2.5.2 (Wes et al. 1976), form not verbatim

critical_numbers: Lab benchmark (Zhang 2020/2022 via Lund): D = 300 mm, W = 65 mm, wall 773 K, 6 rpm, N2 350 ± 10 mL/min, LDPE d = 2.5 mm, 300 s of physical time
Derived for the lab benchmark: freeboard gas V/Q ≈ 300 s, Re_ω ≈ 365, sweep Re of order 1, Gr ≈ 6e6 at ΔT = 100 K, Fr ≈ 0.006. Laminar mixed convection; the sweep carries negligible momentum.
Star-CCM+ CFD-DEM: about 2000 particles, 66k–448k cells, 21.6/32.5/46.2 h on 64 cores for 15 s physical. Recommended 1 core per 1500 DEM particles.
Lund vs Zhang 2022 at 100 s: 540 K vs 600 K mean particle temperature. One-way coupling overheats.
Abdy 2023 HDPE fixed bed: VRT 3.76/1.88 s at 450 °C, 3.52/1.76 s at 500 °C, 3.30/1.65 s at 550 °C (2/4 L/min N2). Maximum wax 91.87 wt% at 500 °C and 1.76 s.
Gas-phase cracking: < 30% compositional change at 750 °C in 4 s (van Wyk 2026, via Li 2026)
Five-lump PP: PP→W 3.2e15 1/s, 244 kJ/mol; W→HF 2.0e2, 80; W→LF 1.0e5, 100; W→G 5.0e14, 249; ΔH 542 kJ/kg
Lumped (Lagrangian) plastic particle valid only for d < 2 mm; above 4 mm the internal gradient exceeds 10 K
Barr 1986 pilot kiln 0.406 m × 5.5 m: covered wall→bed < 30% of freeboard→exposed bed. Radiative h 15–55 W/m2K (800–1800 K gas). Convective h about 2–3 W/m2K at Re ≈ 2000.
Wall–solid h typical estimate 50–100 W/m2K (Gorog 1982 via Boateng)
Boateng: bed turned over about 3 times per revolution. PE pellets dp 3.63 mm, 960 kg/m3, static repose 25°. Active layer 14–38% of bed depth at 0.9–5.2 rpm and 3.3–29% fill in a 0.96 m drum.
Le Guen nominal flighted kiln: hbg 102.83, hcg 112.80, hgw 35.23, hsw 242.96 W/m2K; curtain exchange length 9.71 m vs bed 2.32 m
Chaudhuri calciner: 6 in ID × 3 in, 20–50% fill, 10–30 rpm. Rotation speed has minimal effect on heat-up in experiments. DEM runs of 12 s vs 1200 s experiments.
Chrono::GPU on A100: under 1 h per 1e6 particles per 1e5 steps (≥ 2.8e7 particle-steps/s); linear to 123M particles; A100 more than 2× V100
T4: 8.1 TFLOPS FP32, 16 GB GDDR6, 320+ GB/s, 70 W. Derived DEM about 5.7e6 particle-steps/s for an optimized code (uncertain 2–3×).

Derived: a 30 min T4 DEM run gives only about 15 s (about 1.5 rev at 6 rpm) for a 34k-particle slice, so coupled DEM over the full heat-up time is infeasible. Use DEM for calibration and continuum or parcel models for heat and chemistry.
Derived industrial kiln (1 t/h, 2 m × 12 m): vapour V/Q 120–710 s, outlet u ≈ 0.03 m/s, Re ≈ 1e4, Gr ≈ 2e9. Kiln VRT is minutes, not seconds.
Derived linearized surface radiation 4εσT³ ≈ 84 W/m2K at 773 K, ε = 0.8
Xu 2011: simplified DEM, 8000 particles in real time on one CPU; industrial drum on more than 200 GPUs at 1/11 of real time
