CONTINUATION NOTE: this run started fresh for Topic E. No earlier Topic E files were in the scratchpad. The working directory is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Programacao/381db60a-cc64-54cc-aefe-1e483b5b217d/scratchpad/topicE (lund.txt, chrono.txt, intech.txt, flight.txt, abdy.txt, kitfb.txt, ubcft_*.txt hold the extracted full texts).

ACCESS STATUS. Read in full: Lund thesis, Chrono::GPU, Chaudhuri InTech chapter, Le Guen arXiv, Abdy AAM, Li 2026 KIT, and the Boateng 1993 and Barr 1986 UBC theses (UBC Open Collections JSON API: https://oc-index.library.ubc.ca/collections/831/items/<id>, field 'FullText').
- Closed according to Unpaywall: Barr 1989 Parts I and II, Boateng & Barr 1996, Mujumdar & Ranade 2006 and 2008, Marias 2003, Komossa 2015, Chaudhuri 2006, Emady 2016, Zhang 2020 FPT, Fantozzi 2007. Their content here comes from theses, abstracts or the authors' pages.
- No CFD-DEM paper by 'Liu, Dai & Li' on PE pyrolysis in a kiln was found. Treat that reference as unverified.
- No quantitative data were found for co-current vs counter-current vapour offtake, or for freeboard and duct temperatures in plastic kilns. Only qualitative patent and fouling evidence exists.

SPREADS AND CONFLICTS.
(1) Effect of rotation speed on bed heating:
- Chaudhuri's 2005 DEM abstract says it increases.
- Chaudhuri's 2006 experiments and the 2011 chapter find a minimal effect.
- Zhang 2022 says the gain is 'not obvious'.
- Babler 2017 reports strong interplay through residence time.
- Boateng says advection dominates once the bed is rolling.

So rotation mainly removes the static-bed gradient (the stationary vs rotating contrast). Beyond rolling, extra rpm adds little heat-transfer benefit and shortens residence time.

(2) Wall–bed heat transfer coefficient:
- 50–100 W/m2K (Gorog guess).
- 243 W/m2K (Le Guen, asphalt kiln, high-k grains).
- Barr found it greatly reduced in refractory-lined kilns.
- For plastic beds (k about 0.2–0.4 W/mK) expect the low end, then a step change on melting, when a wetted film forms.

(3) Vapour residence time:
- Lab and fluidized beds run at 1–4 s.
- My kiln estimate is minutes (lab drum V/Q about 300 s; industrial about 120–710 s).
- So the KINTEK claim of 'fast vapour removal' must be shown as hot-path residence time, plus freeboard temperature control and the vapour age field. Simply quoting a gas velocity is not enough.

FEASIBILITY ON ONE T4 IN 10–60 MIN.
(a) A fully coupled 3D CFD-DEM of the whole kiln over heat-up times (hundreds of seconds or more) is NOT feasible. Star-CCM+ needed about 1–2 days on 64 cores for 15 s with only 2000 particles, and KIT reports about 1 day per few seconds for a 3D fluidized bed.
(b) Feasible pieces:
- A GPU DEM slice with 10k–50k spheres plus analytic lifters for 2–5 revolutions (minutes).
- A 3D laminar or LES freeboard on 1–4 M cells with the team's existing MAC/IBM PyTorch solver, which needs about 0.1–0.5 GB of fields. The lab case is laminar mixed convection (Re_ω about 365, Gr about 6e6). The industrial case (Gr about 2e9) needs SGS or k-ω SST.
- A 2D transverse continuum bed model and 1D axial models, which run in seconds.
- Lagrangian thermal parcels: 1e5–1e6 parcels with 1D internal conduction cost little.

RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE ('Kiln-Twin', multi-rate, one-way calibration and two-way thermal coupling, all PyTorch):

L0, shell and heater: a 2D (θ, z) rotating-shell conduction model with heater zones (electric or flue-gas jacket, radiative and convective) and inner exchanges: covered wall→bed by penetration plus contact resistance; exposed wall→bed, wall→curtain and wall→gas by surface radiation plus Le Guen/CFD convection. This captures Barr's regenerative wall temperature cycling.

L1, transverse bed:
- (i) GPU DEM slice with lifters, for a few revolutions only. Outputs: velocity field, active-layer depth, curtain mass flux per lifter angle, contact-time distribution, mixing/Lagrangian maps.
- (ii) A continuum 2D cross-section bed: either a Boateng-type active layer plus plug-flow model, or μ(I) granular rheology on the existing MAC/IBM solver (μ(I) from background knowledge, not verified here), driven by or calibrated against (i).
- Validation: Boateng's PE pellet Table 4.2 (active layer %, surface velocity vs rpm and fill), the Chrono Froude regimes, and the Zhang/FAU flighted-drum PTV data.

L2, axial transport: the Saeman/Kramers bed-depth ODE plus axial dispersion. Lifters change hold-up, so use a DEM-calibrated hold-up.

L3, particle thermochemistry: Lagrangian parcels advected by the L1 field and the L2 axial speed. Each parcel carries:
- a 1D radial conduction model (needed because d > 2 mm);
- enthalpy-method melting with the melt → coating/sticky state flagged (no validated kiln agglomeration model exists);
- RS-L2 primary kinetics for HDPE/LDPE/PP/PS (already available), plus a wax→HF/LF/G melt-phase split (Lechleitner) and the DSC heat of pyrolysis.

Vapour is released as a surface flux at the bed free surface and as volumetric sources in the curtain.

L4, 3D freeboard: a low-Mach variable-density NS solver in the drum with a rotating-wall boundary condition, IBM lifters and curtain drag/heat sinks (two-way). Scalars:
- species lumps (N2, wax vapour, HF, LF, G);
- mean age of gas, giving a local vapour residence time;
- optional first-order gas-phase cracking (wax→LF→G), flagged as uncalibrated below about 600 °C;
- dew point and pour point of the heaviest lump (Riazi cut) vs local wall temperature, giving a wax-deposition risk map at the cold ends and outlet duct.

L5, radiation: a net-radiation enclosure method (wall, bed surface, curtain sheets, end walls) with view factors precomputed by the team's SDF ray-marcher. Treat the gas as transparent or grey with low absorptivity.

Coupling and numerics:
- Operator splitting with multi-rate stepping. DEM runs offline with μs steps. Bed, parcels and freeboard advance with Δt of about 0.01–0.05 s (CFL). The shell advances with Δt of about 1 s.
- Bed and freeboard exchange fluxes every 0.1–1 s, then a quasi-steady sweep: Marias/Mujumdar-style iteration between bed, wall and gas until the energy balance closes to under 1%.
- The Chaudhuri time-scaling argument (time ∝ length²) can justify accelerated time in DEM-derived mixing.
- Two-way thermal coupling is mandatory, per the Lund lesson.

VALIDATION LADDER:
- V1: granular regime vs Fr.
- V2: Boateng PE pellets.
- V3: Chaudhuri calciner heat-up (alumina ks 35, 6 in drum, 20 rpm, 50% fill, wall 398 K).
- V4: Le Guen analytic exponential solution, for code verification.
- V5: Zhang 2020/2022 lab drum heat-up (773 K, 6 rpm; Lund reports about 600 K at 100 s).
- V6: Abdy VRT/wax trends and the team's TGA/DTG kinetics.
- V7: global mass and energy balance closure and mesh/particle-count independence.

VISUALS FOR A CFD AUDIENCE:
- Split screen of static vs rotating kiln (charred hot wall layer and cold core vs uniform bed), directly testing the KINTEK claim.
- Particles coloured by temperature or melt fraction as they cascade off curved lifters through the hot upper atmosphere.
- Freeboard pathlines coloured by vapour age, with an isosurface of wax-vapour mass fraction.
- The unwrapped (θ, z) shell temperature map showing regenerative cycling.
- Axial profiles of the 3D model against the 1D Le Guen/Babler-style model.
- Wax-deposition risk map on the outlet duct.
- A product-split gauge (oil/wax/gas/char) responding live to rpm, slope and sweep sliders.
- An explicit cross-check slide against the Star-CCM+ setup from the Lund thesis, which the audience can reproduce.

sweep.topic: TOPIC G: flighted rotary drums and kilns (internal lifters) and the cascading curtain. Covers lifter geometry, holdup and discharge models, design load, curtain properties, curtain and wall heat transfer, transport, DEM and CFD-DEM, whether flights suit plastic pyrolysis kilns and what is used instead, and a modelling recommendation for a Colab/PyTorch T4 demonstrator.

findings.parameter: Flights per circle (rule of thumb for commercial direct dryers)
findings.value: 2.4 to 3.0 x D flights per circle, with shell peripheral speed 60-75 ft/min
findings.units: count (D presumably in ft, since the same sentence uses ft/min; the unit was not shown in the snippet)
findings.context: Modern commercial cascading rotary dryers. The source introduces a Ua correlation for this design class (the equation was cut off in the snippet).
findings.source: Mujumdar-associated chapter '7 Rotary Drying' (Handbook of Industrial Drying chapter, ResearchGate PDF)
findings.evidence: Search snippet: 'For modern commercial dryers that have a flight count per circle of 2.4 to 3.0 D and operate at shell peripheral speeds of 60-75 ft/min, the following equation has been proposed.' I could not confirm the classic 'radial flight height 1/8-1/12 D' rule.

findings.parameter: Kelly flight profiles: EAD (equal angular distribution) and EHD (equal horizontal distribution)
findings.value: EAD is designed for equal angular distribution of the cascading solids. EHD aims for an even spread over a horizontal mid-plane but is 'not practical to implement in the industry due to its complex design for sticky and wet materials'. Kelly-O'Donnell-type models predict EAD-flighted and under-loaded drums poorly. One study gives a flight-profile constant of 0.637 for EAD, meaning unknown.
findings.context: Classic flight-shape design. Primary source is Kelly (1992) 'Flight design in rotary dryers', Drying Technology 10(4) (tandfonline doi 10.1080/07373939208916491). Kelly and O'Donnell 1968/1977 cover holdup and the dynamic friction coefficient.
findings.source: Secondary summaries of Kelly 1992 found via Lee & Sheehan 2010 / Revol 2001 / Sunkara 2013 search results
findings.evidence: Search summary of several papers citing Kelly. I did not retrieve the EAD geometry equations.

findings.parameter: Revol, Briens & Chabagno (2001) flight design model
findings.value: Earlier holdup models assumed the angle of the solids surface in a flight is independent of flight geometry. Revol et al. remove that assumption. 'Curved flights of an appropriate shape ... lift and then release gradually a large amount of solids.' The model gives holdup and cascading rate for inclined or horizontal drums, cocurrent or countercurrent.
findings.source: Revol D., Briens C.L., Chabagno J.M. (2001) The design of flights in rotary dryers
findings.evidence: Abstract fragments quoted in search results

findings.parameter: Sherritt, Caple, Behie & Mehrotra flighted-drum transport model
findings.value: Particle motion is split into an airborne phase and a dense phase, with separate equations for holdup and axial flow rate. It covers cocurrent and countercurrent flow, mixed particle sizes, horizontal or inclined drums, any flight type, and under- or over-loaded drums. Part II adds axial displacement of airborne particles by gas drag, plus validation.
findings.context: Part I: Can. J. Chem. Eng. 71 (1993) 337-346, doi 10.1002/cjce.5450710302. Part II: Can. J. Chem. Eng. 72 (1994) 240-248, doi 10.1002/cjce.5450720210. Applications include coal, grain, wood chips, ore drying, fertilizer cooling and coked oil-sand combustion. NOTE: the published years are 1993/1994, not 2003.
findings.source: Sherritt R.G., Caple R., Behie L.A., Mehrotra A.K.
findings.evidence: Abstract via Semantic Scholar, Wiley and OSTI records

findings.parameter: Lee & Sheehan geometric unloading model
findings.value: Geometry-based unloading profile for a generic two-section (unserrated, straight) flight, validated on a flight-unloading rig. The fit is good but 'highly sensitive to the material surface angle used'. High-speed photography shows unloading is discontinuous, with significant fluctuations.
findings.context: Powder Technology 198(3) (2010) 395-403
findings.source: Lee A., Sheehan M.E. (2010) Development of a geometric flight unloading model for flighted rotary dryers
findings.evidence: JCU repository abstract

findings.parameter: Design load definitions
findings.value: Holdup is classed as under-, over- or at-design-load. Porter (1963) defines design load from the first unloading flight (FUF) contents. Baker (1988) defines it as 2 x the holdup of flights in the upper half of the drum, assuming lower-half flights hold the same. Matchett & Baker (1988) take the design load as the transition point on a log-log plot of holdup vs throughput. Karali et al. (2015) take it as saturation of the FUF cross-sectional area as filling degree increases.
findings.context: The design load is the drum filling at which flights are just saturated and the bottom bed is minimal, which maximises the airborne curtain. Baker's model also gives the number of flights to fit.
findings.source: Ajayi & Sheehan 2012 (Chem. Eng. Sci. 73:400-411) and Karali et al. 2015 (Chem. Eng. Sci. 138:772-779), as summarised in search results
findings.evidence: Search summaries quoting the papers' literature reviews

findings.parameter: Ajayi & Sheehan (2012) design loading tests
findings.value: Dynamic angle of repose 44.7 deg to 62.3 deg (free-flowing to cohesive, made cohesive with a low-volatility fluid). Drum speed 2.5-4.5 rpm. Airborne solids characterised by Eulerian-Eulerian CFD at flow rates listed as '0.703 to 0.134 kg/s'. The gas-borne to flight-borne solids ratio at design loading is 0.042-0.078 (reported by a citing paper).
findings.context: Pilot-scale horizontal flighted dryer, photographic (image-analysis) design-load estimation
findings.source: Ajayi O.O., Sheehan M.E. (2012) Design loading of free flowing and cohesive solids in flighted rotary dryers, Chem. Eng. Sci. 73:400-411
findings.evidence: Abstract fragments. The 0.042-0.078 ratio comes from a citing paper (secondary).

findings.parameter: Karali et al. 2015 optimum-loading drum
findings.value: Drum D = 1.0 m, L = 0.3 m. 12 and 18 flights. 1, 3 and 5 rpm. Measured as a continuous function of flight angular position: kinetic angle of repose in the flight, individual flight holdup, final discharge angle, cascading rate, and height and time of the falling curtains.
findings.source: Karali M.A., Sunkara K.R., Herz F., Specht E. (2015) Experimental analysis of a flighted rotary drum to assess the optimum loading
findings.evidence: Abstract and search summary

findings.parameter: Karali et al. 2018 unloading at optimum loading
findings.value: Drum D = 0.5 m, L = 0.15 m, 1-5 rpm, 12 and 18 flights, flight length ratios 0.375 and 0.75. Flight holdup is mainly influenced by the flight length ratio. The maximum falling-curtain height occurs at optimum loading, because the bottom solid bed no longer exists (unlike in over-loaded drums). Measured fall height was compared with a literature correlation.
findings.context: Powder Technology 333 (2018) 347-352, doi 10.1016/j.powtec.2018.04.052
findings.source: Karali M.A., Specht E., Herz F., Mellmann J., Refaey H.A. (2018) Unloading characteristics of flights in a flighted rotary drum operated at optimum loading
findings.evidence: Abstract and highlights via search

findings.parameter: Optimum filling degree of flighted drums (Karali group)
findings.value: Practical optimal filling degree is 15%-20%. The filling needed for optimum loading depends more on flight geometry than on rotation speed.
findings.context: Rectangular (two-section) flights, lab drums 0.5-1.0 m
findings.source: Karali group papers (summary in search results). Full thesis: Karali M.A. (2015) Dr.-Ing. thesis, OVGU Magdeburg, 'Analysis study of the axial transport and heat transfer of a flighted rotary drum operated at optimum loading'
findings.evidence: Quoted in search summary: 'In practical applications, the optimal filling degree ranged between 15% and 20%.' I could not open the thesis PDF (proxy blocked).

findings.parameter: Sunkara et al. 2013 flight design effect on particle distribution
findings.value: Mathematical model for rectangular flights that optimises total airborne particle surface area as a function of cascading rate and falling time. Drum 500 mm D x 150 mm L, 12 and 18 flights. As the flight length ratio increases, the cascading rate falls during early discharge but rises rapidly at higher discharge positions. Optimal flight length ratio for maximum effective area is about 1.5 with no gas flow. The final discharge angle was underpredicted (corrected in a 2022 paper).
findings.context: Chem. Eng. Sci. (2013), 'Influence of flight design on the particle distribution of a flighted rotating drum'
findings.source: Sunkara K.R., Herz F., Specht E., Mellmann J. (2013)
findings.evidence: Abstract via academia.edu and ResearchGate listing

findings.parameter: Final discharge angle model (2022)
findings.value: New model from a force balance on a single particle, including the Coriolis force on the last particles sliding down the flight. Validated in 0.5 m and 1.0 m drums with 12 flights, using glass beads and quartz sand. The final discharge angle increases with flight length ratio l2/l1 and with Froude number. Cascading rate and fall height stay high in the final discharge range, depending on l2/l1.
findings.context: Granular Matter 24(4) (2022), doi 10.1007/s10035-022-01283-x (open access; TIB mirror)
findings.source: Modelling the final discharge angle in flighted rotary drums (Specht/Herz group)
findings.evidence: Abstract via search. Full text is open access but WebFetch was blocked in this session.

findings.parameter: Karali et al. 2020 residence-time model at optimum loading
findings.value: Mean residence time from a force balance on a single travelling particle. Inputs are the mean falling-curtain height and the final discharge angle. Validated on a batch drum and a small rotary dryer, cocurrent and countercurrent. A factor is introduced to generalise one literature correlation.
findings.context: Drying Technology 38(4) (2020) 495-505, doi 10.1080/07373937.2019.1582062. PDF hosted by Benha University.
findings.source: Karali, Specht, Mellmann, Refaey, Salem, Elbanhawy (2020) Granular transport through flighted rotary drums operated at optimum-loading: Mathematical model
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: Schofield-Glikin equation validity
findings.value: Applies when the ratio of centrifugal to gravitational force on the particle is < 0.4. Kelly, Baker and Schofield-Glikin models lacked published experimental validation until later image-based studies, which measured the angle in an industrial dryer and back-calculated the friction coefficient.
findings.context: Dynamic angle of repose of material in a flight vs angular position
findings.source: Lisboa et al. (2007) Braz. J. Chem. Eng. 24(3):365-374 and related SciELO papers (search summaries)
findings.evidence: Search summary

findings.parameter: Sheehan, Britton & Schneider (2005) compartment transport model
findings.value: Compartment (paired tanks) model of a countercurrent flighted dryer, covering under-, over- and design-loaded operation. The empirical model needs 4 fitted parameters; the pseudo-physical model (dryer and flight geometry plus solids properties) needs 2. Fitted to an industrial sugar-dryer RTD and solved in gPROMS.
findings.context: Chem. Eng. Sci. 60(15) (2005) 4171-4182. Follow-up: Britton, Sheehan & Schneider (2006) Powder Technol.
findings.source: Sheehan M.E., Britton P.F., Schneider P.A.
findings.evidence: Repository abstract

findings.parameter: Matchett & Baker two-stream residence time model
findings.value: Two-stream model (airborne and flight/bed streams). Part 1 derivation: J. Separ. Proc. Technol. 8 (1987) 11-17. Part 2 application to experimental and industrial data: 9 (1988) 5-13. I did not retrieve the axial-advance-per-cascade equation.
findings.context: Transport/residence time in cascading dryers
findings.source: Matchett A.J., Baker C.G.J.
findings.evidence: Citation lists in search results

findings.parameter: McCormick (1962) Ua exponent
findings.value: Ua = K G^n / D with n between 0.46 and 0.67. 'n = 0.67 is probably the most representative of commercial equipment.' Measured Nu values are often much smaller than calculated ones (Mujumdar 2006). Heat transfer is reported as unaffected by slope and by rotational speed, which mainly affect residence time.
findings.units: Ua W m-3 K-1; G kg m-2 s-1 (gas mass velocity); D m
findings.context: Direct-heat (gas-contact) flighted dryers. A lumped volumetric coefficient that includes the curtain area a.
findings.source: McCormick P.Y. (1962) as summarised in NC State thesis and ScienceDirect 'Rotary Dryers' topic page
findings.evidence: Search summaries

findings.parameter: Ua prefactor (SI) for n = 0.67
findings.value: Ua = 237 G^0.67 / D. Worked example: G' = 0.961 kg m-2 s-1, d = 2 m gives Ua = 115 W/m3K. Another secondary paper quotes the Friedman & Marshall correlation with K = 244.7 (W m-3 C-1, G kg m-2 s-1, D m; exponent not legible in snippet), valid for shell speeds 0.2-0.5 m/s and holdups 2-8%. Baker (1983) says no Ua correlation can be recommended with confidence, but Friedman & Marshall is the most reliable.
findings.context: My own unit conversion of the textbook (Perry-type) form Ua = 0.5 G^0.67/D [Btu h-1 ft-3 F-1; G lb h-1 ft-2; D ft] gives 236.9 G^0.67/D in SI, which matches the 237 example.
findings.source: chempds blog worked example (secondary); SciELO fertilizer rotary dryer paper (secondary); unit conversion done here
findings.evidence: Search snippets: 'U_a = [237 x (G')^0.67]/d = [237 x (0.961)^0.67]/2, U_a = 115 W/m^3 K' and 'K = 244.7 for Ua in W m-3 C-1 ... shell speeds of 0.2 to 0.5 m/s and holdups of 2 to 8%'

findings.parameter: Friedman & Marshall (1949) Ua constants (conflicting secondary value)
findings.value: K = 44 and n = 0.16 with G in kg m-2 h-1 and D in m (one review). Another secondary snippet gives Ua = 0.247 Ms rho_s V^0.5 G^0.16. A patent says the F&M equation predicted 6 Btu/(h ft3 F) for a 7-ft drum. Friedman & Marshall ran 134 cocurrent and countercurrent tests on four sands.
findings.context: Friedman S.J., Marshall W.R. (1949) Studies in rotary drying Part II, Chem. Eng. Prog. 45:573-588. These constants conflict with the n = 0.67 form; use with caution.
findings.source: Secondary reviews (Oregon State 'Engineering Analysis of a Rotary Dryer'; ResearchGate review) and US patent 4506453
findings.evidence: Search summaries only

findings.parameter: Myklestad Ua correlation
findings.context: Myklestad (1963) was among the first rotary dryer models. Units were unknown in the snippet.
findings.source: Secondary design-guide snippet in search results
findings.evidence: Search summary: 'Myklestad's simpler form is Ua=420xG0.8'

findings.parameter: Wall-to-waste heat transfer coefficient with lifters, externally heated pyrolysis kiln
findings.value: Six lifters, 200 mm high: mean k(m-w) rises from 38.6 to 45.3 W/m2K at 2.7 rpm, and to 50.1 W/m2K at 4.0 rpm. More lifters and taller lifters both increase the coefficient.
findings.context: Batch-type externally heated rotary kiln pyrolyser with simulant municipal waste. Companion paper JTST 3(3):523-531 measures k from wall thermocouple pairs. A later plastic-waste paper cites about 40 W/m2K, rising to about 50 W/m2K with heat-transfer parts on the retort inner wall. This is the closest literature analogue to the KINTEK lifter drum.
findings.source: Suzuki T., Okazaki T., Yamamoto K., Nakata H., Fujita O. (2008) Improvements in Pyrolysis of Wastes in an Externally Heated Rotary Kiln (Experimental Study on Heat Transfer Enhancement), J. Thermal Sci. Technol. 3(3):532-539, doi 10.1299/jtst.3.532
findings.evidence: Abstract quote: 'When six lifters 200 mm in height were attached to the inner wall of the kiln, the mean value of k_m-w increased from 38.6 W/m^2K to 45.3 W/m^2K at 2.7 rpm. In addition, k_m-w increased to 50.1 W/m^2K when the rotating speed was increased to 4.0 rpm.'

findings.parameter: Overall HTC in indirectly heated kilns without internals
findings.value: about 31-35
findings.context: Cited by a 2025 paper that builds on Hwan's segmented-lifter kiln work. Lifter-fitted designs in that paper reached higher values.
findings.source: Secondary citation in search result for Hwan I.H. (2009) PhD thesis, Curtin University (segmented lifters, ANSAC pilot hot kiln)
findings.evidence: Search summary

findings.parameter: Segmented lifters in an indirectly heated kiln (Hwan 2009)
findings.value: Segmented lifters give flatter bed-depth profiles and stronger axial transport than bar lifters. Good heat transfer comes at low rotational Reynolds number with strong axial mixing. Heat transfer pathways: freeboard gas to exposed bed, covered wall to covered bed, freeboard gas to falling particles.
findings.context: Cold-kiln tests at Curtin and hot pilot kiln at ANSAC Bunbury. Dimensional analysis for scale-up.
findings.source: Hwan I.H. (2009) Heat transfer mechanisms in an indirectly heated rotary kiln with lifters and its role in scaling, PhD thesis, Curtin University
findings.evidence: Thesis abstract

findings.parameter: Wall-to-solid HTC in flighted kilns (Bongo Njeng et al.)
findings.value: Measured by energy balance in an indirectly heated pilot kiln. Variables: rotation speed, filling degree, lifter shape, wall temperature (100-500 C). A dimensional-analysis correlation is proposed. Existing models are the right order of magnitude but fail to capture trends with operating conditions.
findings.context: Exp. Thermal Fluid Sci. 91 (2018) 197-213. HAL open copy hal-01624450. AIChE 2015 abstract: kiln 1.95 m long, quartz sand, with and without lifters.
findings.source: Bongo Njeng A.S., Vitu S., Clausse M., Dirion J.-L., Debacq M.
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: Seidenbecher et al. flighted-drum thermal experiments
findings.value: Indirectly heated drum L = 1.76 m, D = 0.5 m, L-shaped flights, glass beads, batch. Flight length ratio 0.375-2.0, number of flights 6-18. Secondary: ratios of 1, 1.5 and 0.75 gave better heat transfer. Companion 2020 paper: higher rotational speed and air flow give faster temperature change; higher filling degree gives a slower temperature drop. Curtain density decides whether gas bypasses or penetrates the curtain; if it penetrates, the whole inner curtain area (sum of particle surfaces) is exposed.
findings.context: Chem. Eng. Sci. 240 (2021) 116652 and 229 (2020) 115972. Contact-HT paper: Thermal Sci. Eng. Prog. 47 (2024) 102265, which found an existing unflighted-drum contact model agreed with measurements in the flighted drum. Dissertation: Seidenbecher 2021, Halle (open repository).
findings.source: Seidenbecher J., Herz F., Meitzner C., Specht E., Wirtz S., Scherer V., Liu X.
findings.evidence: Abstracts and Halle record via search. The 'best ratio' statement is secondary.

findings.parameter: Curtain heat transfer experiment (Wardjiman & Rhodes)
findings.value: Duct 0.15 x 0.60 m. Horizontal air 0.9-1.2 m/s. Curtain thickness 4-10 cm. Solids 0.031-0.040 kg/s. A single-particle model predicts particle temperatures well but gas temperatures poorly.
findings.context: Powder Technology 191(3) (2009) 247-253
findings.source: Wardjiman C., Rhodes M. (2009) Heat transfer in a particle curtain falling through a horizontally-flowing gas stream
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: Curtain hydrodynamics (Wardjiman et al. 2008)
findings.value: Sand d = 204 um, 0.031-0.047 kg/s, inlet curtain thickness 0.02-0.10 m, air 0-1.2 m/s. CFD agrees with experiment; the single-particle model is less satisfactory because the real gas flow is non-uniform. Thesis: a 2 cm inlet curtain diverges as it falls; at 4 cm or more it becomes slightly converging.
findings.context: Powder Technology 188(2) (2008) 110-118
findings.source: Wardjiman C., Lee A., Sheehan M., Rhodes M.
findings.evidence: Abstract and Monash thesis abstract

findings.parameter: CFD-derived reduced model of curtain heat transfer (Afshar et al.)
findings.value: Silica spheres rho = 2634 kg/m3, 200/400/600 um, 400 K, 0.041-0.2 kg/s from a slot. Changing the slot size at 0.041 kg/s (400 um) can raise convective heat transfer per unit mass by up to 13%. A reduced-order model predicts curtain centreline particle temperature, with a drag coefficient tuned to size and mass flow.
findings.context: Prog. Comput. Fluid Dyn. 15(2) (2015) 71-80. Open 2012 CFD conference paper at JCU.
findings.source: Afshar S., Sheehan M., Fazlollahi (2015) Using CFD to derive reduced order models for heat transfer in particle curtains
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: Minimal model for convection and radiation in flighted kilns (Le Guen et al.)
findings.value: Gas, granular suspension (curtain) and bed exchange heat in a channel. Without radiation, temperature profiles are exponential. With radiation, the profiles fit stretched exponentials whose parameters are the same for all phases. An efficiency criterion sets the optimal kiln length.
findings.context: Can. J. Chem. Eng. 95 (2017) 100-110. Open full text on arXiv 1612.05762. Related: Piton et al. (2015) Appl. Therm. Eng. 75, 1-D coupled thermal-granular flighted-kiln model validated on an asphalt plant.
findings.source: Le Guen L., Piton M., Henaut Q., Huchet F., Richard P.
findings.evidence: Abstract (full text not read; fetch blocked)

findings.parameter: DEM: effect of lifters on heat transfer (Xie et al. 2017)
findings.value: Citing papers say the specific heat transfer coefficient of the particle flow increases with rotating speed but decreases with more and higher lifters. Another citation reports heat transfer efficiency rising with lifter height and falling slightly with lifter number. The secondary reports conflict.
findings.context: Powder Technology 314 (2017) 175-181, doi 10.1016/j.powtec.2016.09.022, 'DEM investigation of heat transfer in a drum mixer with lifters'
findings.source: Xie Q., Chen Z., Hou Q., Yu A.B., Yang R.
findings.evidence: Statements from citing papers only

findings.parameter: DEM: baffles/lifters and wall heat conduction (Ardalani/Rutgers, AIChE 2018/2020)
findings.value: Heat transfer first improves significantly as the number and size of baffles increase, but an excessive number of baffles can reduce the heat transfer rate. This is conduction-only DEM.
findings.context: Conduction-dominated (indirectly heated) drums. Relevant to an externally heated pyrolysis kiln.
findings.source: Ardalani et al., AIChE Annual Meeting 2020 paper 263g; Yohannes/Muzzio et al. AIChE 2018 paper 224c
findings.evidence: Conference abstract

findings.parameter: PTV + DEM of flighted drum (Zhang et al. 2020)
findings.value: Lab drum with 4 rectangular flights and plastic particles. 10, 20, 30 rpm. Filling 10, 15, 20%. DEM in LIGGGHTS. Higher speed raises holdup ratio and cascading rate of an individual flight. Average velocity and granular temperature rise with speed and fall with filling. PTV and DEM agree well. Follow-up (Particuology 2020, doi 10.1016/j.partic.2020.09.010): 1/4/8/12 flights, 15% fill. 8 and 12 flights give a larger and more stable dilute-phase ratio. DEM matches PTV; literature models deviate significantly.
findings.context: Powder Technology 363 (2020) 23-37, doi 10.1016/j.powtec.2019.12.035. PhD thesis by L. Zhang (OVGU 2020) also covers MPT.
findings.source: Zhang L., Jiang Z., Weigler F., Herz F., Mellmann J., Tsotsas E.
findings.evidence: Abstracts

findings.parameter: DEM: inclined flights (Zhu et al. 2023)
findings.value: Maximum mass of particles in the active phase at 37 rpm, joint angle 139 deg, inlet 7.83 kg/s. Inclined flights raise axial speed by 26% vs a drum without them.
findings.context: Processes 11 (2023) 1363 (open access)
findings.source: Zhu, Xie, Xu, Zhang (2023) DEM Simulation of a Rotary Drum with Inclined Flights Using the Response Surface Methodology
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: DEM: aligned vs separated flights, waste-heat drum (He, E, Jiang 2025)
findings.value: Heat exchange capacity tracks filling degree, which is most sensitive to inclination angle. Separated flights make a spiral curtain and a more uniform distribution, but exchange less heat than aligned flights and cost more than 30% more to build. Total system power stayed below 20% of the recovered power.
findings.context: Processes 13 (2025) 1594 (open access)
findings.source: He Y., E D., Jiang Z. (2025) Particle Motion and Gas-Solid Heat Exchange Enhancement in Rotary Drums with Aligned/Separated Flight
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: Eulerian (CFD) vs Lagrangian (DEM) for flighted drums
findings.value: DEM resolves individual particles and their length of fall. Eulerian is cheaper and did better when the number of flights changed. Lowering the shear modulus in DEM is valid, mainly at low rotation speed.
findings.context: Comput. Part. Mech. (2021), doi 10.1007/s40571-021-00407-z. UFU (Brazil) thesis.
findings.source: UFU group (Duarte/Barrozo school), Comparison between the Eulerian (CFD) and the Lagrangian (DEM) approaches in the simulation of a flighted rotary drum
findings.evidence: Abstract and thesis summary

findings.parameter: GPU-DEM cost benchmarks
findings.value: Mill with lifters: 12 h of compute per mill revolution at time step 4e-6 s on one NVIDIA Tesla P100. Industrial drum with 9.6 million particles run quasi-real-time (simplified contact). 8 million particles for 30 s of process time 'within a day' on a laptop GPU. GPU speed-ups of 45-75x over CPU are reported.
findings.context: Order-of-magnitude feasibility for a T4. The cited works use different hardware and contact models, so they are not directly comparable.
findings.source: Search summaries of GPU-DEM papers (Development of 3D GPU DEM code, mineral processing 2025; BlazeDEM3D-GPU; quasi-real-time rotating drum GPU)
findings.evidence: Search summaries

findings.parameter: Cohesive powders in flighted kilns (Debacq et al. 2013)
findings.value: Unloading of cohesive uranium-based powders filmed at ambient and high temperature. A geometry-based constitutive law (powder volume in lifter vs angular position) agrees well with the measurements.
findings.context: Powder Technology (2013), doi 10.1016/j.powtec.2013.04.007. Relevant to sticky or cohesive feeds.
findings.source: Debacq M., Vitu S., Ablitzer D., Houzelot J.-L., Patisson F.
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: Lifters in a tyre pyrolysis rotary kiln (Syamsiro et al. 2019)
findings.value: Kiln D = 260 mm, L = 400 mm, lifter segment length 28 mm, semi-batch at 300 C. Without lifters, 15 rpm gave the highest liquid yield. Lifters reduced liquid and solid products and increased gas.
findings.context: Waste tyre, Indonesia. Liquid yields were low in all runs.
findings.source: Syamsiro M. et al. (2019) Development of a rotary kiln reactor for pyrolytic oil production from waste tire
findings.evidence: Abstract quotes: 'the use of lifter reduced the liquid and solid products while the gaseous product increases'

findings.parameter: Solid heat carrier instead of flights for plastic pyrolysis kilns
findings.value: Quartz-sand heat carrier at 5%-15% loading (EDEM + C++ heat model). At 5% the bed slips on the wall from time to time. Above 10% the bed rolls. More carrier speeds up volatilisation, shortens vapour residence time, and gives more oil and less gas. A related PE/PP/PS kiln study (sand, 0-20% fill, 500 C) says the rolling carrier mixes particles, evens out temperature, prevents agglomeration and overcomes the 'low thermal conductivity and sticky nature of plastic waste'.
findings.context: Gao & Bao 2020 (Chinese Science Bulletin, doi 10.1360/TB-2020-0765). 'Liquid oils produced from pyrolysis of plastic wastes with heat carrier in rotary kiln', Fuel Process. Technol. (2020) S0378382020301508. 'Exergy and energy analysis...' PSEP (2020).
findings.source: Gao Y., Bao J. (2020); Fuel Process. Technol. 2020 heat-carrier kiln paper
findings.evidence: Abstracts

findings.parameter: Heating rate with solid heat carrier in a rotary kiln (plastics)
findings.value: up to 200
findings.context: Claim for integrating solid heat carriers in rotary kilns for plastic pyrolysis (in-situ catalytic, Ni/ZSM-5, Fuel 2025)
findings.source: Search summary of Fuel 2025 'In-situ catalytic pyrolysis of plastic waste in the rotary kiln with solid heat carrier coupled with Ni/ZSM-5'
findings.evidence: Search summary

findings.parameter: Steel balls as heat carrier / chains (biomass kilns)
findings.value: 1.0-1.5 mm steel balls or about 1 mm quartz or SiC sand used as heat carrier. Henrich et al. found steel balls gave the best results. A chain curtain in a rotary kiln was hypothesised to crush char.
findings.context: Biomass/biochar screw and kiln reactors. I found no plastic-specific study on steel balls.
findings.source: Review: Screw reactors and rotary kilns in biochar production (J. Anal. Appl. Pyrolysis 2023)
findings.evidence: Search summary

findings.parameter: Spiral/helical internals and tyre-wire problem (patents)
findings.value: Double rotary kiln: spiral flights add heating area and conveying, and their pitch controls residence time of about 5-45 min. Tyre reactor patent: stirring parts add cost and get entangled by steel wire, blocking the reactor. Plastic-evaporation kiln patent: preferred D 0.9-2 m at about 700 C. Batch tyre reactors use a spiral agitator or baffle plate to discharge carbon black.
findings.context: Industrial practice for tyre and plastic drums
findings.source: US 5662052 (double rotary kiln); US 8475726 B2 (tyre reactor); US patent 'Rotary kiln for the evaporation of thermoplastic waste' (USPTO 11988382); CA 2706159 / EP0853114
findings.evidence: Patent text snippets in search results

findings.parameter: Wall fouling by molten plastic
findings.value: Sticky plastic can form a thick film on the kiln shell that blocks heat transfer, and the kiln sometimes needs mechanical cleaning (informal). Agglomeration comes from a thin adhesive layer. Residual char and inorganics left in the reactor reduce heat transfer to new feed (patent). Molten plastic forms agglomerates with fluidising sand (fluidised-bed defluidisation).
findings.context: Supports the concern that open lifters foul in the melt zone
findings.source: LinkedIn article (D. Gerlach, 'Pyrolysis of mixed waste', informal); US 10093864 (continuous recycling of waste plastic)
findings.evidence: Search summaries

equations.name: Dynamic angle of repose of solids in a flight (Schofield & Glikin 1962)
equations.expression: tan(gamma) = [ mu + (R_o*omega^2/g)*(cos(theta) - mu*sin(theta)) ] / [ 1 - (R_o*omega^2/g)*(sin(theta) -/+ mu*cos(theta)) ]
equations.variables: gamma = dynamic angle of repose of the free surface in the flight (to horizontal); mu = dynamic friction coefficient (back-calculated from measured gamma; typical gamma 44.7-62.3 deg in Ajayi & Sheehan 2012); R_o = radius of flight tip; omega = drum angular speed (rad/s); g = 9.81 m/s2; theta = angular position of the flight tip
equations.validity: Force balance on a particle about to leave the flight surface. Valid for centrifugal/gravity ratio R_o*omega^2/g < 0.4. The sign in the denominator depends on how theta is measured: the snippet shows (sin theta - mu cos theta), and other papers write (sin theta + mu cos theta), so check against Sunkara 2013 or Lisboa 2007 before coding. Input to any geometric holdup model (Kelly, Baker, Lee & Sheehan, Sunkara).
equations.source: Schofield F.R., Glikin P.G. (1962) Trans. IChemE 40:183-190, as reproduced in Lisboa et al. 2007 / Revol et al. 2001

equations.name: Geometric flight holdup and cascading rate (Kelly / Baker / Lee & Sheehan / Sunkara framework)
equations.expression: h_F(theta) = rho_b * L_d * A_F(theta, gamma(theta), l1, l2, R); cascading mass rate per flight: m_dot_c(theta) = - rho_b * L_d * omega * dA_F/dtheta; total airborne rate: M_dot_air = sum over flights in discharge range of m_dot_c
equations.variables: A_F = cross-sectional area of solids held by a two-section flight (radial base l1, tip l2; flight length ratio l2/l1), bounded by the free surface at angle gamma; rho_b = bulk density; L_d = drum (flight) length; omega = angular speed
equations.validity: Holds at or below design load (flights not over-supplied by a bottom bed). Results are very sensitive to gamma (Lee & Sheehan 2010). The final discharge angle needs the Coriolis-corrected model (Granular Matter 2022). The general form is my restatement; the paper-specific area formulas were not retrieved.
equations.source: Framework of Lee & Sheehan 2010 (Powder Technol. 198:395-403); Sunkara et al. 2013 (Chem. Eng. Sci.); restated here, not verbatim

equations.name: Design load criteria
equations.expression: Baker (1988): H_DL = 2 * sum_{flights in upper half} h_F(theta). Porter (1963): H_DL set by saturation of the first unloading flight (FUF). Karali et al. (2015): design point = filling degree at which the FUF cross-section stops increasing. Matchett & Baker (1988): transition point on log(holdup) vs log(throughput).
equations.variables: H_DL = total drum holdup at design load; h_F = holdup of an individual flight
equations.validity: Practical optimum filling degree is about 15-20% (Karali group). It depends more on flight geometry than on rpm.
equations.source: Ajayi & Sheehan 2012 and Karali et al. 2015 (literature reviews within)

equations.name: Volumetric gas-solids heat transfer coefficient (McCormick 1962 form)
equations.expression: Ua = K * G^n / D, with n = 0.46-0.67 (0.67 recommended). SI: Ua [W m-3 K-1] = 237 * G^0.67 / D (G in kg m-2 s-1, D in m). Equivalent textbook form: Ua = 0.5 G^0.67 / D [Btu h-1 ft-3 F-1; G lb h-1 ft-2; D ft]; 0.5 x 18.63 x 737.35^0.67 / 3.2808 = 236.9 (conversion done here).
equations.variables: U = heat transfer coefficient; a = curtain (airborne particle) surface area per drum volume; G = gas mass velocity based on drum cross-section; D = drum diameter
equations.validity: Direct-contact cascading dryers at about design load, with shell speeds about 0.2-0.5 m/s and holdups 2-8% (F&M range quoted in a secondary source). Lumps convection to curtain and bed. Does not cover radiation-dominated, indirectly heated pyrolysis kilns with low gas flow, where G (sweep gas or pyrolysis vapour) is small, so it will under-predict there. Baker (1983): no Ua correlation can be recommended with confidence.
equations.source: McCormick 1962 via NCSU thesis; SI constant from chempds worked example; secondary K = 244.7 (exponent not legible) from SciELO fertilizer-dryer paper

equations.name: Mean residence time (Friedman & Marshall data; Perry & Chilton form)
equations.expression: tau [min] = 0.23 * L / (D * N^0.9 * tan(alpha)) [+/- gas-drag term]. SI variant with drag: tau [s] = 0.3344 * L / (S * N^0.9 * D) +/- 0.6085 * (...) * d_p^-0.5 (second term garbled in source). '+' for countercurrent, '-' for cocurrent.
equations.variables: L = drum length; D = diameter; N = speed (rpm in first form, rev/s in SI form); alpha or S = drum slope; d_p = particle diameter; G = gas mass velocity
equations.validity: Empirical, for free-flowing granular solids in flighted dryers. The often-quoted textbook drag term '0.6 B L G/F with B = 5 Dp^-0.5' was NOT verified in this session. Do not mix the 0.23 and 0.3344 constants (different units).
equations.source: Perry & Chilton form via secondary sources; SI variant from ScienceDirect 'new corrected formula ... filamentous particles' (2016) and Atlantis Press MME 2016

equations.name: Gas-particle convection in the curtain (Ranz-Marshall)
equations.expression: Nu_p = h_p d_p / k_g = 2 + 0.6 Re_p^0.5 Pr^(1/3); Re_p = rho_g |u_g - v_p| d_p / mu_g
equations.variables: h_p = particle heat transfer coefficient; d_p = particle diameter; k_g, rho_g, mu_g = gas properties; v_p = particle velocity (about g*t during free fall); u_g = gas velocity
equations.validity: Isolated spheres. Wardjiman & Rhodes 2009 found single-particle models predict curtain particle temperatures well but gas temperatures poorly. Dense curtains shield the interior (Afshar 2015: slot geometry changes heat transfer per mass by up to 13%). The Twente rotating-cone study found Ranz-Marshall reasonable for 159-284 um but under-predicting for 428 um particles.
equations.source: Ranz W.E., Marshall W.R. (1952) Chem. Eng. Prog. 48 (standard correlation); applicability per Wardjiman & Rhodes 2009

equations.name: Falling-curtain kinematics and per-cascade heat pickup (derived)
equations.expression: t_f = sqrt(2 y_f / g) (drag-free); v_p(t) = g t; per-pass particle energy balance: m_p c_p dT_p/dt = h_p pi d_p^2 (T_g - T_p) + eps_p sigma pi d_p^2 F_view (T_w^4 - T_p^4); number of cascades = tau_res / (t_f + t_flight), where t_flight is about (theta_discharge - theta_load)/omega
equations.variables: y_f = fall height from discharge point to bed or opposite wall (Karali 2018: maximum at design load); t_f = fall time; T_w = wall temperature; eps_p = particle emissivity; F_view = effective view factor (reduced by curtain shielding)
equations.validity: Derived here from basic kinematics and an energy balance; this is not a literature correlation. For d_p > ~0.5 mm, terminal velocity is not reached over typical drum falls of 0.2-2 m. Particle Biot number must be small (polymer granules or tyre chips over a few mm violate this: use intra-particle conduction).
equations.source: Derived (standard kinematics + lumped-capacitance balance); single-particle approach as used by Wardjiman & Rhodes 2009

equations.name: Curtain solids fraction and radiative opacity (derived)
equations.expression: phi_c = m_dot'_c / (rho_p * delta_c * v_p); optical thickness tau_c = 1.5 * Q_ext * phi_c * delta_c / d_p (Q_ext about 1 for large opaque spheres, geometric optics); curtain emissivity / opacity eps_c = 1 - exp(-tau_c)
equations.variables: m_dot'_c = curtain mass flow per unit drum length (kg m-1 s-1); delta_c = curtain thickness; v_p = particle velocity; rho_p = particle density; phi_c = solid volume fraction
equations.validity: Derived here (Beer-Lambert for monodisperse spheres: projected area per volume = 1.5 phi/d_p). Assumes a uniform, dilute curtain. Falling-particle solar receivers measured opacities of 0.5-1, with phi dropping from about 0.6 at release to below 0.1 within 0.5 m of fall (Sandia, J. Sol. Energy Eng. 2017). Use it to split wall-to-curtain vs wall-to-bed radiation.
equations.source: Derived; supporting data: Sandia 'Characterization of Particle Flow in a Free-Falling Solar Particle Receiver' (2017)

equations.name: Axial advance per cascade (Saeman/Matchett-Baker type, derived)
equations.expression: dz_cascade = y_f * sin(alpha) +/- dz_drag, with dz_drag of order (1/2) * a_drag * t_f^2 and a_drag = (3/4) C_D (rho_g/rho_p) |u_g - v_p| (u_g - v_p) / d_p; mean axial solids velocity u_s = dz_cascade / (t_f + t_flight) (+ bed rolling contribution)
equations.variables: alpha = drum slope; y_f = fall height; u_g = axial gas velocity (+ cocurrent); C_D = drag coefficient
equations.validity: Derived here as the kinematic basis of Matchett & Baker (1987/88) and Sherritt et al. (1993/94) airborne-phase transport. Their exact closures were not retrieved. Over-loaded drums add a rolling-bed (kiln-type) transport term.
equations.source: Derived; framework of Matchett & Baker 1987-88 and Sherritt et al. 1993-94

equations.name: Critical (centrifuging) speed and Froude number
equations.expression: Fr = omega^2 R / g; n_c [rpm] = (60 / (2 pi)) * sqrt(g / R) = 42.3 / sqrt(D [m])
equations.variables: R = drum radius; D = diameter; omega = angular speed
equations.validity: Standard mechanics. Flighted dryers and kilns run at small Fr (typically 1-5 rpm in 0.5-1 m lab drums per Karali et al.). The Schofield-Glikin limit R_o omega^2/g < 0.4 applies.
equations.source: Standard mechanics (derived)

equations.name: Wall-to-bed overall coefficient definition (Suzuki et al. 2008)
equations.expression: q_w = k_m-w * (T_wall - T_waste); measured k_m-w = 38.6 (no lifters) -> 45.3 (6 x 200 mm lifters) W m-2 K-1 at 2.7 rpm; 50.1 W m-2 K-1 at 4.0 rpm with lifters
equations.variables: q_w = heat flux through the drum wall (from wall thermocouple pairs); k_m-w = overall wall-to-waste coefficient
equations.validity: Batch externally heated waste-pyrolysis kiln. Gives a direct multiplier for lifters of about 1.17x at 2.7 rpm and about 1.30x when also going to 4.0 rpm.
equations.source: Suzuki et al. (2008) J. Therm. Sci. Technol. 3(3):532-539

key_sources.citation: Suzuki T., Okazaki T., Yamamoto K., Nakata H., Fujita O. (2008) Improvements in Pyrolysis of Wastes in an Externally Heated Rotary Kiln (Experimental Study on Heat Transfer Enhancement). J. Therm. Sci. Technol. 3(3):532-539 (+ companion 3(3):523-531)
key_sources.why: The only quantitative data found for lifters in an externally heated waste-pyrolysis kiln, matching the KINTEK concept. Wall-to-waste k is 38.6 W/m2K without lifters, 45.3 with them, and 50.1 at 4 rpm. Open on J-STAGE.

key_sources.citation: Karali M.A. et al. (2015) Chem. Eng. Sci. 138:772-779; (2018) Powder Technol. 333:347-352; (2020) Drying Technol. 38(4):495-505; Karali Dr.-Ing. thesis OVGU 2015
key_sources.why: The design/optimum-loading programme: holdup, final discharge angle, cascading rate, curtain fall height and time, axial transport and curtain heat transfer. The thesis is open access and the best single source for curtain-model equations and validation data.

key_sources.citation: Sunkara K.R., Herz F., Specht E., Mellmann J. (2013) Influence of flight design on the particle distribution of a flighted rotating drum. Chem. Eng. Sci.; plus 'Modelling the final discharge angle in flighted rotary drums', Granular Matter 24 (2022)
key_sources.why: Geometric holdup and cascading-rate model for rectangular flights, optimising airborne surface area. The open-access 2022 paper adds Coriolis-corrected final discharge. Lab data: 0.5 and 1.0 m drums, 12-18 flights.

key_sources.citation: Lee A., Sheehan M.E. (2010) Powder Technol. 198(3):395-403; Ajayi O.O., Sheehan M.E. (2012) Chem. Eng. Sci. 73:400-411; Sheehan, Britton, Schneider (2005) Chem. Eng. Sci. 60:4171-4182
key_sources.why: JCU school: geometric unloading model, design-load criteria for free-flowing and cohesive solids, and compartment transport models suitable for 1-D process simulation.

key_sources.citation: Sherritt R.G., Caple R., Behie L.A., Mehrotra A.K. (1993/1994) The movement of solids through flighted rotating drums, Parts I and II. Can. J. Chem. Eng. 71:337-346; 72:240-248
key_sources.why: Classic airborne/dense-phase holdup and transport model with gas drag, valid for any flight type and under- or over-loading. Note it was published in 1993/94, not 2003.

key_sources.citation: Revol D., Briens C.L., Chabagno J.M. (2001) The design of flights in rotary dryers. Powder Technol. 121:230-238
key_sources.why: Holdup/cascade model where the surface angle depends on flight geometry. Covers curved flights like the KINTEK infographic.

key_sources.citation: Le Guen L., Piton M., Henaut Q., Huchet F., Richard P. (2017) Heat convection and radiation in flighted rotary kilns: A minimal model. Can. J. Chem. Eng. 95:100-110 (arXiv:1612.05762)
key_sources.why: Open-access minimal gas/curtain/bed heat-exchange model with radiation. A good template for a cheap GPU curtain-heat-transfer module.

key_sources.citation: Bongo Njeng A.S., Vitu S., Clausse M., Dirion J.-L., Debacq M. (2018) Wall-to-solid heat transfer coefficient in flighted rotary kilns. Exp. Therm. Fluid Sci. 91:197-213 (HAL open copy)
key_sources.why: Indirectly heated pilot kiln with lifters, 100-500 C. Dimensional-analysis correlation for wall-to-solid HTC including lifter shape. The most relevant validation for an externally heated flighted pyrolyser.

key_sources.citation: Seidenbecher J. et al. (2020) Chem. Eng. Sci. 229:115972; (2021) Chem. Eng. Sci. 240:116652; (2024) Therm. Sci. Eng. Prog. 47:102265; Seidenbecher Dissertation 2021 (Halle, open)
key_sources.why: Indirectly heated flighted drum (0.5 x 1.76 m): flight length ratio 0.375-2.0, 6-18 flights, separate contact and curtain-convection heat transfer. The open dissertation has the curtain heat-transfer analysis.

key_sources.citation: Wardjiman C., Rhodes M. (2009) Powder Technol. 191:247-253; Wardjiman et al. (2008) Powder Technol. 188:110-118; Afshar, Sheehan, Fazlollahi (2015) Prog. CFD 15:71-80
key_sources.why: Experimental and CFD curtain hydrodynamics and gas-curtain heat transfer, including limits of single-particle models. Use for curtain closure validation.

key_sources.citation: Zhang L., Jiang Z., Weigler F., Herz F., Mellmann J., Tsotsas E. (2020) PTV measurement and DEM simulation of the particle motion in a flighted rotating drum. Powder Technol. 363:23-37; + Particuology 2020 (number of flights)
key_sources.why: DEM (LIGGGHTS) validated against PTV for flighted drums at 10-30 rpm and 10-20% fill. A benchmark for a DEM-slice demonstrator.

key_sources.citation: Gao Y., Bao J. (2020) The simulation of particle movement and heat transfer in rotary kiln for plastic waste pyrolysis. Chinese Science Bulletin, doi 10.1360/TB-2020-0765
key_sources.why: Plastic-specific DEM with a sand heat carrier (5-15%) instead of flights. Shows the industrial alternative to lifters for sticky plastics.

key_sources.citation: Hwan I.H. (2009) Heat transfer mechanisms in an indirectly heated rotary kiln with lifters and its role in scaling. PhD thesis, Curtin University (open via CORE)
key_sources.why: Open full-text thesis on an indirectly heated kiln with segmented lifters: heat-transfer pathway split (wall-bed, gas-bed, gas-falling particles) and scaling criteria.

key_sources.citation: Syamsiro M. et al. (2019) Development of a rotary kiln reactor for pyrolytic oil production from waste tire
key_sources.why: Small tyre-pyrolysis kiln tested with and without lifters. Lifters cut liquid yield and raised gas, a cautionary data point for the KINTEK claim that flights give 'less secondary cracking'.

critical_numbers: Flights per circle in commercial dryers: 2.4-3.0 x D (D apparently in ft), shell speed 60-75 ft/min (Mujumdar chapter, secondary)
Optimum (design) filling degree of flighted drums: 15-20% of drum volume (Karali group, secondary)
Lab flighted drums used for validation: D 0.5 m x L 0.15 m and D 1.0 m x L 0.3 m, 12 or 18 flights, flight length ratio l2/l1 0.375 and 0.75, 1-5 rpm (Karali 2015/2018)
Optimal flight length ratio for maximum airborne effective area: ~1.5, no gas flow (Sunkara 2013, abstract)
Indirectly heated flighted drum: D 0.5 m, L 1.76 m, flight length ratio 0.375-2.0, 6-18 flights (Seidenbecher 2021)
Dynamic angle of repose range, free-flowing to cohesive: 44.7-62.3 deg at 2.5-4.5 rpm (Ajayi & Sheehan 2012)
Gas-borne to flight-borne solids ratio at design load: 0.042-0.078 (secondary, citing Ajayi & Sheehan 2012)
Schofield-Glikin validity: R*omega^2/g < 0.4
Ua = K G^n/D, n = 0.46-0.67 (0.67 recommended); SI Ua = 237 G^0.67/D W m-3 K-1 (G kg m-2 s-1, D m), equivalent to 0.5 G^0.67/D in Btu/(h ft3 F)
Friedman & Marshall Ua validity range (secondary): shell speed 0.2-0.5 m/s, holdup 2-8%; K = 244.7 W m-3 C-1 (exponent not visible)
Externally heated pyrolysis kiln wall-to-waste coefficient: 38.6 W/m2K without lifters, 45.3 W/m2K with 6 x 200 mm lifters at 2.7 rpm, 50.1 W/m2K at 4.0 rpm (Suzuki et al. 2008)
Indirectly heated kilns without internals: overall HTC ~31-35 W/m2K (secondary)
Curtain experiments: 0.15 x 0.60 m duct, air 0-1.2 m/s, sand 204 um, 0.031-0.047 kg/s, curtain 0.02-0.10 m thick (Wardjiman 2008/2009)
Curtain slot geometry changes convective heat transfer per unit mass by up to 13% (Afshar 2015)
Falling-particle receiver curtain: phi drops from ~60% at release to <10% within 0.5 m of fall; opacity 0.5-1 (Sandia 2017)
DEM flighted drum (PTV-validated): 4 flights, 10/20/30 rpm, 10/15/20% fill (Zhang 2020); 8-12 flights give larger and more stable dilute phase
Inclined flights raise axial speed by 26% vs straight (Zhu 2023 DEM); separated flights cost >30% more to build and exchange less heat than aligned flights (He 2025)
Plastic kiln sand heat carrier: 5% loading slips, >10% rolls (Gao & Bao 2020); 0-20% fill at 500 C (FPT 2020); heating rate up to 200 C/s claimed (secondary)
Biomass kiln steel-ball heat carrier: 1.0-1.5 mm (Henrich et al., via review)
Tyre kiln D 260 mm x L 400 mm: lifters (28 mm segment) reduced liquid and raised gas yield; best liquid without lifters at 15 rpm (Syamsiro 2019)
GPU-DEM order of magnitude: 12 h per mill revolution at dt = 4e-6 s on one P100 (mill with lifters); 8e6 particles x 30 s process time in about 1 day on a laptop GPU (secondary)

CORRECTIONS TO THE BRIEF:
- Sherritt et al. was published in 1993 (Part I) and 1994 (Part II) in Can. J. Chem. Eng., not 2003.
- The Kelly holdup work found was dated 1968, 1977 and 1992, not 1969.
- I could not verify the radial flight height rule (1/8-1/12 D) or the Friedman-Marshall residence-time drag term '0.6 B L G/F, B = 5 Dp^-0.5'. Treat both as unverified.
- Secondary sources give conflicting Friedman-Marshall Ua constants (n = 0.67 vs n = 0.16).
- I excluded one search summary that attributed the numbers 656.88 K and 151.15 W/m2K to Seidenbecher 2021, because they appear to come from a different (baffled-drum) paper.

PHYSICS TAKEAWAYS FOR THE KINTEK-STYLE KILN:
1. Flights help in two ways. They raise wall-to-bed contact heat transfer modestly: Suzuki 2008 measured about +17% at 2.7 rpm and about +30% when also going to 4 rpm, for an externally heated pyrolysis kiln. They also create a curtain that exchanges heat with the freeboard gas and radiatively with the hot upper wall. In an externally heated kiln with little sweep gas, the curtain mainly receives radiation from the uncovered hot wall, and gas-convective Ua correlations (built for hot-gas dryers with high G) do not apply directly.
2. The design load (filling about 15-20% for typical two-section flights) maximises the curtain. Over-loading adds a rolling bottom bed and shortens the fall.
3. Plastics: between melting (PE/PP roughly 110-170 C, not from these sources) and devolatilisation, the charge is a viscous, sticky melt. Open lifters cannot hold a free-flowing load and foul. Wall films block heat transfer and kilns sometimes need mechanical cleaning (informal source). Published plastic-kiln work uses a solid heat carrier (sand 5-20% fill, which prevents agglomeration and lets the melt coat carrier particles) rather than flights. Biomass kilns use steel balls (1-1.5 mm) or chains. Tyre and plastic drums use spiral/helical flights or a spiral agitator for conveying and carbon-black discharge. Tyre wire entangles stirrers. A small tyre kiln test (Syamsiro 2019) found lifters lowered liquid yield and raised gas, which cuts against the marketing claim of less secondary cracking.
4. Curtains therefore only make physical sense for free-flowing solids: inert heat-carrier particles, char or carbon black after devolatilisation, or tyre chips. A realistic demonstrator should model a melt/heat-carrier bed zone (no curtain) followed by a char/carrier zone with flights.

RECOMMENDED MODELLING APPROACH FOR THE COLAB/PyTorch T4 DEMONSTRATOR (my engineering recommendation, not from a source):

(A) Production model: a reduced-order 'flight holdup + curtain' model, fully vectorised in torch.
- Per axial slice and per flight angular position theta, compute gamma(theta) from Schofield-Glikin, then the two-section-flight holdup area A_F(theta). Build A_F by polygon clipping, or precompute it as a lookup table.
- Cascading rate = -rho_b L omega dA_F/dtheta.
- The design-load check is Baker's 2x upper-half holdup. Excess holdup goes to a rolling bottom bed handled by the bed-regime module from the parallel research.
- Represent curtains as Lagrangian parcels (about 1e5-1e6 parcels is cheap on a T4). Release them at the flight tip with tangential velocity omega R_o and let them fall ballistically with drag. Heat them by Ranz-Marshall convection plus radiation from the exposed wall, using a curtain-optical-thickness shielding factor (eps_c = 1 - exp(-1.5 phi delta/d_p)).
- Get axial advance per cascade from y_f sin(alpha) plus drag, giving residence time and RTD.
- Close the gas side with the freeboard model and couple pyrolysis vapours.

(B) Calibration and visual 'wow': a thin periodic DEM slice in PyTorch.
- Soft-sphere linear spring-dashpot, cell-list neighbour search, slice thickness about 5-10 d_p.
- Use a few 1e4 to about 2e5 spheres with a reduced shear modulus, which the UFU study found acceptable at low rpm.
- Reproduce the Karali/Sunkara 0.5 m drum (12 flights, l2/l1 = 0.375 or 0.75, 1-5 rpm, glass beads) and the Zhang 2020 PTV case (4 flights, 10-30 rpm).
- Check per-flight holdup, final discharge angle and curtain fall height against the reduced model.
- Benchmark T4 timings yourself; the literature GPU figures are on different hardware.

(C) Validation targets:
- Holdup and discharge vs angular position: Karali 2015/2018, Sunkara 2013, Lee & Sheehan 2010.
- Design-load filling of 15-20%.
- Wall-to-bed HTC uplift from lifters: Suzuki 2008 (38.6 to 45.3 to 50.1 W/m2K) and Bongo Njeng 2018.
- Curtain heat transfer: Wardjiman & Rhodes 2009, Afshar 2015.
- Optional consistency check against Ua = 237 G^0.67/D, for hot-gas drying cases only.

(D) For the Star-CCM+ team: the same geometry can be run as DEM in Star-CCM+ for a high-fidelity reference slice. The reduced model is the fast, explainable twin.

verdicts.parameter: Schofield-Glikin dynamic angle of repose: sign in the denominator
verdicts.claimed: tan(gamma) = [mu + n(cos theta - mu sin theta)] / [1 - n(sin theta -/+ mu cos theta)], sign uncertain
verdicts.corrected_value: tan(gamma) = [mu + n(cos theta - mu sin theta)] / [1 - n(sin theta + mu cos theta)], with n = R_o omega^2/g and theta measured from the horizontal on the rising (lifting) side of the drum.
verdicts.source_checked: WebSearch snippet of the SciELO paper 'Modeling and experimental study of hydrodynamic and drying characteristics of an industrial rotary dryer' (bjce sRmbXjnPYwMTx9gNkrnKQWS), which shows tan psi = (mu + n(cos theta - mu sin theta))/(1 - n(sin theta + mu cos theta)). I re-derived it independently: effective gravity in the rotating frame (n cos theta, n sin theta - 1) tilts the normal by beta with tan beta = n cos theta/(1 - n sin theta), and tan(beta + atan mu) gives the + sign.
verdicts.note: Use the '+' form. Another search rendering of the equation was garbled. In the original model mu is the tangent of an angle of repose and is usually back-calculated from photographs (Lisboa 2007).

verdicts.parameter: Curtain optical thickness tau = 1.5 Q_ext phi delta / d_p; eps_c = 1 - exp(-tau)
verdicts.claimed: Derived Beer-Lambert expression
verdicts.source_checked: Own derivation: projected area per volume = (6 phi/(pi d^3)) (pi d^2/4) = 1.5 phi/d. phi_c = m'_c/(rho_p delta v_p) is dimensionally consistent.
verdicts.note: 1 - exp(-tau) is the curtain opacity (extinction fraction), not its emissivity. The effective emissivity also needs the particle emissivity and scattering. The Sandia values (phi 0.6 at release to <0.1 within 0.5 m; opacity 0.5-1) were not verified.

verdict_blocked_network.summary:
ACCESS: WebFetch failed with DNS errors on every host, and curl through the egress proxy could not reach any academic host: J-STAGE, arXiv, CORE, d-nb, Halle, HAL, SciELO, MDPI, Springer, JCU, Semantic Scholar, Crossref and OpenAlex all returned no connection, and only GitHub was reachable. About 12 extended WebSearch calls ran before the per-turn search budget, shared with other agents, ran out. All checks below therefore rest on search-returned abstract or snippet text plus my own arithmetic and derivations. No full text was read.

CONFIRMED (abstract or secondary level):
- Suzuki et al. 2008 k_m-w: 38.6, 45.3 and 50.1 W/m2K, quoted verbatim from the abstract. The abstract adds two design rules. Lifters give about +10% when lifter height / waste-layer thickness > 0.45. The NUMBER of lifters dominates during the pyrolysis phase of plastic-based waste.
- Karali 2018 geometry: 0.5 x 0.15 m drum, 1-5 rpm, 12/18 flights, flight length ratios 0.375/0.75.
- Flights per circle 2.4-3.0D, with D in ft, at 60-75 ft/min (secondary).
- McCormick exponent 0.46-0.67, with 0.67 most reliable (secondary).
- Myklestad Ua = 420 G^0.8, no diameter dependence (secondary).
- Ua = 237 G^0.67/D and the 115 W/m3K example. The 237 constant is attributed to Treybal 1981. G must be in kg m-2 s-1: my conversion gives 236.88, and one handout's kg m-2 h-1 is wrong.
- Critical speed 42.3/sqrt(D), re-derived.
- Curtain optical-thickness algebra, re-derived. Note that 1 - exp(-tau) is opacity, not emissivity.
- 'No published validation of the S-G, Kelly and Baker models' (snippet).
- Lisboa 2007 bibliographic details.

CORRECTED:
1. Karali et al. 2015 (CES 138) used a 0.50 m x 0.15 m drum with flight length ratios 0.375/0.75, not D = 1.0 m x L = 0.3 m. The list of measured quantities the thread gives belongs to the 2018 paper. The critical-numbers line 'D 1.0 m x L 0.3 m' is unsupported as attributed.
2. Schofield-Glikin sign: use tan gamma = [mu + n(cos theta - mu sin theta)] / [1 - n(sin theta + mu cos theta)], with n = R_o omega^2/g and theta measured from the horizontal on the rising side. A SciELO paper snippet shows this form and my own rotating-frame derivation gives the same result.
3. Friedman & Marshall n = 0.16 is that author's own exponent. Exponents by author: F&M 0.16, Aiken & Polsak 0.37, Miller 0.60, McCormick 0.67, Myklestad 0.80. This is not a 'conflict' within one correlation, and the 237 G^0.67 form is McCormick/Treybal, not F&M.

UNVERIFIABLE (not seen):
- S-G validity limit < 0.4.
- F&M K = 244.7 and its 0.2-0.5 m/s, 2-8% ranges.
- The '6 Btu for a 7-ft drum' patent figure. The snippet instead shows measured Ua up to 45 Btu/h ft3 F.
- The 'Ua = 0.5 G^0.67/D in Perry' citation. The arithmetic is consistent, but the source was not seen.
- Optimum filling 15-20%. Perry & Green via a secondary source gives flights carrying about 10-15% of dryer volume.
- Ajayi & Sheehan numbers. The reversed '0.703 to 0.134 kg/s' range looks like a transcription error.
- Sunkara ratio 1.5.
- Direction of the 2022 final-discharge-angle trends. Only the dependence on Fr and flight length ratio was seen.
- Sherritt years.
- Syamsiro lifter yield effect.
- Gao & Bao slip/roll thresholds.
- 200 C/s heating rate (implausible for a kiln bed).
- 31-35 W/m2K indirect-kiln HTC.
- Zhang, Zhu and He DEM numbers.
- Sandia curtain values.
- F&M residence-time constants.
- Axial advance per cascade: y_f sin(alpha) vs y_f tan(alpha) depends on how y_f is defined; the difference is negligible at 1-5 deg slope.

DECISION IMPACT: The Suzuki data are the only confirmed quantitative lifter effect for an externally heated pyrolysis kiln. The +17% at 2.7 rpm is a lifter effect; the +30% mixes lifters with a speed change. Validation geometry for a DEM slice should be the 0.5 x 0.15 m drum. Fix the Schofield-Glikin sign before coding.

Leads to check in a session with web access: Waste Management 2025 S0956053X25005045 (medical-waste indirectly heated kiln HTC), Exp. Therm. Fluid Sci. 2014 S0894177714000296 (baffled-kiln wall HT correlation), and Particuology 2024 S1674200124000580, which cites Suzuki 2008a.

verdicts.parameter: Wall-to-waste overall HTC k_m-w with lifters (Suzuki et al. 2008, JTST 3(3):532-539)
verdicts.claimed: 38.6 W/m2K without lifters; 45.3 W/m2K with 6 x 200 mm lifters at 2.7 rpm; 50.1 W/m2K at 4.0 rpm with lifters
verdicts.corrected_value: Same values. Rotation alone, without lifters, raises k_m-w from 38.6 to 43.4 W/m2K at 4.0 rpm (Fig. 3c text). So the pure lifter factor is 45.3/38.6 = 1.17 at 2.7 rpm and 50.1/43.4 = 1.15 at 4.0 rpm. The combined lifter + speed factor is 1.30. The values are means over the whole batch pyrolysis.
verdicts.source_checked: Full text read, J-STAGE PDF https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jtst/3/3/3_3_532/_pdf (Sec. 3.2, Table 1, Fig. 3a-c)
verdicts.note: Feed is simulated MSW, dry basis: paper 30, wood 25, PE 15, PP 15, PS 5, grain 10 wt%, plus 10% moisture. Wall at 555 C. Six cases with lifters and two cases at 4 rpm (Table 1).

verdicts.parameter: Suzuki 2008 lifter design rule (H_l/H_w > 0.45; arc-length ratio)
verdicts.claimed: About +10% when H_l/H_w > 0.45 'or when L_l/L_w was larger than 1' (abstract)
verdicts.corrected_value: The body text (Sec. 3.2-3.3) and Conclusion (3) say L_l/L_w (or L_l/L_c) must be LESS than 1, i.e. at least one lifter inside the bed-wall contact arc. The abstract's 'larger than 1' is a misprint. The H_l/H_w (or H_l/H_c) > 0.45 criterion is confirmed. Measured by phase: in phase 1 (water) 200 mm lifters give +18% and 50 mm lifters have little effect. In phase 3 (plastics) even 50 mm lifters give >10%. With 100 mm lifters, phase 3 gains +6% with 3 lifters and +17% with 6.
verdicts.source_checked: Full text, J-STAGE PDF (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 4, Tables 3-4, Conclusions)
verdicts.note: Table 3 gives H_l/H_w = 0.12/0.23/0.47 and H_l/H_c = 0.45/0.91/1.82 for 50/100/200 mm lifters. Table 4 gives L_l = 3.14/1.05/0.52 m for 0/3/6 lifters, with L_l/L_c = 4.62/1.54/0.77.
