verdicts.corrected_value: Karali's thesis recommends 5-15% of drum volume. Measured design-load fill in the 0.5 m drum was 4.5-5.8% (l2/l1 = 0.375, 12 flights), 8.1-10.2% (0.75, 12 flights) and 12.7-14.8% (0.75, 18 flights), rising slightly with rpm (1-5 rpm). The 1.0 m drum needed about 9% lower fill on average. Perry & Green (1999) give 10-15%.
verdicts.source_checked: Karali M.A. Dr.-Ing. thesis OVGU 2015, full text (https://d-nb.info/1076590195/34): Sec. 2.5-2.6, Table 2.3, Fig. 3.7
verdicts.note: 20% fill is used in Sunkara 2013 and Granular Matter 2022 explicitly as OVER-loaded. Lisboa 2007 found 7 flights best with at least 16% fill in a 0.25 m drum, i.e. different flights and scale.

verdicts.parameter: Karali et al. drum geometries
verdicts.claimed: Thread: 2015 paper used D = 1.0 m, L = 0.3 m; earlier verdict: 0.5 x 0.15 m
verdicts.corrected_value: 0.5 m x 0.15 m drum (thesis Ch. 2, matching the CES 2015 abstract): 12/18 flights, l1 = 0.05 m, l2/l1 = 0.375/0.75, 1/3/5 rpm. A 1.0 m x 0.3 m drum (L/D = 0.3) was used for scale-up in thesis Ch. 3 with l2/l1 = 0.375, 0.75 and 1.0 (1.0 with 12 flights only).
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis full text, Tables 2.1 and 3.1
verdicts.note: l2/l1 = 0 works only in over-loaded drums. l2/l1 = 1.0 with 18 flights 'throttles' the solids and forms a bottom bed.

verdicts.parameter: Karali et al. 2018: maximum curtain fall height at design (optimum) loading
verdicts.claimed: Maximum fall height occurs at optimum loading because the bottom bed disappears
verdicts.corrected_value: Measured mean fall height in the 0.5 m drum was 28.2-31.0 cm (h/D = 0.56-0.62) at design load and 3 rpm.
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis Sec. 4.7.1 and Table 4.1 (full text)
verdicts.note: Thesis level. The 2018 Powder Technol. paper itself was not opened (Elsevier).

verdicts.parameter: Sunkara et al. 2013: optimal flight length ratio
verdicts.claimed: About 1.5 for maximum airborne surface area, no gas flow
verdicts.corrected_value: Maximum particle surface area occurs at l2/l1 = 1.5 (no gas flow, no particle shielding), with little change between 1 and 1.5. The author recommends l2/l1 close to 1 and n_F close to the theoretical number (about 18), because shielding rises above 1. For l1/R = 0.1 the maximum shifts to l2/l1 = 2.2.
verdicts.source_checked: Sunkara K.R. (2013) Dr.-Ing. thesis OVGU 'Granular flow and design studies in flighted rotating drums', full text https://d-nb.info/1054420610/34 (Sec. 6.7, Ch. 8)
verdicts.note: Drums 500 and 1000 mm in diameter, 150 and 300 mm long, 12 and 18 flights, l2/l1 0-1.0, l1/R = 0.2. Quartz sand, glass beads and limestone.

verdicts.parameter: Final discharge angle model (Granular Matter 2022)
verdicts.claimed: Coriolis force included; delta_L increases with l2/l1 and Fr; validated in 0.5 and 1.0 m drums with 12 flights
verdicts.corrected_value: Confirmed. Authors are Seidenbecher, Herz, Sunkara and Mellmann, GM 24:123. Drums 0.5/1.0 m x 0.15/0.3 m, l1/R = 0.2, 0.5-10 rpm, fill 20% (over-loaded). Glass beads 0.7 mm (Theta = 28.0 deg) and quartz sand 0.2 mm (32.4 deg). The new model fits within about 10%, and within 5% for sand at Fr < 0.005. A larger drum gives a larger delta_L. Old model: delta_L = 90 deg + alpha + gamma_L.
verdicts.source_checked: Full text, Springer OA PDF (link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10035-022-01283-x.pdf, fetched with a plain curl user-agent)
verdicts.note: Eq. (6) of this paper prints the Schofield-Glikin denominator with a minus sign; see the next verdict.

verdicts.parameter: Schofield-Glikin kinetic angle of repose: sign in the denominator
verdicts.claimed: tan(gamma) = [mu + n(cos theta - mu sin theta)] / [1 - n(sin theta + mu cos theta)], '+' form
verdicts.corrected_value: General published form: tan(gamma) = [mu cos(alpha) + Fr (rH/R)(cos delta - mu sin delta)] / [cos(alpha) - Fr (rH/R)(sin delta + mu cos delta)], with Fr = omega^2 R/g, tan(alpha) = l2/rH, rH = R - l1, delta = flight-tip angle above the 9 o'clock horizontal. It is identical to the '+' form with n = omega^2 r_HS/g, where r_HS = rH/cos(alpha).
verdicts.source_checked: Sunkara thesis Eq. 3.12 with the force-balance derivation (Eqs. 3.6-3.11); Karali thesis Eq. 4.4; own re-derivation. Granular Matter 2022 Eq. (6) prints '(sin delta - mu cos delta)'.
verdicts.note: Two full texts plus the derivation support '+'. The GM 2022 minus sign looks like a typesetting error. In practice the two forms differ by less than 0.5 deg for Fr up to 0.013 (computed for mu = tan 35 deg), so the sign barely matters at kiln speeds. Sunkara: valid only for free-flowing solids, 'not to highly cohesive solids, sticky and wet materials'.

verdicts.parameter: Schofield-Glikin validity R_o omega^2/g < 0.4
verdicts.claimed: Valid when the centrifugal/gravity ratio < 0.4
verdicts.source_checked: Sunkara thesis Sec. 3.3, Karali thesis Sec. 4.3, Lisboa 2007 (SciELO HTML), Granular Matter 2022: none states a 0.4 limit
verdicts.note: Sunkara only notes that gamma tends to the dynamic angle of repose as Fr tends to 0. Kiln and dryer Fr is 3e-4 to 1.3e-2 (Karali validity table), far below any such limit.

verdicts.parameter: Design-load models (Porter, Kelly & O'Donnell, Baker, Ajayi & Sheehan)
verdicts.claimed: Baker (1988): design load = 2 x holdup of the upper-half flights
verdicts.corrected_value: Porter 1963: H_Tot = H_FUF x n_F/2. Kelly & O'Donnell 1977: H_Tot = H_FUF x (n_F+1)/2. Baker 1988: H_Tot,flights = 2 x sum(H_i, from FUF to LUF) - H_FUF. Ajayi & Sheehan 2012: H_Tot = 1.24 x (2 sum H_i - H_FUF)(1+S), S = 0.042-0.078. Karali 2015 (rectangular flights): H_Tot = 1.38 x (2 sum H_i - H_FUF). Here H is holdup per unit length (m3/m or cm2) and f_design = H_Tot/(pi R^2).
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis Table 1.1, Eqs. 1.1-1.5 and 2.1 (full text, page image checked)
verdicts.note: Ajayi & Sheehan's model deviated by -16.6 to +26.8% from Karali's data, and the Porter and K&O models by up to 40% (Table 2.3).

verdicts.parameter: Ajayi & Sheehan 2012 numbers
verdicts.claimed: Dynamic angle of repose 44.7-62.3 deg; 2.5-4.5 rpm; '0.703 to 0.134 kg/s'; airborne/flight-borne ratio S = 0.042-0.078; Eulerian-Eulerian CFD
verdicts.corrected_value: Confirmed: 44.7-62.3 deg (cohesion set with a low-volatility fluid), 2.5-4.5 rpm, S = 0.042-0.078, pilot drum D = 0.75 m x L = 1.15 m with angular flights, image analysis plus CFD. Not confirmed: the '0.703 to 0.134 kg/s' flow rates and that the CFD was Eulerian-Eulerian (Karali writes only 'CFD').
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis Sec. 1.5 and 2.6 (full text; secondary to Ajayi & Sheehan)
verdicts.note: The original CES 73:400-411 was not read.

verdicts.parameter: Sherritt et al. publication years
verdicts.source_checked: Reference list of Suzuki et al. 2008 (refs 2-3), full text
verdicts.note: Bibliographic only.

verdicts.parameter: Lisboa et al. 2007 study
verdicts.claimed: Braz. J. Chem. Eng. 24(3); two-segment flight holdup and length of fall
verdicts.corrected_value: Lisboa, Vitorino, Delaiba, Finzer, Barrozo. Drum 0.25 m in diameter x 0.60 m long. Single superphosphate (Sauter 2.76 mm). 2.65 and 5.55 rpm; 0.33 and 0.67 kg/min. Measured dynamic friction coefficient mu = 0.994. Best result with 7 flights at 16.0% or more fill. Saeman & Mitchell fitted the residence time best.
verdicts.source_checked: SciELO HTML full text (https://www.scielo.br/j/bjce/a/dGNdtNDQFjKfrJ7jHRfCF4L/)
verdicts.note: The equations are images and were not transcribed. Lisboa also quotes Perry & Green: flights should carry 10-15% of dryer volume.

verdicts.parameter: No published experimental validation of the S-G, Kelly and Baker models
verdicts.claimed: Models lacked published validation
verdicts.corrected_value: Ajayi & Sheehan 'argued that none of those models had been validated experimentally and most were non-generic'.
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis Sec. 1.5 (full text)
verdicts.note: Secondary to Ajayi & Sheehan 2012.

verdicts.parameter: SI volumetric coefficient Ua = 237 G^0.67/D and worked example
verdicts.corrected_value: Ua [W m-3 K-1] = 237 G^0.67/D with G in kg m-2 s-1 and D in m. The example gives 115.4. Converting 0.5 G^0.67/D [Btu h-1 ft-3 F-1; lb h-1 ft-2; ft] gives 236.88.
verdicts.source_checked: NPTEL mod4.pdf full text (p. 18 formula; p. 20 example)
verdicts.note: NPTEL labels G' as 'kg/m2.h', which is a unit error: with h the result would be about 240 times smaller. The source of the 0.5 G^0.67/D imperial form was not seen. Valid only for direct hot-gas dryers.

verdicts.parameter: McCormick exponent n = 0.46-0.67 (0.67 most representative)
verdicts.source_checked: No full text found. Sunkara thesis Eq. 2.6 instead quotes Friedman & Marshall as U A_C = (0.477/D)((n_F - 1)/2) G^0.46 (units not given).
verdicts.note: Keep as a secondary-source statement. The 0.46 exponent also appears in one rendering of Friedman & Marshall, so the attributions are muddled.

verdicts.parameter: Friedman & Marshall Ua constant K = 244.7 (exponent illegible)
verdicts.claimed: K = 244.7 W m-3 C-1, validity 0.2-0.5 m/s shell speed and 2-8% holdup
verdicts.corrected_value: 244.7 is the SI form of Ua = 15 G^0.16/D [Btu h-1 ft-3 F-1; G lb h-1 ft-2; D ft], which converts to Ua = 245.0 G^0.16/D [W m-3 K-1; G kg m-2 s-1; D m] (own conversion). So the exponent belonging to 244.7 is 0.16, not 0.67. The validity ranges (0.2-0.5 m/s, 2-8%) remain unverified.
verdicts.source_checked: NPTEL mod4.pdf full text (p. 27: 'Ua = 15(G_G)^0.16/D', G_G = maximum superficial air mass velocity lb/ft2 h, D ft; example gives 5.57 Btu/h ft3 F). Conversion done in Python.
verdicts.note: NPTEL gives no attribution; the Friedman & Marshall (1949) attribution comes from secondary sources. This is a different correlation from the 237 G^0.67/D (McCormick/Treybal-type) form.

verdicts.parameter: Myklestad Ua = 420 G^0.8
verdicts.claimed: Ua = 420 G^0.8, units unknown
verdicts.corrected_value: Karali's thesis instead gives U_V = 0.52 (m_a/A)^0.8 [kW m-3 K-1], with m_a/A in kg m-2 s-1, attributed to Foust et al. 1960 and Myklestad 1963. This equals 520 G^0.8 W m-3 K-1. It also gives a shell-loss coefficient U_e = 0.022 (m_a/A)^0.879 [kW m-2 K-1] (Douglas 1993; Arruda 2009).
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis Eqs. 6.5 and 6.7 (raw-text exponents checked)
verdicts.note: The 420 prefactor was not seen in any full text. Both forms are for convective hot-gas dryers and coolers.

verdicts.parameter: Friedman-Marshall / Perry mean residence time
verdicts.claimed: tau = 0.23 L/(S N^0.9 D) +/- drag term; 'B = 5 Dp^-0.5' unverified; SI variant 0.3344
verdicts.corrected_value: SI form: theta [min] = 0.23 L/(S N^0.9 d) +/- 1.97 B L G'/F, with B = 5 dp^-0.5 (dp in micron), L and d in m, S slope in m/m, N in rpm, G' and F in kg m-2 h-1. The sign is + for countercurrent and - for cocurrent. 1.97 = 0.6 x 3.2808, from Perry's 0.6 B L G/F with L in ft. Karali writes the first term as tau [s] = 13.8 L/(tan(beta) N^0.9 D), where 13.8 = 0.23 x 60.
verdicts.source_checked: NPTEL mod4.pdf p. 18 (full text); Karali thesis Eq. 5.2
verdicts.note: The 0.3344 SI variant is unverified; do not mix constants. Perry & Green general form: tau = K L/(tan(beta) N^0.9 D). Karali fitted K = 22.7 (tau in s) for his 0.5 m drum (12 flights, l2/l1 0.75, design load); Friedman & Marshall under-predicted his model by 27-50% (Table 5.1).

verdicts.parameter: Axial advance per cascade
verdicts.claimed: dz = y_f sin(alpha) +/- drag term (derived, closures not retrieved)
verdicts.corrected_value: Karali Eqs. 5.9-5.26: X_avg = 0.5 g sin(beta) t_fall^2 -/+ 0.5 k u_r^2 t_fall^2, with t_fall = sqrt(2 h_fall/g), so the gravity term equals h_fall sin(beta). k = 1.5 C_D rho_a/(d_p rho_p), with Schiller-Naumann C_D (24/Re form written as 12 with 1.5 prefactor) and Re from u_r = u_a +/- u_x. Number of cascades C = L/X; t_lift = 2 delta_avg/omega; tau = C (t_lift + t_fall).
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis Ch. 5 (full text)
verdicts.note: Here beta is the drum slope and h_fall the vertical fall height. Karali neglects rolling and bouncing in the bed.

verdicts.parameter: Overall HTC 31-35 W/m2K 'in indirectly heated kilns without internals'
verdicts.claimed: About 31-35 W/m2K for kilns without internals (secondary)
verdicts.corrected_value: 31-35 W/m2K is Hwan's overall coefficient U from the FLUE GAS to the solid bed (resistances in series: flue gas to outer wall, wall, covered wall to covered bed). It applies to an indirectly heated pilot kiln WITH segmented lifters: D_iw = 0.498 m, L = 3.98 m, lifter height 0.08 m, low-rank coal 260-325 kg/h, fill 14-17%, MRT about 15 min. U rose from 31 to 35 W/m2K when recycled off-gas fell from 52 to 26 kg/h.
verdicts.source_checked: Hwan I.H. (2009) PhD thesis, Curtin, full text via figshare (https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/62348503): abstract, Eq. 6.17, Table 6.2, Sec. 6.3
verdicts.note: Hwan identifies covered-wall-to-covered-bed transfer as the limiting step. This value is not a wall-to-bed coefficient and not a 'no internals' value.

verdicts.parameter: Syamsiro et al. 2019 tyre kiln with lifters
verdicts.claimed: D 260 mm x L 400 mm, lifter segment 28 mm, semi-batch at 300 C; best liquid without lifters at 15 rpm; lifters cut liquid and solid, raise gas
verdicts.corrected_value: As claimed. IOP Conf. Ser.: Earth Environ. Sci. 245 (2019) 012044.
verdicts.source_checked: Abstract on the UNAIR scholar page (fetched). The IOP PDF was blocked by a JavaScript challenge.
verdicts.note: Abstract level only. At 300 C liquid yields were low in all runs, which makes this a weak data point.

verdicts.parameter: Gao & Bao 2020 sand heat carrier: 5% slips, >10% rolls
verdicts.claimed: 5-15% loading; slip at 5%; rolling above 10%
verdicts.source_checked: WebSearch summaries only (SciEngine connection reset; ResearchGate 403)
verdicts.note: The summaries agree: Chinese Sci. Bull. 65(26):2895-2902 (2020), quartz-sand carrier 5-15%, EDEM + C++ heat model; more carrier gives more oil and char and less gas. Zhang et al. (FPT 206, 2020) reportedly found 15% best for oil (secondary).

verdicts.parameter: Heating rate up to 200 C/s with a solid heat carrier (Fuel 2025)
verdicts.claimed: up to 200 C/s
verdicts.source_checked: Not reachable (Elsevier)
verdicts.note: Implausible for a kiln bed; do not use.

verdicts.parameter: Zhang et al. 2020 PTV + DEM; Particuology 2020 number of flights
verdicts.claimed: 4 flights, 10/20/30 rpm, fill 10/15/20%; 8-12 flights give a larger and more stable dilute phase
verdicts.source_checked: Abstracts via the Semantic Scholar API (DOI 10.1016/j.powtec.2019.12.035; 10.1016/j.partic.2020.09.010)
verdicts.note: Plastic particles. The follow-up used 1/4/8/12 flights at 15% fill. Literature models deviate significantly from the measurements.

verdicts.parameter: Zhu et al. 2023 inclined flights +26% axial speed
verdicts.claimed: +26% axial speed; best active-phase mass at 37 rpm, joint angle 139 deg, 7.83 kg/s
verdicts.source_checked: Abstract via the Semantic Scholar API (Processes 11:1363)
verdicts.note: Context: a gas-liquid drum filled with beads used as fillers, compared with a drum without inclined flights. Not a pyrolysis kiln.

verdicts.parameter: He, E, Jiang 2025 aligned vs separated flights
verdicts.claimed: Separated flights give a spiral curtain and more uniform distribution but less heat exchange, and cost more than 30% more; system power below 20% of recovered power
verdicts.source_checked: Abstract via the Semantic Scholar API (Processes 13:1594)
verdicts.note: Waste-heat-recovery drum, DEM study.

verdicts.parameter: Critical speed
verdicts.claimed: n_c = 42.3/sqrt(D[m]) rpm
verdicts.source_checked: Own calculation
verdicts.note: Standard mechanics.

verdicts.parameter: Curtain solids fraction and opacity (Sandia 2017)
verdicts.claimed: phi falls from about 0.6 at release to <0.1 within 0.5 m; opacity 0.5-1
verdicts.corrected_value: Confirmed. In addition: opacity >95% within 0.7 m for 9.53 and 11.1 mm slots, and 80% within 0.6 m for a 6.35 mm slot. Particles 280 micron ceramic. Curtain about 2 cm thick. Velocities in the first 2 m match drag-free fall because entrained air reduces drag.
verdicts.source_checked: Full text, Ho et al., J. Sol. Energy Eng. (2017), DOI 10.1115/1.4035258 (Sandia PDF)
verdicts.note: 1 - exp(-tau) remains a derived opacity (Beer-Lambert), not an emissivity.

verdicts.parameter: Wardjiman et al. 2008 curtain hydrodynamics
verdicts.claimed: Sand 204 um, 0.031-0.047 kg/s, curtain 0.02-0.10 m, air 0-1.2 m/s, duct 0.15 x 0.60 m
verdicts.corrected_value: Also: particle density 2640 kg/m3. Eulerian-Eulerian CFD agreed with experiment; the single-particle model was less satisfactory.
verdicts.source_checked: JCU repository abstract (researchonline.jcu.edu.au/7041)
verdicts.note: Abstract level.

verdicts.parameter: Afshar & Sheehan curtain CFD
verdicts.claimed: Silica 2634 kg/m3, 200/400/600 um, 400 K, 0.041-0.2 kg/s; up to +13% convective HT per unit mass by changing the slot
verdicts.corrected_value: Also: box 0.45 x 0.9 x 0.225 m; slots 10, 30, 60 and 80 mm; 4 mm mesh; 3-D Eulerian-Eulerian; the +13% is for 400 um particles at 0.041 kg/s.
verdicts.source_checked: Karali thesis Sec. 6.1 (full text, secondary summary of Afshar & Sheehan 2012)
verdicts.note: Secondary.

verdicts.parameter: Lee & Sheehan 2010 and Sheehan et al. 2005
verdicts.claimed: Geometric unloading model sensitive to surface angle; compartment model with 4 or 2 parameters
verdicts.source_checked: JCU repository abstracts (items 11956 and 6068)
verdicts.note: Abstract level.

verdicts.parameter: Le Guen et al. 2017 minimal model
verdicts.claimed: Exponential profiles without radiation; stretched exponentials with radiation; efficiency criterion
verdicts.corrected_value: Confirmed; full closures listed under additional findings.
verdicts.source_checked: arXiv:1612.05762 full text (Tables I-V page image checked)
verdicts.note: Assumes dilute curtain (<10%), Stokes >> 1 and Bi < 0.1. Developed for an asphalt plant (direct-fired).

verdicts.parameter: Bongo Njeng et al. 2018 wall-to-solid HTC
verdicts.claimed: Values not retrieved; dimensional-analysis correlation
verdicts.corrected_value: h_cw-cb is of order 1e2 W m-2 K-1: measured 45-1132 W m-2 K-1 over 100-500 C and 2-12 rpm. Rectangular lifters > no lifters > straight lifters. Correlation Eq. 16 with fitted parameters is listed under additional findings.
verdicts.source_checked: HAL author PDF full text (hal.science/hal-01624450/file/publiAlexWTSHTC_pourHAL.pdf), Table 3 and Eq. 16 checked on page image
verdicts.note: Sand in a 0.101 m kiln, so a large extrapolation to waste kilns.

verdicts.parameter: Hwan 2009 segmented lifters
verdicts.claimed: Flatter bed-depth profiles, good heat transfer at low rotational Reynolds number with strong axial mixing
verdicts.corrected_value: Flat bed profile at low Re_omega, with Pe < 50 or Dz = 1e-5 to 1e-3 m2/s. The limiting step is covered wall to covered bed.
verdicts.source_checked: Hwan thesis full text (abstract, Ch. 6)
verdicts.note: Ch. 6 was originally confidential and is now in the open copy.

verdicts.parameter: Seidenbecher flighted-drum thermal experiments
verdicts.claimed: L 1.76 m, D 0.5 m, l2/l1 0.375-2.0, 6-18 flights; faster temperature change with higher speed and air flow
verdicts.corrected_value: Only the CES 229 (2020) 115972 abstract was confirmed: indirectly heated batch drum with glass beads; higher rpm and air flow give quicker temperature changes; higher fill gives a gradual decrease in the temperature drop.
verdicts.source_checked: Semantic Scholar abstract. The Halle dissertation is behind an Anubis anti-bot challenge, which I did not bypass.
verdicts.note: The geometry numbers remain unverified.

verdicts.parameter: Eulerian vs DEM (UFU) claim
verdicts.claimed: The Eulerian approach did better when the number of flights changed; reduced shear modulus valid at low rpm
verdicts.source_checked: Abstract (Nascimento, Lima, Brandao, Santos, Duarte, Barrozo 2021, Comput. Part. Mech.)
verdicts.note: The abstract says only that the choice of approach 'proved to be of great importance'. It does not state which was better.

verdicts.parameter: GPU-DEM cost benchmarks; Xie et al. 2017 DEM lifters; Kelly EAD constant 0.637; patent '6 Btu' figure
verdicts.claimed: As in the thread
verdicts.source_checked: Xie 2017 abstract is elided on Semantic Scholar; the others were not reachable
verdicts.note: Not used for the model.

verdicts.parameter: Curtain/flight claims on the KINTEK FAQ page
verdicts.claimed: Rotation lifts and showers material; less secondary cracking
verdicts.corrected_value: The page has no numbers and does not name flights. It says rotation 'lifts the waste material and pours it through the hotter upper atmosphere' and that removing gases from the hot zone 'avoids unwanted secondary reactions (cracking)'. It lists drive wear, dynamic seals and motor energy as trade-offs.
verdicts.source_checked: pt.kintekfurnace.com FAQ page, full text fetched
verdicts.note: Marketing text. Syamsiro 2019 (lifters raised gas yield) cuts against the cracking claim.

additional_findings.parameter: Suzuki batch externally heated kiln geometry (validation case)
additional_findings.value: Inner cylinder SUS310S, wall 25 mm, ID 1.0 m, L 1.5 m; heating-gas jacket gap 34 mm; natural-gas flue gas 700-800 C; inner wall mean 555 C (700 C gas) or 630 C (800 C gas); N2 purge; lifters were 25 mm thick, 1500 mm long boards, 50/100/200 mm high, 3 or 6 of them
additional_findings.context: Batch rotary pyrolyser for simulated MSW (35 wt% PE/PP/PS dry basis). Rotation 2.7, 4.0 and 4.3 rpm.
additional_findings.source: Suzuki T. et al. (2008) J. Therm. Sci. Technol. 3(3):523-531 and 532-539
additional_findings.evidence: 523 Sec. 2.2 and Fig. 2; 532 Sec. 2.3-2.4 and Table 1

additional_findings.parameter: Time evolution of the wall-to-waste coefficient k_m-w (no lifters)
additional_findings.value: 22 -> 55 W/m2K at 555 C wall; 27 -> 55 W/m2K at 630 C wall; peak wall heat flux about 11 kW/m2 (555 C) and 16.5 kW/m2 (630 C); initial wall-to-waste dT about 450 K and 520 K
additional_findings.units: W m-2 K-1; kW m-2; K
additional_findings.context: k_m-w = q_m/(A (T1 - T_w)), with q_m from wall conduction lambda (T2 - T1)/[(D1/2) ln(D2/D1)]. Evaluated only while T_waste < 450 C. k rises as the waste heats up; bulk waste volume shrinks from 0.48 to 0.07 m3. Waste reached 460 C 30 min after feeding.
additional_findings.source: Suzuki et al. (2008) JTST 3(3):523-531

additional_findings.parameter: Batch pyrolysis time vs wall temperature, lifters and speed (Suzuki)
additional_findings.value: 42 min (555 C, no lifters, 2.7 rpm); 30 min (630 C); 40 -> 33 min (6 lifters, 50 -> 200 mm); 42 -> 37 -> 35 min (0/3/6 lifters, 100 mm); 38 min (no lifters, 4.3 rpm per text); 31 min (6 x 200 mm lifters, 4.0 rpm)
additional_findings.context: Gas production shows three peaks: water, then cellulosics, then plastics. Lifters plus 4 rpm match the effect of raising the wall from 555 to 630 C.
additional_findings.source: Suzuki et al. (2008) JTST 3(3):532-539
additional_findings.evidence: Sec. 3.1, Fig. 2a-d, Conclusion (1)

additional_findings.parameter: Bed geometry in the Suzuki batch drum (fill check)
additional_findings.value: Waste layer 430 mm deep, arc 1420 mm just after feeding; char layer 110 mm deep, arc 680 mm after pyrolysis. My segment geometry with V = 0.48 and 0.07 m3 in a 1.178 m3 drum gives fill 40.7% (depth 0.427 m, arc 1.425 m) and 5.9% (depth 0.11 m, arc 0.675 m).
additional_findings.context: The drum runs at about 41% bulk fill, far above flighted-drum design load (5-15%). The lifters work as bed mixers and contact-area enhancers, not as curtain-forming flights.
additional_findings.source: Suzuki et al. 2008 (JTST 532 Sec. 3.2; JTST 523 Sec. 3.4); fill computed here
additional_findings.evidence: Measured values from the text; geometric check derived here (circular segment)

additional_findings.parameter: Horizontal-kiln bed-depth equation and lifter-count design example (Suzuki)
additional_findings.value: F = 0.74 (H_f/D)^2.05 x D^4 N cot(beta) rho / l. Example: D 2 m, L 20 m, 3 rpm, 70 kg/min, rho_b 150 kg/m3, repose angle 40 deg gives H_w about 1.0 m and L_w about 3.1 m at the inlet. The lifter count rises from 2 at the inlet to 3 (from 15 m), 4 (15-18 m), 5 (18-19 m) and 6 (to the end).
additional_findings.units: F kg/min; D, H_f, l m; N rpm; rho kg/m3; beta angle of repose
additional_findings.context: Solved section by section from the outlet. Source cited: Assoc. Powder Process Industry & Engineering, 'Kilns for Processes' (1985) p. 66 (Japanese). Design rules: H_l/H_w > 0.45 and L_l/L_w < 1.
additional_findings.source: Suzuki et al. (2008) JTST 3(3):532-539, Eq. (1), Table 5, Figs. 6-8
additional_findings.evidence: Eq. (1) checked on the page image

additional_findings.parameter: Design-loading filling degree correlation (Karali)
additional_findings.units: D, d_p, l1 m; rho_b kg/m3; Fr = omega^2 R/g
additional_findings.context: Valid ranges: D 0.5-1.0 m; L 0.15-0.3 m (L/D = 0.3); 1-5 rpm; Fr 2.79e-4 to 0.013; d_p 0.2-2 mm; Theta_A 25.7-62.3 deg; rho_b 1550-4630 kg/m3; n_F 12-18; l2/l1 0.375-1.0; l1 0.05-0.1 m; rectangular flights, free-flowing solids. My check gives 9.39% vs 9.3% measured (glass beads 0.7 mm, 3 rpm, 12 flights, l2/l1 = 0.75) and 5.25% vs 5.3% (l2/l1 = 0.375).
additional_findings.source: Karali M.A. (2015) Dr.-Ing. thesis OVGU, Eq. 3.1/5.33 and Table 3.2
additional_findings.evidence: Eq. 3.1 checked on page image (thesis p. 54); validity table p. 55

additional_findings.parameter: Measured design-load fill and FUF holdup (0.5 m drum)
additional_findings.value: Quartz sand 0.2 mm (12 flights, l2/l1 0.75): 8.7/9.4/10.0% at 1/3/5 rpm. Same with 18 flights: 12.7/13.7/14.8%. Glass beads 0.7 mm, l2/l1 0.375: 4.8/5.3/5.8%. FUF cross-section about 25-26 cm2 (l2/l1 0.75) and about 16 cm2 (0.375).
additional_findings.source: Karali thesis Tables 2.2 and 2.3
additional_findings.evidence: Table 2.3 rows 1-29

additional_findings.parameter: Mean curtain fall height: Blumberg & Schluender correlation (conflicting renderings)
additional_findings.value: Karali Eq. 4.7: h_fall = 0.85 R (1-f)(1 + Theta_A^2)(l2/l1)^0.13. Sunkara Eq. 3.89: h_F/R = 0.85 (1-f_D)(1.3 + Theta_A^2)(l2/l1)^0.13. Theta_A in rad. Validity: 0.2 <= f <= 0.4, Theta_A pi/8 to pi/4 (0.4-0.8 rad), l2/l1 0.75-1.0 (over-loaded drums).
additional_findings.context: Karali's Table 4.1 'B&S' values (24.4 and 22.4 cm) reproduce only with the 1 + Theta^2 form. The 1.3 form gives 30.0 and 28.0 cm, close to the measured 30.2 and 31.0 cm. The original (Chem. Eng. Process. 35 (1996) 405-411) was not read, so treat the constant as uncertain.
additional_findings.source: Karali thesis Sec. 4.7.2 and Table 4.1; Sunkara thesis Sec. 3.9.2
additional_findings.evidence: Both equations transcribed; numbers recomputed in Python

additional_findings.parameter: Geometric flight holdup and cascading rate for rectangular flights (Sunkara model)
additional_findings.value: Flight filling f_F,i(delta) = A_F,i/(pi R^2), in three regions. R-I (delta <= gamma): Eq. 3.26. R-II (gamma < delta <= gamma + alpha + beta): f = (1/2pi)[pi(gamma + eps* - phi)/180 - sin(eps*) cos(eps*) - cos^2(eps*)/tan(delta - gamma) - (rH/R)(l2/R)]. R-III (to delta_L): f = (1/2pi)(l2/R)^2 / tan(delta - gamma - alpha). Cascading rate m_F,i/(rho_b omega pi R^2 L) = -df_F,i/d delta (derivatives in Eqs. 3.43-3.45). Active flights n_F,a = (delta_L/360) n_F.
additional_findings.context: Auxiliary angles: tan(alpha) = l2/rH, tan(beta) = l2/l1, kappa = 90 + delta, phi = kappa - alpha, eps* = arccos[(rH/R) cos(kappa - gamma)/cos(alpha)]. The angle pi(gamma + eps* - phi)/180 uses degrees. Mean flight filling is (1/delta_L) times the integral of f_F,i over 0..delta_L. Assumes free-flowing, design- or over-loaded, no gas flow.
additional_findings.source: Sunkara K.R. (2013) Dr.-Ing. thesis OVGU, Sec. 3.4-3.5 (Eqs. 3.19-3.45)
additional_findings.evidence: Eqs. 3.21-3.38 transcribed from pdftotext. Check the region-I expression (3.26) against the PDF before coding.

additional_findings.parameter: Theoretical number of flights, maximum flight length ratio and final discharge (Sunkara)
additional_findings.value: tan(upsilon0) = (1 - (rH/R)/cos(alpha)) tan(gamma at delta = 0); n_F = 360/(alpha + upsilon0). (l2/l1)_max = sqrt(1 - (rH/R)^2)/(l1/R). Mellmann final discharge: delta_L = 90 + alpha + gamma_L, with gamma_L from S-G evaluated at delta_L (iterate).
additional_findings.context: n_F about 18 is the theoretical optimum in Sunkara's lab cases
additional_findings.source: Sunkara thesis Eqs. 3.48-3.49 and 3.81-3.83

additional_findings.parameter: Curtain fall height, fall time and particle surface area (Sunkara)
additional_findings.value: Sector 1 (impact on bed): h_F/R = cos(eps_B)/cos(Theta_A) + (rH/R)(sin(delta) - tan(Theta_A) cos(delta))/cos(alpha). Impact on shell: h_F/R = (rH/R) sin(delta)/cos(alpha) + sqrt(1 - (rH/R)^2 (cos(delta)/cos(alpha))^2). Impact on flight sheets: h_F/R = 2 (rH/R) sin(delta)/cos(alpha). Fall time t_F = (1/omega) sqrt(2 Fr h_F/R). Curtain area A_cs,i/(L R) = 3 pi (rho_b/rho_s)(D/d_p) f_cs,i, with f_cs,i = sqrt(2 Fr h_F/R) (-df_F,i/d delta).
additional_findings.context: eps_B = bed filling half-angle; eps_A = arccos(cos(alpha) cos(eps_B)/(rH/R)). Assumes no shielding (curtain porosity about 1).
additional_findings.source: Sunkara thesis Eqs. 3.84-3.99

additional_findings.parameter: Kinetic angle of repose in the flight vs S-G prediction (measured)
additional_findings.value: The measured angle rises by 2-7 deg early in discharge and then falls. S-G predicts an almost constant angle. More flights (18 vs 12) raise the angle; l2/l1 has almost no effect.
additional_findings.context: 0.5 m drum, design load, 1 and 5 rpm
additional_findings.source: Karali thesis Sec. 4.3, Figs. 4.2-4.3
additional_findings.evidence: Text Sec. 4.3

additional_findings.parameter: Flight cascading-rate definition and measured trend (Karali)
additional_findings.value: f_F(delta) = H_F(delta)/V_drum per unit length; -df_F/d delta = m_F(delta)/(rho_b omega pi R^2 L). Per-flight rates are of order 1e-4 to 6e-4 kg/s in the 0.5 x 0.15 m drum. The rate is high at the start, dips to a minimum, peaks again and then falls sharply to zero.
additional_findings.context: Quartz sand, 3 rpm, 12/18 flights; glass beads, l2/l1 0.375/0.75
additional_findings.source: Karali thesis Eqs. 4.5-4.6, Fig. 4.7
additional_findings.evidence: Fig. 4.7 axis tick 0.0006 kg/s (read from figure text)

additional_findings.parameter: Rotary cooler and dryer gas-solid model constants (Karali)
additional_findings.value: U_V = 0.52 (m_a/A)^0.8 kW m-3 K-1; U_e = 0.022 (m_a/A)^0.879 kW m-2 K-1. Industrial cooler case: D 5 m, L 40 m, 18 flights, l2/l1 0.75 (l1 0.5 m), siderite 38.8 kg/s at 800 C, air 34.7 kg/s. Results: U_V 0.75 kW m-3 K-1, solids out 202 C, air out 540 C, shell loss 36% of Q_s. Curtains: 8 active, mean fall 3.1 m, thickness 0.18 m.
additional_findings.units: kW m-3 K-1; kW m-2 K-1; m; kg/s; C
additional_findings.context: Convective direct-contact devices. A flat-plate approach (Nu = 0.037 Re^0.8 Pr^0.33) and a sphere approach (Ranz-Marshall, assumed curtain solid fraction 0.8) are offered to define the curtain area.
additional_findings.source: Karali thesis Ch. 6 (Eqs. 6.5-6.14, Tables 6.1-6.3)
additional_findings.evidence: Exponents confirmed in raw text

additional_findings.parameter: Le Guen/Piton flighted-kiln heat-transfer closures
additional_findings.value: h_bg = 0.4 (3600 m_g/A_g)^0.62 (valid range 50-100 W/m2K). h_cg = (k_s/d_s)(2 + A Re^a + B Re^b Pr^c), with Re < 200: B 0.6, b 1/3, c 1/3. h_gw = (k_g/D_h)(0.02 Re^0.93 + 8.5e-6 Re_omega^1.45), valid 1100 < Re_omega < 58000 and Re < 30000. h_sw = (k_s/(eps_B D_D)) 11.6 (2 eps_B D_D^2 omega/(2 a_s))^0.3, printed validity omega 3.5-10 rad/s. l_cg = n_F 3 pi (rho_b/rho_s)(D_D^2/(2 d_p)) F_t alpha_cg; l_bg = D_D sin(eps_B); l_bw = D_D eps_B.
additional_findings.context: Nominal asphalt-plant case: d_s 5 mm, alpha_cg 3%, m_s 33.98 kg/s, m_g 3.74 kg/s, Tg0 1873 K, Ts0 298 K. Gives h_bg 102.83, h_cg 112.80, h_gw 35.23 and h_sw 242.96 W/m2K, and l_bg 2.32, l_cg 9.71, l_gw 3.55, l_sw 1.79 m. As printed, h_cg uses the solid conductivity k_s and l_gw = D_D pi eps_B; both look like typos. The omega range equals 33-95 rpm, implausible for kilns. Check the originals (Piton et al. 2015) before use.
additional_findings.source: Le Guen L. et al. (2017) Can. J. Chem. Eng. 95:100-110 (arXiv:1612.05762), Tables I-V
additional_findings.evidence: Page 9 image checked for Tables IV-V; nominal values in text

additional_findings.parameter: Measured wall-to-solid HTC in an indirectly heated pilot kiln with lifters (Bongo Njeng)
additional_findings.value: h_cw-cb at 2 rpm and 100 C: no lifters 106-163, straight lifters 61-147, rectangular lifters 129-249. At 300 C: 82-353. At 500 C: 181-685. At 4-12 rpm and 500 C: 285-1132. Averaged examples: 293 +/- 32 (zone 2) and 249 +/- 29 (zones 1 + 2) W/m2K.
additional_findings.context: Kiln D 0.101 m, L 1.95 m, Inconel 6.5 mm wall (eps 0.9), two 0.4 m electric zones. Slope 3 deg, 2-12 rpm, 0.5-3.2 kg/h, exit dam 23.5-33.5 mm. 4 rows of 10 mm lifters. Sand 0.55 mm (rho_b 1422, cp 835, k_b 0.1836, eps 0.76). No forced gas flow. Neglecting radiation would overestimate h by about 7/13/16% at 100/300/500 C; convection is negligible (about 0.05%).
additional_findings.source: Bongo Njeng A.S. et al. (2018) Exp. Therm. Fluid Sci. 91:197-213 (HAL author version)
additional_findings.evidence: Tables 1-3, Sec. 4.1, Fig. 8

additional_findings.parameter: Wall-to-solid HTC correlation for flighted, indirectly heated kilns (Bongo Njeng Eq. 16)
additional_findings.value: h_cw-cb = K (k_b/l_psi) (K_a omega D^2/a_b)^alpha (K_b l_psi/D)^beta (K_g HU%)^gamma (K_d T_w k_b^0.4 c_pb^0.6/(rho_b^0.4 D^2.8))^delta. K = 2.1371 (95% CI -3.88 to 8.16), alpha = 0.4531, beta = -0.3507, gamma = 0.9693, delta = 1.4177. K_a = 1e-3, K_b = 10, K_g = 1e-2, K_d = 1e-4.
additional_findings.units: W m-2 K-1 (omega rad/s, HU in %, T_w as used by the authors)
additional_findings.context: Valid for 100-500 C walls, outside radiation-dominated conditions. Fits within +/-20%. Wes et al. 2 sqrt(k rho c/(pi t_c)), Tscheng-Watkinson and Li et al. are the right order of magnitude but miss the trends. The confidence interval on K spans zero, so extrapolation is risky.
additional_findings.source: Bongo Njeng et al. (2018), Eq. 16 and Table 4
additional_findings.evidence: Page 16 image checked

additional_findings.parameter: Tscheng-Watkinson wall-to-bed correlation (conflicting secondary renderings)
additional_findings.value: Bongo Njeng Eq. 2: h = 11.6 (k_b/l_psi)(N R^2/(a_b psi))^0.3. Le Guen Table IV: h = (k_s/(eps_B D))11.6 (2 eps_B D^2 omega/(2 a_s))^0.3.
additional_findings.context: The filling angle sits in the denominator in one version and the numerator in the other. Original: Tscheng & Watkinson, Can. J. Chem. Eng. 57 (1979) 433 (not read). Hwan Table 6.1 gives Tscheng-Watkinson gas-side forms: h_ew-g = 1.54 (k_g/D_H) Re_g^0.575 Re_w^-0.292 and h_eb-g = 0.46 (k_g/D_H) Re_g^0.535 Re_w^0.104, valid 1600 < Re_g < 7800 and 20 < Re_w < 800, with D_H = 0.5 D (2pi - theta + sin(theta))/(pi - theta/2 + sin(theta/2)).
additional_findings.source: Bongo Njeng 2018 Eq. 2; Le Guen 2017 Table IV; Hwan 2009 Table 6.1
additional_findings.evidence: All three read in full text; the original was not

additional_findings.parameter: Rotary dryer/kiln drive power (Perry eq. 20-44 as used by NPTEL)
additional_findings.value: bhp = N (4.75 d w + 0.1925 D' W + 0.33 W)/100000, with N rpm, d shell diameter ft, w live (material) load lb, D' riding-ring diameter = d + 2 ft, W total rotating load lb. SI conversion done here: P [W] = N (0.2562 d w + 0.01038 D' W + 0.00543 W), with d and D' in m (D' about d + 0.61 m) and w, W in kg.
additional_findings.context: NPTEL worked example: d 8.07 ft, w 35,268 lb, D' 10.07 ft, W 66,520 lb, 3 rpm gives 45.08 bhp (33.6 kW). Recomputed: 45.08. The SI form reproduces 33.6 kW.
additional_findings.source: NPTEL Chemical Engineering Design II, Module 4, p. 32-33 (citing Perry eq. 20-44)
additional_findings.evidence: Worked example transcribed; arithmetic verified in Python

additional_findings.parameter: Vendor drive power vs size, direct rotary dryers (FEECO)
additional_findings.context: Typical data for fertilizer (60 lb/ft3, up to 10% moisture removal). Chain/sprocket drives up to 55 kW and gear drives above; friction drive for drums of 1.8 m and under. FEECO notes sticky sludge-like feeds stick to the shell, and a 'bald' (flightless) section is used for fragile feeds.
additional_findings.source: FEECO International, The Rotary Dryer Handbook (vendor datasheet), p. 7, 11, 15
additional_findings.evidence: Table 'Typical rotary dryer data'

additional_findings.parameter: Batch rotary tyre/plastic pyrolysis drum datasheet (vendor)
additional_findings.value: 2200 x 6000 mm: 27 t, 23 m3, 5 t/d. 2200 x 6600: 29 t, 25 m3, 6 t/d. 2600 x 6000: 32 t, 32 m3, 8 t/d. 2600 x 6600: 34 t, 35 m3, 9 t/d. 2800 x 6000: 35 t, 37 m3, 10 t/d. 2800 x 6600: 38 t, 41 m3, 12 t/d. Power 8-11 kW (2200 models) and 12-17 kW (2600/2800). Speed 0.4 r/min. Internal gear drive, horizontal rotation, direct (external) firing.
additional_findings.units: mm; t; m3; t/day; kW; rpm
additional_findings.context: Unverified marketing data (INNOVIC listing on SupplierGO). Other vendor pages: Beston BLJ-6 D2.2 x L6.0 m, 6 t/d, 24 kW and BLJ-10 D2.6 x L6.6 m, 8-10 t/d, 30 kW; a rotary pyrolysis reactor vendor quotes 0.5-3 rpm. Weibold: vertical batch tyre reactors about 2 m ID x 5 m give only 5-6 t/day each, with cycles up to about 14 h.
additional_findings.source: SupplierGO/INNOVIC listing; mswrecyclingplant.com (Beston); harshaengineersindia.in; weibold.com
additional_findings.evidence: Spec tables read from fetched pages

additional_findings.parameter: Drive-power check for a batch drum (derived)
additional_findings.value: About 3.1 kW for the drum drive
additional_findings.context: Perry/NPTEL correlation (SI form) applied to a 2.6 m x 6.6 m drum at 0.4 rpm with a 34 t shell and an assumed 9 t charge (W = 43 t). Vendor total plant power of 12-17 kW also covers fans and pumps, so the two are consistent.
additional_findings.source: Derived here from the NPTEL/Perry correlation and the vendor datasheet

additional_findings.parameter: Hwan hot pilot kiln with segmented lifters (validation data)
additional_findings.value: L 3.98 m; D_iw 0.498 m; D_ow 0.510 m; heating tube D_ii 1.2 m. Lifter height 0.08 m, thickness 6 mm. k_b 0.4 W/mK; rho_b 600 kg/m3. Coal 260-325 kg/h; fill 14-17%; Pe 71-77; Re_omega 215 -> 172; MRT 15 -> 14.6 min; heat-transfer efficiency 51 -> 80%.
additional_findings.units: m; W m-1 K-1; kg m-3; kg/h; %; min
additional_findings.context: Indirectly heated by counter-current flue gas; radiation neglected below 1073 K. Coal pyrolysis: A = 0.2-0.6 s-1, Ea = 46-197 kJ/mol.
additional_findings.source: Hwan I.H. (2009) PhD thesis, Curtin University, Table 6.2 and Sec. 6.3
additional_findings.evidence: Table 6.2; Sec. 6.3 text

additional_findings.parameter: Saeman-Mitchell residence time and Porter curtain-loading limit
additional_findings.value: tau = L/[f(H) D N (tan(beta) +/- m' u_g)], with cascade factor f(H) between 2 and pi, rising with holdup. Porter: cascade rate divided by exposed curtain surface should not exceed 1.3 min-1.
additional_findings.context: Lisboa 2007 found Saeman-Mitchell fits the residence time best. Sign conventions differ between sources; Lisboa and Karali write + for cocurrent.
additional_findings.source: Lisboa et al. 2007 (SciELO HTML); Karali thesis Eq. 5.3; Sunkara thesis Sec. 2.3 (Porter, secondary)
additional_findings.evidence: Text of Lisboa 2007; Sunkara Sec. 2.3

additional_findings.parameter: Friedman & Marshall volumetric coefficient as quoted by Sunkara
additional_findings.context: The (n_F - 1)/2 factor stands for the number of curtains. Ua was smaller with no flights, rose significantly with 2 and 4 flights, and barely changed at 8. This conflicts with the 15 G^0.16/D form, so treat the F&M attribution as uncertain.
additional_findings.source: Sunkara thesis Eq. 2.6 (secondary)
additional_findings.evidence: Sec. 2.3

additional_findings.parameter: Applicability of flight models to sticky feeds (plastics melt zone)
additional_findings.value: S-G and geometric holdup models apply only to free-flowing solids, 'not to highly cohesive solids, sticky and wet materials'. Karali's study was limited to dry free-flowing solids. FEECO says sticky sludge-like feeds stick to the shell and can become a fire risk.
additional_findings.context: Supports modelling the plastic melt zone as a rolling/agglomerating bed without curtains, and adding curtains only where char or heat carrier is free-flowing
additional_findings.source: Sunkara thesis Sec. 3.3.1; Karali thesis Sec. 7.2; FEECO handbook p. 11
additional_findings.evidence: Quoted statements

verdict_fulltext.summary:
This time I read most key sources in full via curl: Suzuki 2008 (both JTST papers), the Karali 2015 and Sunkara 2013 OVGU theses, Seidenbecher et al. (Granular Matter 2022, Springer OA), Le Guen arXiv:1612.05762, Bongo Njeng 2018 (HAL author PDF), the Hwan 2009 thesis (figshare), Lisboa 2007 (SciELO), Sandia 2017, NPTEL Module 4 and vendor datasheets. I did not bypass anti-bot challenges: the Halle repository (Seidenbecher dissertation), the CORE, IOP and ResearchGate PDFs, and SciEngine stayed blocked.

Main corrections:
(1) The optimum (design-load) filling is 5-15%, not 15-20%. Karali measured 4.5-14.8%; Perry & Green give 10-15%.
(2) The 31-35 W/m2K figure is Hwan's flue-gas-to-bed overall U in a kiln WITH segmented lifters, not a no-internals value.
(3) In the Suzuki abstract, 'L_l/L_w larger than 1' is a misprint; the body requires L_l/L_w < 1. Rotation alone raises k_m-w from 38.6 to 43.4 W/m2K, so the pure lifter factor is about 1.15-1.17.
(4) Baker's design-load model is 2 sum(H_i) - H_FUF. Ajayi & Sheehan use factor 1.24 (with (1+S)); Karali uses 1.38.
(5) The secondary K = 244.7 is the SI form of Ua = 15 G^0.16/D (exponent 0.16), not the 0.67 form.
(6) The Schofield-Glikin '+' sign is confirmed by two full texts and a derivation. Granular Matter 2022 prints '-', but the difference is under 0.5 deg at kiln Froude numbers.
(7) Karali's 1.0 x 0.3 m drum is from thesis Ch. 3, not the 2015 paper.

Gaps filled:
- Sunkara's full geometric holdup, cascading-rate, fall-height, curtain-area and theoretical-flight-number equations.
- Karali's design-load fill correlation (validated here to within 0.1-0.3 points of Karali's measurements) and his axial-advance/residence-time model (K = 22.7).
- Measured wall-to-bed coefficients: Suzuki 22-55 W/m2K for waste, and Bongo Njeng 45-1132 W/m2K with the Eq. 16 correlation and its fitted parameters.
- Le Guen/Piton closures.
- Perry/NPTEL drive-power correlation with an SI conversion checked against the worked example.
- Rules of thumb: radial flight height D/12-D/8 now confirmed.
- FEECO drive-power data and batch-drum datasheets: 2.2-2.8 m x 6-6.6 m drums, 0.4 rpm, 8-17 kW, 5-12 t/d (unverified marketing data).

Still unverifiable: the S-G 0.4 limit, McCormick's 0.46-0.67 range, Myklestad's 420 prefactor, the Seidenbecher geometry, the Gao & Bao numbers (search summaries only), the 200 C/s heating rate, and the GPU-DEM costs. Physics takeaway for the model: the flight and curtain models apply only to free-flowing solids (Sunkara says so explicitly). The Suzuki waste kiln ran at about 41% fill, where lifters act as bed mixers, not curtain formers. So the plastic melt zone should be modelled as a rolling bed without curtains.

sweep.topic: TOPIC H: static vs rotating heating of a pyrolysis bed, batch rotary tyre/plastic drums, kiln sealing and inerting, and drive power/torque

findings.parameter: Thermal bed mixing time vs rotational speed and filling degree (Nafsun et al. 2017)
findings.value: Mixing time falls as speed rises and as filling falls; at high speed the filling degree has little effect; at low speed the values fall inside the Schlünder-Mollekopf (1984) penetration-model range
findings.context: Batch drum D = 0.6 m, L = 0.45 m, filled with two layers of granular material at different temperatures; thermocouples at several bed heights. Reported as time constant, number of bed revolutions, peak time and mixing number. Faster mixing at higher speed is attributed to more bed revolutions per minute and more particle interaction.
findings.source: Nafsun A.I., Herz F., Specht E. et al., Thermal bed mixing in rotary drums for different operational parameters, Chem. Eng. Sci. 160 (2017) 346-353, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2016.11.005
findings.evidence: Abstract and highlights via search extract: 'rotational speed and filling degree ... varied in the range of n=1-6 rpm and F=10-20%'; 'thermal mixing time decreases with higher rotational speed and lower filling degree'; 'influence of filling degree ... not significant at high rotational speed'

findings.parameter: Thermal mixing vs material properties, particle size and drum diameter (Nafsun, Herz, Liu 2018)
findings.value: Rotational speed matters more than particle size. Larger particles and smaller penetration depth improve thermal mixing. Mixing time rises with higher filling, smaller particles, lower rpm and larger drum diameter.
findings.context: Same 0.6 m x 0.45 m batch drum; quartz sand, glass beads, expanded clay, steel spheres. Thermal mixing depends on conduction and on radial segregation.
findings.source: Nafsun A.I., Herz F., Liu X., Influence of material thermal properties and dispersity on thermal bed mixing in rotary drums, Powder Technol. 331 (2018) 121-128, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2018.01.072
findings.evidence: Highlights: 'Rotational speed dominates the mixing process compared to particle size'; 'Larger particle sizes as well as lower penetration depth improved thermal mixing'

findings.parameter: Temperature field inside a heated rotating bed (Nafsun & Herz 2016)
findings.value: In the passive layer the temperature falls from the wall to the active/passive boundary. In the active layer it rises from the boundary to the bed surface. The gradient is smaller in the upper bed because of particle mixing.
findings.context: Indirectly heated drum; glass beads; constant filling and speed; thermocouples on rotating and fixed rods measured radial and circumferential profiles.
findings.source: Nafsun A.I., Herz F., Experiments on the temperature distribution in the solid bed of rotary drums, Appl. Therm. Eng. 103 (2016) 1039-1047, doi:10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2016.04.128
findings.evidence: Abstract: temperature gradient in upper part smaller than lower part 'due to mixing of particles'

findings.parameter: Transverse mixing time in a drum with strips (flights)
findings.value: Transverse mixing 'virtually completed within 2 revolutions'
findings.units: drum revolutions; valid for n > 5 rpm and filling < 15 %
findings.context: Horizontal rotary drum reactor fitted with strips. This is the classic benchmark for a flighted drum mixing the cross-section within a few turns. At 0.5 rpm, 2 revolutions take 240 s.
findings.source: Wes G.W.J., Drinkenburg A.A.H., Stemerding S., Solids mixing and residence time distribution in a horizontal rotary drum reactor, Powder Technol. 13 (1976) 177-184, doi:10.1016/0032-5910(76)85002-4
findings.evidence: Search extract of abstract: 'in a drum provided with strips for rotational speeds above 5 r.p.m. and a degree of filling less than 15%, the transverse mixing was virtually completed within 2 revolutions of the drum'

findings.parameter: Contact heat-transfer test matrix (Herz et al. 2012, IJHMT)
findings.value: D = 600 mm, L = 450 mm; n = 1, 3, 6 rpm; F = 10-20 %; d_p = 0.7-2.0 mm; quartz sand, glass beads, copper beads. Of four literature models, only one agreed well with the data.
findings.context: Wall-to-bed contact heat-transfer coefficient measured in a batch drum. Useful as a validation set for wall-to-bed boundary conditions.
findings.source: Herz F., Mitov I., Specht E., Stanev R., Influence of operational parameters and material properties on the contact heat transfer in rotary kilns, Int. J. Heat Mass Transfer 55 (2012) 7941-7948, doi:10.1016/j.ijheatmasstransfer.2012.08.022
findings.evidence: Abstract via search extract

findings.parameter: Contact HTC trends (Herz et al. 2012, CES)
findings.value: h_ws falls as particle diameter rises (higher contact resistance at the first particle layer) and rises with the bed's effective thermophysical properties. An extended penetration theory is given; its fitted chi parameter is about 0.096 < chi < 0.198 (garbled snippet).
findings.context: Covered-wall to solid-bed heat transfer in rotary drums
findings.source: Herz F., Mitov I., Specht E., Stanev R., Experimental study of the contact heat transfer coefficient between the covered wall and solid bed in rotary drums, Chem. Eng. Sci. 82 (2012) 312-318, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2012.07.042
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'as the particle diameter increases, the contact heat transfer coefficient decreases ... higher contact resistance'; chi range read from a garbled ResearchGate snippet

findings.parameter: Penetration-theory wall-to-bed coefficient (formula)
findings.value: alpha = 2*sqrt(lambda*rho*c_p/(pi*t)), with contact time t = gamma*60/(2*pi*n) (gamma = filling angle in rad, n in rpm)
findings.context: Bulk (bed) properties lambda, rho, c_p. The model leaves out the wall/first-particle contact (gap) resistance, which Schlünder-Mollekopf and Lehmberg add in series. Measured coefficients plot as straight lines against sqrt(n).
findings.source: Moumin G. et al., Int. J. Heat Mass Transfer 177 (2021) 121473 (DLR)
findings.evidence: Search extract quoting the paper's equation and the definition t = gamma*60/(2*pi*n)

findings.parameter: Conductive heating time scales in a rotary drum (Emady et al. 2016)
findings.value: tau/tau_c collapses onto one monotonic curve of phi = tau_p/tau_c. Low phi: conduction dominates and the bed heats quickly as a solid body. High phi: granular convection dominates and the bed heats slowly but nearly uniformly. Intermediate phi: cool core with warmer outer layers.
findings.context: DEM of wall-to-bed conduction. Bed heating time tau, particle thermal time constant tau_p, particle-wall contact time tau_c. Lets tau be predicted a priori.
findings.source: Emady H.N., Anderson K.V., Borghard W.G., Muzzio F.J., Glasser B.J., Cuitino A., Prediction of conductive heating time scales of particles in a rotary drum, Chem. Eng. Sci. 152 (2016) 45-54, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2016.05.022
findings.evidence: Abstract text via search extract

findings.parameter: Mixing vs heat conduction in tumblers (Figueroa et al. 2010)
findings.value: Faster mixing can raise or lower heat-transfer efficiency depending on the Peclet number. Nusselt is correlated against Pe.
findings.context: Rotating tumblers heated at the wall; Pe identifies whether conduction or convection dominates
findings.source: Figueroa I., Vargas W.L., McCarthy J.J., Mixing and heat conduction in rotating tumblers, Chem. Eng. Sci. 65 (2010) 1045-1054, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2009.09.058
findings.evidence: Abstract and citing papers via search extract

findings.parameter: DEM heating trends (Chaudhuri et al. 2006)
findings.value: Heating is faster with smaller particles, higher rotation rate, lower fill, lower heat capacity and higher conductivity. A 2010 calciner follow-up found rotation speed had minimal impact on heat transfer.
findings.context: DEM heat transfer in rotating vessels
findings.source: Chaudhuri B., Muzzio F.J., Tomassone M.S., Modeling of heat transfer in granular flow in rotating vessels, Chem. Eng. Sci. 61 (2006) 6348-6360, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2006.05.034
findings.evidence: Summary in a 2024 citing paper; 2010 follow-up quoted in search extract

findings.parameter: Effect of rpm on thermal time in drums with and without baffles (DEM)
findings.value: From 3 to 30 rpm, thermal time drops 4 % with no baffles and 18 % with 16 baffles. RPM improves temperature uniformity without much shortening of thermal time.
findings.context: Baffles act like flights. Attribution is uncertain: the figures come from a search summary of the DEM baffled-drum papers (Chem. Eng. Sci. 2022, S0009250922000604; Powder Technol. 2023, S0032591023006630) and the exact paper was not confirmed.
findings.source: Scale-up of heat transfer in a rotary drum equipped with baffles, Powder Technol. (2023)
findings.evidence: Search extract: 'thermal time decreases by 4% for a drum without baffles, while for a drum with 16 baffles, the thermal time drops by 18% from 3 RPM to 30 RPM'; highlights: 'RPM increases temperature uniformity without reducing thermal time significantly'

findings.parameter: Thermal conductivity of solid polymers
findings.value: PE 0.3-0.5; PP 0.17-0.22 (one TPS measurement on PP: 0.28)
findings.context: These are solid-polymer values. A loose flake or pellet bed is lower because of the gas gaps (see the derived Zehner-Schlünder estimate).
findings.source: Thermtest application note and search-compiled polymer data
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: Thermal diffusivity of polymer melts and solid LDPE
findings.value: Molten LDPE 6.92e-7; molten PP 5.53e-7; solid LDPE about 1.7e-7 (0.17 mm2/s)
findings.context: Melt values measured near the melting temperature by an unsteady method. The solid LDPE value comes from a materials database.
findings.source: Yánez et al., LDPE and PP thermal diffusivity in molten state, Ingeniería e Investigación (2013); makeitfrom.com
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'alpha = 6.92x10^-7 m2/s for LDPE and alpha = 5.53x10^-7 m2/s for PP'

findings.parameter: Packed-bed vs solid conductivity (order-of-magnitude analogue)
findings.value: Solid limestone 2.0 vs a 25 %-porosity limestone aggregate bed about 0.15. Adsorbent bed 0.188 (10 C) and 0.204 (80 C); catalyst bed about 0.12.
findings.context: Shows how contact-point conduction pulls a bed's conductivity far below the solid's. There is no measured value for a polymer-flake bed; none was found in the open literature.
findings.source: USPTO patent 10921273 (apparatus for effective conductivity of aggregate beds); SFU Bahrami group (Rouhani et al. 2018)
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: DERIVED: effective conductivity of a static plastic-flake bed (Zehner-Schlünder, no radiation)
findings.context: My own calculation with Zehner-Schlünder (C = 1.25): k_s = 0.2-0.45, k_gas = 0.026 (25 C), 0.040 (300 C) and 0.050 (450 C) W/mK, porosity 0.5-0.7. Radiation adds to this at high temperature. Consistent with the brief's 0.1-0.2 W/mK.
findings.source: Derived (this work) using the Zehner-Schlünder model (Tsotsas & Martin 1987 review)
findings.evidence: Python calculation in scratchpad

findings.parameter: DERIVED: thermal penetration time of a static layer, t = L^2/alpha
findings.context: Bed alpha = k/(rho_b*c_p) with k = 0.10-0.20 W/mK, rho_b = 300-400 kg/m3, c_p = 1900-2000 J/kgK. Latent heat of melting and the pyrolysis endotherm would lengthen these times. The melt is too viscous for useful natural convection.
findings.source: Derived (this work)
findings.evidence: Python calculation

findings.parameter: DERIVED: rotating-bed renewal in a 2.6 m x 6.6 m drum
findings.value: Contact time t_c = 16-59 s; h_pen = 47-93 W/m2K; penetration depth per contact 3-6 mm; lumped bed heating constant tau = m*c_p/(h*A_cw) = 0.5-2.0 h (1.2-3.7 t bed at F = 10-30 %, n = 0.4-1 rpm)
findings.units: s, W m^-2 K^-1, mm, h
findings.context: Penetration model with bed k = 0.15, rho_b = 350, c_p = 2000; covered-wall area A_cw = eps*R*L. Contact resistance and freeboard radiation are left out. Compared with a static 0.1-0.3 m layer, rotation shortens the characteristic heating time by roughly 10-100x. One revolution takes 60-150 s.
findings.source: Derived (this work) from the penetration model (Moumin 2021; Schlünder & Mollekopf 1984)
findings.evidence: Python calculation

findings.parameter: DERIVED: wall superheat, static vs rotating, at the same wall heat flux
findings.value: Static semi-infinite bed (effusivity e = 324 W s^0.5 m^-2 K^-1): dT_wall = 2q*sqrt(t/pi)/e, which gives about 1045 K after 1 h at q = 5 kW/m2 (so in practice the wall climbs to flue-gas temperature). Rotating bed: dT = q/h of about 60-100 K at 5 kW/m2.
findings.context: Quantifies the infographic's 'charred at wall, cold centre' panel: a static bed cannot carry the heat away, so the wall and the first layer overheat and char/coke while the centre stays cold.
findings.source: Derived (this work)
findings.evidence: Python calculation

findings.parameter: Fixed-bed plastic pyrolysis thermal behaviour
findings.value: Low conductivity of plastic gives non-uniform heat distribution. The heating rate slows between 419 and 483 C in the lower (feedstock) zone. The wall must run hotter than the reaction temperature.
findings.context: Lab fixed-bed reactor (Univ. Banja Luka) with thermocouples at bottom, middle and top plus CFD; mixed plastic, biomass and blends.
findings.source: Đurđević M., Papuga S., Kolundžija A., Analysis of the thermal behavior of a fixed bed reactor during the pyrolysis process, Hem. Ind. 78(1) (2024) 29-40, doi:10.2298/HEMIND221217024D
findings.evidence: Search extract of full-text snippets: 'decrease in the heating rate in the temperature interval from 419 to 483 C of the lower reactor part'

findings.parameter: Stirring effect in LLDPE pyrolysis
findings.value: Unstirred runs gave more methane. Stirring improved temperature uniformity, cut hot-spot overcracking and shifted selectivity toward C14-C20 condensables.
findings.context: Microwave-heated batch vs continuous-stirred LLDPE pyrolysis, with and without HZSM-5
findings.source: Comparative study of continuous-stirred and batch microwave pyrolysis of LLDPE in the presence/absence of HZSM-5 (2021)
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: Wall overheating causing char in plastic pyrolysis (patent statement)
findings.value: Heat entering through the wall sets up a large temperature gradient; the fluid next to the wall is much hotter than the bulk and makes excess char; uniform heating should lower char yield
findings.context: PVC-containing mixed plastic pyrolysis reactor patent
findings.source: US Patent 11987756, Process for PVC-containing mixed plastic waste pyrolysis in a reactor handling three phases of products
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: Fixed bed vs moving (agitated) bed tyre pyrolysis at 600 C
findings.value: Full rubber conversion in both. Liquid: fixed bed >50 % vs moving bed 43.2 %. Gas: 7.5 % vs 17.1 % (third-party figures). The moving bed cracks more severely (faster heating, longer gas residence); fixed-bed solid residence time is longer.
findings.context: Moving-bed unit takes up to 15 kg/h; N2 atmosphere
findings.source: Aylón E. et al., Waste tire pyrolysis: comparison between fixed bed reactor and moving bed reactor, Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 47 (2008) 4029-4033, doi:10.1021/ie071573o
findings.evidence: Abstract states the qualitative points; the yield numbers come from an academia.edu summary and were not checked against the paper

findings.parameter: Batch rotary tyre reactor DY-1-10 (Henan Doing)
findings.value: D 2600 mm x L 6600 mm; 10 t tyres per 24 h; 0.4 turn/min; total installed power 19 kW; Q245R boiler plate, 16 mm; batch time 16-20 h; after 2 h parking, carbon black discharged by rotating the reactor (1.5-2 h); water condensers about 40 m2
findings.units: mm, t, rpm, kW, h, m2
findings.context: 'Fuel oil + carbon black' class of plant; burner furnace under the drum. Sister model 2200 x 6000 mm, 6 t, 0.4 rpm.
findings.source: Henan Doing vendor catalogue pages (DY-1-10 reactor and plant)
findings.evidence: Search extracts of vendor tables: 'D2600mm*L6600mm', '0.4turn/minute', 'Total power 19KW', 'one batch time 16-20 hour'

findings.parameter: Batch tyre drum motor and reducer sizing (vendor)
findings.value: 2200 x 6000 drum: 350 reducer with a 4 kW motor; larger drums: 400 or 500 reducer with 5.5 kW. Another vendor gives the 2200 x 6000 drum 6 t per batch and a 12 h total cycle.
findings.context: Drive motor is a few kW, compared with hundreds of kW of burner duty
findings.source: Sihai Energy Tech 5-20 t tyre pyrolysis plant page; wastetireoil.com 6/8/10 t plant page
findings.evidence: Search extracts of vendor tables

findings.parameter: Beston BLJ-10 / BLJ-16 batch rotary reactors
findings.value: BLJ-10: D2.6 x L6.6 m, rotary, total power 30 kW, 8-10 t/day (batch). BLJ-16: D2.8 x L7.1 m, 54 kW (listed as semi-continuous on a directory page; Beston itself says batch, 1 batch/day).
findings.context: The vendor sources conflict; the directory page is about 6.5 years old
findings.source: Beston Group product pages and a directory listing
findings.evidence: Search extracts

findings.parameter: Huayin HY2800x6600 batch reactor
findings.value: 10 t/batch; power 9-15 kW plus 5.5 kW vacuum unit and 11 kW auto-feeder; a 10 t batch of plastic takes about 20 h per cycle
findings.context: Ma & Zhong (2018) describe Huayin as a catalytic batch process of 10 t per batch
findings.source: Huayin made-in-china listing and Huayin news page; Ma J., Zhong Q., Comparison of Chinese pyrolysis processes (Columbia/WTERT 2018)
findings.evidence: Search extracts

findings.parameter: Batch tyre plant product yields (vendor)
findings.value: 10 t batch example: 45 % oil (4.5 t), 35 % carbon black (3.5 t), 13 % steel (1.3 t). Passenger tyres: 45-50 % oil, 30-35 % CB, 8-10 % steel, 10-15 % syngas. Truck/bus tyres: 15-20 % steel.
findings.context: Marketing figures, not measured mass balances
findings.source: Vendor pages (pyrolysisunit.com, gasificationplant.com, Guanma)
findings.evidence: Search extracts

findings.parameter: First commercial batch rotary tyre plant in Bangladesh (Islam et al. 2013)
findings.value: 2 units, horizontal-axis rotary batch reactor, 4.5 t/run, about 6 m long x 2 m diameter; 420 C at 0.03 bar over-pressure. Heated externally by burning product oil for the first 3 h, then pyro-gas for the remaining 5 h. Oil yield 45 wt% (char 35, gas 10, steel cord 10 wt% per a second summary, not verified).
findings.context: Radiant Renewable Energy Ltd., Gazipur. A real-plant example of a 'fuel oil + carbon black' batch drum with slight positive pressure and self-fuelled burners.
findings.source: Islam M.R., Islam M.N., Mustafi N.N., Rahim M.A., Haniu H., Thermal recycling of solid tire wastes for alternative liquid fuel: the first commercial step in Bangladesh, Procedia Eng. 56 (2013) 573-582, doi:10.1016/j.proeng.2013.03.162
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'operates at 420 C under 0.03 bar pressure ... heated externally by burning product pyrolysis liquids for first three hours and by burning product pyro-gas for rest five hours'; char, gas and steel split from a secondary summary

findings.parameter: 10 t rotary tyre reactor in a review (Lewandowski et al. 2019)
findings.value: Cylindrical rotary reactor D = 2.8 m, L = 6.6 m; 40-45 % oil, 8-10 % gas, 30-35 % carbon. The same review is cited for a rotary reactor giving a maximum 44 wt% oil at 550 C with HHV 39.3 MJ/kg. Another commercial tyre kiln: about 2.2 m ID x 6.6 m at 0.5-3 rpm.
findings.context: Review of tyre pyrolysis reactor types
findings.source: Lewandowski W.M., Januszewicz K., Kosakowski W., Efficiency and proportions of waste tyre pyrolysis products depending on the reactor type - a review, J. Anal. Appl. Pyrol. 140 (2019) 25-53, doi:10.1016/j.jaap.2019.03.018
findings.evidence: Search summary of the review's table (refs [117],[118] not opened)

findings.parameter: Rotary-kiln tyre pyrolysis yields at about 450 C
findings.value: Gas 15 +/- 3, oil 40 +/- 4, recovered carbon black 45 +/- 4
findings.context: Industrial-route review summary
findings.source: Advances in the pyrolysis of end-of-life tires: a critical review of reactors (Univ. Porto repository)
findings.evidence: Search extract: '15 +/- 3 wt % TPG, 40 +/- 4 wt % TPO, and 45 +/- 4 wt % RRCB at approximately 450 C for rotary kiln technology'

findings.parameter: Chinese plastic/tyre rotary processes (Ma & Zhong 2018)
findings.value: Kingtiger: continuous, 50 t/d, near-horizontal rotary kiln with catalyst; 45 % fuel oil, 40 % carbon black, 15 % gas from mixed plastics. Henan Doing: continuous, 100 t/d; oil 45-52 %, carbon black 30 %, gas 18-25 %. Huayin: catalytic batch, 10 t per batch.
findings.context: Columbia University / WTERT MS report
findings.source: Ma J., Zhong Q., Comparison of Chinese pyrolysis processes, WTERT/Columbia (2018)
findings.evidence: Search extracts of the report

findings.parameter: Heat demand of tyre pyrolysis and self-sufficiency
findings.value: Reaction heat 1.41-2.16 kJ/g tyre (698-848 K). Burning 30-50 % of the pyrolysis gas covers it. Gas LHV averages 37.3 MJ/kg, 71-73 wt% hydrocarbons. Poor insulation can break self-sufficiency.
findings.context: For a 10 t batch: 3.9-6.0 MWh, i.e. 390-750 kW averaged over 8-10 h (derived)
findings.source: Gamboa et al., Thermodynamic evaluation of the energy self-sufficiency of the tyre pyrolysis process, Energies 16(24) (2023) 7932, doi:10.3390/en16247932
findings.evidence: Abstract

findings.parameter: Batch 10 t plant fuel per batch and electricity (vendor)
findings.value: Fuel per batch: about 300 kg diesel, or 300-400 kg pyrolysis oil, or about 150 m3 CNG, or 100-150 kg LPG, or 700-800 kg wood, or about 500 kg coal (column mapping inferred). Average electrical power about 30 kW over about 10 h.
findings.context: Non-condensable gas is mostly recycled to the furnace as heating fuel
findings.source: wastetireoil.com FAQ, energy cost of running a tyre pyrolysis plant
findings.evidence: Search extract of vendor table

findings.parameter: Electricity use of tyre pyrolysis (LCA)
findings.value: Pilot plant: 155.51 kWh/t tyres including pre-treatment. Maga et al. 2023: 549 kWh/t ELT for pyrolysis, cooling and CHP own use.
findings.context: System boundaries differ; drive power is a small part of either figure
findings.source: Maga D. et al., A comparative life cycle assessment of tyre recycling using pyrolysis compared to conventional end-of-life pathways, Resour. Conserv. Recycl. (2023)
findings.evidence: Search extracts of the LCA inventories

findings.parameter: Target O2 and pressure window for tyre pyrolysis (patent)
findings.value: O2 kept at or below 1 % during pyrolysis. N2 purge removes air from the voids between shreds and air absorbed in them. Operation near neutral pressure, about +/-3 in WC (about +/-0.75 kPa). Negative pressure lets air leak in; positive pressure lets flammable gas escape through gaskets and seals.
findings.context: Directly relevant to the infographic's 'sealing to keep the drum anaerobic' trade-off
findings.source: US 8,888,961 and US 9,777,159, Pyrolysis process and products
findings.evidence: Patent text via search extract: 'Preferably, the oxygen level is maintained at or below 1% during the pyrolysis process'; '+/-3 inches WC'

findings.parameter: Alternative: slight negative pressure with plug seals
findings.value: Reactor run at -0.02 to -0.1 in WC, with a rubber plug at the inlet and a char seal at the outlet, to prevent significant air infiltration
findings.context: Older tyre and waste pyrolysis apparatus
findings.source: US 5,167,772, Apparatus for pyrolysis of tires and waste
findings.evidence: Patent text via search extract

findings.parameter: Explosion case study: inerting failure in a pyrolysis prototype
findings.value: Two explosions (2020 and 8 Oct 2021, the second destroying the plant). The N2 purge was stopped after 2 min when gas bubbled at a downstream water seal. The written procedure required N2 pressurization to 40 kPa, which was never verified by measurement. The reactor was not rotating, and gases likely ignited when the wall exceeded their autoignition temperature.
findings.context: Danish plastic-pyrolysis prototype (P4O). Shows the need for verified O2 measurement before burners light, and how a non-rotating heated drum overheats locally.
findings.source: Hedlund F.H., Inherent hazards and limited regulatory oversight in the waste plastic recycling sector - repeat explosion at pyrolysis plant, Chem. Eng. Trans. 99 (2023) 241-246, doi:10.3303/CET2399041
findings.evidence: Search extracts of the full text

findings.parameter: NFPA 69 oxygen safety margin for inerting
findings.value: Continuously monitored: at least 2 vol% below the worst-case LOC if LOC >= 5 %, otherwise <= 60 % of LOC. Not monitored (2019 ed.): 4.5 vol% below LOC if LOC >= 7.5 %, otherwise <= 40 % of LOC.
findings.context: With H2 present (LOC 5 %), a monitored system must stay at or below about 3 % O2, so a 1-2 % O2 target is consistent
findings.source: NFPA 69, Standard on Explosion Prevention Systems (2002 and 2019 editions)
findings.evidence: Search extracts of the standard text (5.7.2.5 in 2002; 7.7.2.8 in 2019)

findings.parameter: Limiting oxygen concentration, N2 diluent
findings.context: Main flammable components of pyrolysis gas. Ethylene and CO values were not confirmed (see the NIOSH Zlochower & Green data).
findings.source: Wikipedia 'Limiting oxygen concentration' table (secondary, citing NFPA 69/Zabetakis)
findings.evidence: Search extract of the table

findings.parameter: Relative leakage of rotary-drum seal types (FEECO)
findings.value: Labyrinth >> 5 %; single leaf << 3-5 %; double leaf about 25 % of a single leaf (about 1-3 %); bellows with a graphite face seal << 1 %
findings.context: Vendor ranking. Labyrinth suits only cases where air ingress does not matter; a graphite-face bellows or a purged double seal is needed for pyrolysis.
findings.source: FEECO, Seal Options for Rotary Dryers and Kilns; Rotary Drum Seals
findings.evidence: Search extracts of FEECO pages

findings.parameter: Purged double seals and purge-gas penalty
findings.value: N2 is injected between two seal sets and flows outward, blocking air inflow. Kilns under negative pressure need 'fairly large quantities' of N2 or steam purge, which dilutes the process gas and enlarges downstream vapour handling.
findings.context: Indirectly heated kilns needing an O2-free interior. Graphite-block seals (Davy patent; thyssenkrupp polysius graphite seal) are spring-pressed contact seals.
findings.source: ispatguru.com, Characteristic features of rotary kilns; USPTO 5869810
findings.evidence: Search extracts

findings.parameter: Seal face pressure and leakage trade-off (spring-loaded seal bars)
findings.value: Nominal face pressure about 5 psi between seal bars and the rotating disc, set by spring preload and seal-air pressure. Raising seal-air pressure reduces bar loading, so ingress has to be balanced against wear.
findings.context: PREPP waste kiln seal case study
findings.source: OSTI EGG-M--89466, PREPP rotary kiln seals - problem and resolution
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: Vendor dynamic seal pressure and N2 feed inerting
findings.value: Dynamic seal pressure 3 kPa; N2 replaces the air in the feeding system
findings.context: Continuous tyre pyrolysis plant (vendor claim, no O2 setpoint given)
findings.source: Beston Group, Continuous tyre pyrolysis plant page
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: Floating seal leakage improvement
findings.value: Seal leakage air flow 75-95 % lower than the best labyrinth designs
findings.context: Summary page with little detail on the test method
findings.source: science.gov topic page 'rotary kiln seal'
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: Power draw for material movement (Liu et al. 2016)
findings.value: Explicit regression model of power vs kiln length and diameter, inclination, feed rate, rpm, repose angle and bulk density, validated on an industrial cement kiln. Material movement reportedly about 70-75 % of the total motor requirement (unverified snippet).
findings.context: Its mechanistic basis is lifting the bed against gravity. The equation itself was not visible.
findings.source: Liu X., Xu X., Wu W., Herz F., Specht E., A simplified model to calculate the power draw for material movement in industrial rotary kilns, Powder Technol. 301 (2016) 1294-1298, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2016.08.005
findings.evidence: Abstract via search; the 70-75 % figure appeared only in one search summary

findings.parameter: DEM power draw vs speed, filling and axis offset
findings.value: Peak and mean power draw are proportional to rotational speed and to filling degree. Axis offset makes the power periodic at the rotation frequency; it barely changes the mean but largely sets the overshoot.
findings.context: Experimentally validated DEM with multi-sized particles
findings.source: Wu W., Liu X., Zhang Z., Hu Z., DEM investigation of the power draw for material movement in rotary drums with axis offset, Chem. Eng. Res. Des. 144 (2019) 310-317
findings.evidence: Highlights via search extract

findings.parameter: Large-kiln drive power benchmark
findings.value: A 6 m x 60 m kiln needs about 800 kW to turn at 3 rpm (implied torque about 2.55 MN m). Typical speeds 0.5-2 rpm; modern cement kilns 4-5 rpm.
findings.context: Scale reference only
findings.source: Wikipedia, Rotary kiln
findings.evidence: Article text via search

findings.parameter: Drive sizing margins
findings.value: Size the motor for 1 1/3 x normal speed: worked example 49.3 HP x 4/3 = 65.8 HP, so a 75 HP standard motor. Metso: drive torque demand up to 250 % of normal running torque. Another source: starting torque 3-5x running torque.
findings.context: Batch drums restart fully loaded and hot, so starting torque governs the gearmotor choice
findings.source: Allis-Chalmers bulletin, Horsepower to drive rotary kilns, coolers or dryers; Metso Rotary kiln handbook (2025)
findings.evidence: OCR text via search extract

findings.parameter: Drive type vs power (FEECO)
findings.value: Chain and sprocket or direct drives up to about 75 hp (about 55 kW); gear and pinion for heavier duty. Higher bulk density needs more horsepower.
findings.context: Batch tyre drums at 4-5.5 kW sit well inside the chain-drive range
findings.source: FEECO drive assemblies pages and Rotary Kiln Handbook
findings.evidence: Search extract

findings.parameter: Kiln drive power from manufacturer tables
findings.value: YZ1225 (1.2 m x 25 m): 22 kW; YZ3060 (3.0 m x 60 m): 90 kW; metallurgical 3.0 m x 45 m: 75 kW; 3.0 m x 48 m (precalciner): 100 kW
findings.context: Continuous mineral kilns, for scale only
findings.source: Zhihu table of rotary kiln parameters; Henan Hongxing metallurgical kiln page

findings.parameter: Measured drive power of an indirectly heated rotary dryer
findings.value: Idle 3.11 kW; in operation 3.22 kW at 470 kg/h feed
